tab_title: The RIGHT Way to Unbrick a Netgear R9000 (No Serial Cable Needed!)
description:
Stuck on DD-WRT, OpenWRT, or dealing with a bricked Netgear Nighthawk X10 R9000? Don't break out the soldering iron or open the case for a serial cable just yet!

Responding to a question from viewer @GenericDude6551, this tutorial walks through the proper, foolproof method to restore your Netgear R9000 back to official stock firmware using NMRPFlash. We cover the crucial gotchas—like dealing with the standard TFTP block rollover limits, choosing the right initial firmware version size (V1.0.0.68) before upgrading, and setting up Npcap and NMRPFlash on Windows.

⚠️ The Two Critical Fixes Explained in This Guide:
The Firmware Size Trap: Flashing the newest Netgear firmware directly fails over TFTP because file sizes over 32MB trigger block rollover errors. We fix this by first flashing the initial release image (V1.0.0.68.img) before performing an official web GUI update to the latest build.

The NMRPflash Version Quirk: Modern builds of NMRPflash cause upload rejections on Windows with this router. We use NMRPflash v0.9.25 (Win32) paired with Npcap to ensure reliable communication.

🔧 Software Tools Used:
NMRPflash (v0.9.25 Win32): https://github.com/jclehner/nmrpflash...
Npcap (WinPcap compatibility mode enabled): https://npcap.com/#download

tab_title: Explaining U0101 Code: Lost Communication with TCM (Transmission Control Module)
description:
In this video I explain what the U0101 code means, how the CAN bus works, and some basic can check to find the problem.

A U0101 code is set when the TCM (transmission control module) is not communicating with the other vehicle computers (ECM/PCM). 

How to Test Alternator Video 
   • How to Test an Alternator with a Multi Met...  

0:00 Intro
0:09 What Is a U0101 Code?
0:36 How the CAN Bus Works
1:39 Possible Causes
1:42 Blown Fuse
2:07 Charging or Battery Issues
3:23 TCM Circuit (Power and Ground)
4:06 CAN Bus Wiring and Connectors
5:05 Faulty TCM
5:43 Wrap Up

Modern vehicle computers (ECM/ABS/TCM) communicate over what's called the CAN bus. 

The CAN bus is the wires that run to each computer, along with the protocols to talk to each other. 

A TCM can be a standalone computer or combined with the ECM into one package (PCM).

Troubleshooting a U0101 Code can be difficult at times since it involves computers and wiring, but there are basic, easy things that can be checked and ruled out. 

Possible Causes of the U0101 Code
Blown Fuse (Check and Test Fuses)
Charging or Battery Issues (Test Alternator and Battery) 
Problems with the TCM circuit (Test Power - Ground - Open - Short)
Problems with the Data CAN bus (Check Connectors and Wiring)
Faulty TCM

title: Explaining U0101 Code: Lost Communication with TCM (Transmission Control Module)

Hands-on review of the Thermal Master Thor 002 handheld thermal camera. I walk through the settings menu, the four view modes, and every color palette, then put it to work on real jobs: scanning an electrical panel for hot spots, balancing radiant floor heating loops, and finding cold air infiltration from poor insulation. I also show how to pull images into the Thor TM PC software for analysis and reports.

🔍 REAL-WORLD USES SHOWN:

*⚡ Electrical Panel Inspection*
Spot overheating breakers and loose connections
Compare circuit temperatures side by side
Catch problems before they become a fire

*🔥 Radiant Floor Heat Balancing*
See which loops are flowing and which are starved
Adjust manifold valves by watching the floor, not guessing
Confirm even heat across the whole slab

*🏠 Insulation & Air Leak Detection*
Cold air infiltration shows up as dark streaks around windows, doors, outlets
Find missing or settled insulation in walls and ceilings
Best results with a 15-20°F indoor/outdoor temperature difference

*💻 Thor TM PC Software*
Transfer images via USB-C
Adjust palette, emissivity, and spot measurements after the fact
Generate inspection reports

📊 THOR 002 KEY SPECS:
IR resolution: 256×192 (512×384 with X³IR Super Resolution)
Temp range: -4°F to 1022°F (-20 to 550°C)
Accuracy: ±2°C or ±2%
Thermal sensitivity: 40mK
3.5" IPS display, 640×480
25Hz frame rate, 40°×30° field of view
View modes: Fusion, IR, Picture-in-Picture, Visual (2MP camera)
Palettes: White Hot, Black Hot, Lava, Iron, Rainbow, Rainbow HC, Black Red
Spot meter: Center/Max/Min + 3 custom spots
5000mAh battery, 8 hr runtime, 18W fast charge (4 hr)
32GB storage, MP4 video recording, laser pointer, LED work light
Wi-Fi + app, IP54, hard case and tripod mount included

🆚 THOR 001 vs THOR 002:
The 001 adds a macro lens (8cm min focus vs 30cm), ±1.5°C accuracy, 35mK sensitivity, 6 custom spots, and two extra highlight palettes. For panel scans, heating work, and building envelope checks, the 002 covers what most DIYers and homeowners need.

⚠️ SAFETY NOTES:
Thermal imaging is NOT a substitute for de-energizing before working in a panel
Keep hands clear of live bus bars when scanning with the cover off
Never look into the laser pointer

💡 PRO TIPS:
Set emissivity for the surface (shiny metal reads low - use tape or paint as a target)
Let the camera acclimate 5-10 minutes when moving between cold and warm spaces
Scan panels under load - an idle circuit won't show a bad connection
For radiant floors, run the system 30+ minutes before scanning
Use Iron or Rainbow HC for subtle temperature differences, White Hot for panels

Energy audit: $200-500 per visit
Electrical inspection: $150-300
Finding one bad breaker or one starved heating loop pays for the camera

tab_title: What to do when air conditioner freezes up: Air conditioner tips for summer
description:
In this video we share what to do when air conditioner freezes up.
One of our air conditioner tips for summer is knowing what to do when you have a frozen evaporator coil, or a frozen air conditioner.  A frozen air conditioner is a common air conditioner problem and you can help yourself by first turning everything off.  You need to get the ice off the coil in order to fix the problem with your air conditioner.  If your air conditioner is not blowing cold air, it could be a frozen coil so after you confirm that your coil is frozen and you turn everything off, you should change your furnace air filter.  Air flow is a common air conditioner problem and could cause your air conditioner to freeze.  You should also have a professional air conditioner tune up to check to make sure you have a proper refrigerant charge.  You should also check to make sure something is not stuck on.  

These air conditioner tips for summer will help you save on an air conditioner repair and know what to do when air conditioner freezes up.  If you keep a clean air filter and maintain a proper refrigerant change to your air conditioner.  We also explain more about why does your air conditioner freeze up and more helpful air conditioner information for homeowners from One Hour Heating and Air Conditioning.

tab_title: Before You Shut Your AC Down This Fall, Do This (Or Pay for It Next Spring)
description:
🔧 Everything I learned fixing HVAC for 25 years, in one plain-English book.
📘 THE HVAC SURVIVAL GUIDE - get it here: https://raydutton.com

Your air conditioner is still earning its keep in this heat. But in a few weeks, when you go to shut it down for the season, you have a choice to make, and it is worth about a couple thousand dollars. Do it the way most folks do - throw a cover over it, cut the power, walk away feeling responsible - and there is a real good chance that the first warm morning you switch it back on, the fellow who comes out says the one word you never want to hear about the most expensive part in the machine. The compressor. Or you spend five minutes now, the right way, and it wakes up next spring like nothing happened. Twenty-five years I spent on these systems, the fall shutdowns and the spring startups both, for the same companies that mail out that spring repair quote.

The 3 fall-shutdown moves, cheapest first:
Take it out of cooling for the season (so a warm afternoon can't wake it in cold air) - free
Do NOT wrap the whole unit (moisture rot + a mouse mansion in the wiring) - cover the top only
Do NOT cut the power all winter (it kills the crankcase heater and slugs the compressor come spring) - leave it on for a few dollars a month
And the reason nobody ever warned you: a fall mistake makes no sound. It waits all winter and hands you the bill in spring.

Chapters:
0:00 The choice that costs you a compressor

description:

How does tap water actually get clean? Most people think the treatment plant pours in chlorine and that is the treatment. Chlorine is real and it works, but it is the last step. By the time it goes in, most of the cleaning is already done, and the thing doing most of that cleaning is dirt grabbing more dirt.

This video follows the water from the river, lake or aquifer to your kitchen tap: why germs hide in cloudy water, how coagulation, flocculation and sedimentation make the mud clump, grow and sink, how sand and coal filters catch what chlorine can't, why disinfection depends on dose and time, what the leftover chlorine in your pipes is for, how Florida's groundwater plants differ, what home water filters really do, and what Orlando ran short of in the summer of 2021.

I'm a licensed builder, not a water plant operator. Everything I ask you to check here is reading, smelling and looking: your utility's water quality report, the tap water, the faucet aerator and your filter's NSF number.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Is chlorine the treatment?
0:38 This one's for two of you
0:56 A glass of muddy water
1:13 Why chlorine can't do it alone
1:46 Where the water comes from
2:03 Step 1: coagulation
2:42 Step 2: flocculation
3:00 Step 3: sedimentation
3:34 Step 4: filtration
4:19 Step 5: disinfection
5:02 Typhoid and Jersey City, 1908
6:05 Step 6: pH, pipes and fluoride
6:33 What plant operators watch
7:15 Florida's groundwater
7:51 Home water filters
8:21 Things to check tonight
9:04 What Orlando ran out of
9:47 Where the water goes next

What's covered in this video:

Germs hide behind specks of dirt, so the federal rule is written around turbidity (how clear the water is), not just chlorine. The CDC says Cryptosporidium can survive for days at normal chlorine levels.
Fine clay specks all carry the same negative charge and push each other apart. A coagulant such as alum cancels it, so the specks stick, then slow paddles grow them into floc for 10 to 30 minutes.
Sedimentation basins hold the water for hours (a typical state rule says at least four) while the floc sinks into sludge.
Filters are about two feet of anthracite coal over about a foot of fine sand over gravel, and get backwashed for 10 to 15 minutes. For surface water, filtration plus disinfection must remove at least 99.99% of viruses.
Disinfection depends on CT, concentration times time. A clearwell makes the water take the long way, and a chlorine residual is left in for the trip through the pipes.
Jersey City began routine disinfection in 1908. Typhoid fell from about 100 cases per 100,000 people in 1900 to about 0.1 by 2006, and one study of 25 big cities (1900 to 1940) found a filtration plant cut typhoid deaths by nearly 40%.
About 92% of Floridians drink groundwater, so plants here mostly fight hydrogen sulfide smell and hardness. Pitcher and fridge filters are for taste or metals, not germs: NSF 42 is taste and odor, 53 is health claims, 58 is reverse osmosis.

tab_title: Why Japan Doesn't Use Central Heating Like America
description:
Get The 30-Year HVAC Bible — Make Your Heating And Cooling System Last Decades Longer → https://liibro.com/l/hvac/john-the-hv...

Japan has some of the most advanced heat pump technology in the world, yet most Japanese homes are heated one room at a time rather than with a central system. This video breaks down exactly why that is, tracing the answer back to centuries of building tradition, the economics of Japanese housing, and a building code that only became mandatory for new homes in April 2025. The workhorse of the Japanese home is the ductless inverter split — the eakon — a technology Japan pioneered as far back as 1981 and that American homes are only beginning to adopt. But the room-by-room approach comes with serious consequences, including a startling gap between bathtub drowning deaths and traffic fatalities among Japanese seniors. The video also exposes a quiet flaw in American systems: the SEER2 efficiency rating on your outdoor unit is a lab number that stops at the cabinet and ignores duct leakage, static pressure, and the rooms nobody is using. Hokkaido, Japan's coldest region, turns out to hold the lesson both countries need.

#heating #heatpump #hvac #japan #energyefficiency #homeimprovement #construction #technology #winterliving #realestate

tab_title: Drolet ECO-55 ST vs EasyFire EF3801C: Best Pellet Stove Value
description:
In this pellet stove comparison, we look at the EasyFire EF3801C vs Drolet ECO-55 ST to help you decide which heating unit is the better long-term investment for your home. Both stoves deliver around 39,000 BTUs of heat, but they differ significantly in hopper capacity, blower design, warranty terms, and price.

The Drolet ECO-55 ST features an 80 lb hopper (69-hour burn time), a quiet variable-speed blower, a limited lifetime heat exchanger warranty, and an affordable price tag of around $2,649. In contrast, the EasyFire EF3801C offers a 50 lb hopper, a single-speed blower, a 3-year heat exchanger warranty, and 12V battery backup readiness, priced near $3,963.

If off-grid power backup is your primary concern, EasyFire is worth a look. However, for most homeowners seeking maximum value, convenience, and low maintenance costs, the Drolet ECO-55 ST is my top technician recommendation.

tab_title: Your Attic Might Need This Makeover Before Winter
description:
Before winter, take a closer look at what’s hiding in your attic. Air leaks, poorly sealed ducts, and incomplete air barriers can let heating and cooling escape—even when insulation is already in place.

In this attic makeover, I show a supply duct that still had a gap after being “fixed,” a hidden connection beside an upstairs bathroom, and why attic air sealing and insulation need to work together.

You’ll learn what to look for around recessed lights, wiring, pipes, and attic walls; how expanding foam helps seal gaps; and how an energy audit with a blower door test can help uncover hidden air leakage.

Before adding insulation, ask: *What needs to be sealed before we cover it up?* Ask for pictures of the gaps and the completed repairs so you understand what’s being fixed.

tab_title: Before You Pay $600 For a Fridge Repair, Check These 6 Things (5 Minute Fix)
description:
🔗 Save Thousands on Repairs, Replacements and Power Bills with my Complete Appliance Blueprint:
https://nakamurasecrets.com

Nobody watches this video because they want to. You are watching because you opened your refrigerator this morning and the milk was warm, and there is a number sitting in the back of your mind. You are thinking compressor. Let me take that off your shoulders right now: after thirty years of walking into kitchens exactly like yours, the compressor is almost never what it is.

Here is the shortcut, free, before you watch anything. Go look at your freezer. If the freezer is still cold and only the refrigerator side has gone warm, your compressor is fine. It has to be, because the same system cools both compartments. What you have is an air problem, and air problems are ordinary parts.

I fixed appliances in other people's homes for thirty years, and I want to be honest about why I made this video. I got paid to do a lot of these repairs. A man calls, I drive out, I spend twenty minutes, and I hand him a bill for something he could have done himself with a screwdriver and a vacuum cleaner. I took that money because it was my trade. It never sat right with me. This video is me giving it back.

The six things I check, in the order I check them:

Dirty condenser coils, which is the most common cause by a wide margin
A stopped condenser fan, which makes the compressor shut itself down to protect itself
A failed start relay, and the ten second shake test that tells you
A block of ice on the back wall of your freezer, meaning the defrost system quit
A swollen defrost thermostat or a dead defrost heater
An evaporator fan that stopped turning, so the cold never travels

What this saves you: a technician charges seventy-five to a hundred and fifty dollars just to arrive and tell you what is wrong. A normal repair runs three hundred to six hundred. A start relay, one of the six above, is fifty to two hundred if somebody else does it. And a compressor, the thing you are dreading, is seven hundred to twelve hundred and fifty by the time you count the part and the labor.

I also tell you exactly where to stop, and that part is not about your skill. If all six check out, what is left is the sealed system, and under Section 608 of the EPA's rules only a certified technician may legally open, empty or charge a refrigerant circuit. You cannot legally buy the refrigerant, and the penalties for venting it run into tens of thousands of dollars a day. Six things are yours. What is behind them is not.

One honest note. Several of these really are five minute jobs. Cleaning the condenser coils properly is closer to twenty. I say so in the video rather than pretending otherwise. And unplug the refrigerator before you touch anything; there is one point where we plug it back in on purpose and I tell you exactly when.

Nothing good should ever be wasted. Not the machine in your kitchen, and not the knowing of how to keep it.

description:
Your outdoor AC unit isn't broken. It isn't the wrong brand. It's dirty. And the fix is a garden hose.

The average American summer electric bill is ~$178/month (EIA forecast). Air conditioning is 12–17% of your home electricity nationally — and 40–50% in hot-climate states. Five specific problems are inflating that number, and three of them cost you nothing or close to nothing to fix this weekend.

— Why a dirty condenser coil cuts cooling capacity 7%, raises power draw 10%, and reduces net compressor efficiency 16% (DOE FEMP data — not the misquoted "30%" figure from commercial chiller studies that every contractor blog repeats)

tab_title: Danfoss thermostat TP5001 SETUP & MENU
description:
TP5001M, TP5001B, TP5001RF thermostat menu:

P01 01 - Manual temperature operation
P01 02 - Schedule timer 5/2 day
P01 03 - Schedule timer 24h
P02 01 - ON/OFF Load compensation is enabled. ON/Off load compensation is a feature of temperature control products such as room thermostats and programmable thermostats.
On/Off load compensation is a proven method of minimising energy use by calculating the demand from a thermostat. As the temperature approaches the required setting, the boiler will fire for shorter periods of time, ensuring a constant temperature is maintained. This not only enhances comfort levels, but also uses less energy. On/Off load compensating products are ideal for use with modern systems in well-insulated houses. Recommended for use with gas condensing boilers. Thermostat prevents boiler working for too long period of time. In this way, the heating works more efficiently, as the return temperature of the heating return is lowered. Condensation is better. Less gas is consumed.
P02 02 - ON/OFF standart operation. Boiler is ON till set temperature is reached. 
P03 01 - Normal start control.
P03 02 - Delayed start of heating. TP5001 thermostat includes an optional delay start feature to hold off the heating for a time on mild days when the room temperature at the start of an event is close to the programmed value. Recommended for use with gas condensing boilers in order to use less gas. In other words, it is an economic mode.
P03 03 - Optimised start control. TP5001 thermostat includes an optional optimum start control. This feature allows you to set the time at which you require a room temperature by. The thermostat then calculates how soon before the event time the system must be turned up to ensure that the room is at the temperature by the required time. Heating can be started maximum 120 min before schedule. 
P04 - Temperature limitation high
P05 - Temperature limitation low
P06 - Frost protect temperature
P07 - Away mode temperature
P08 01 - Timer display 24h
P08 02 - Timer display 12h
P09 - Service due setup. Installer setting only
P10 00 - RF Pairing mode OFF (TP5001RF only) 
P10 01 - RF Pairing mode ON (TP5001RF only) 
P11 01 - Auto daylight saving ON
P11 02 - Auto daylight saving OFF

Old code numbers
TP5001M 087N7930
TP5001B 087N7931
TP5001 RF + RX1-S 087N7934 

New code numbers
TP5001M V2 087N7935
TP5001 RF + RX1-S V2 087N7936

Error Messages
E1 - Sensor failure
EE  - EEPROM failure
Lo - Measured temperature below 0°C
Hi - Measured temperature above 50°C
E3 - RF Pairing failed
E4 - RF Signal lost
E6 - Real Time Clock (RTC) failure

description:
Your air conditioner doesn't make cold air. It moves heat out of your house and dumps it outside. Once you understand that, one nearly free fix makes obvious sense: get your outdoor unit out of the direct sun. In this one I explain the physics in plain English, show you the right way to shade a condenser without ever choking its airflow, and the common mistake that quietly cooks your system instead of helping it.

Why "cold" isn't real, and what your AC is actually doing every second it runs
Why a condenser baking in full sun can't shed heat, and what that costs you
The wrong way to shade it (a tarp or a box will wreck your system)
The right way: shade cloth, planted shade, awnings, and safe clearances
What kind of temperature drop you can honestly expect, and what you can't
Two more free things that help your unit breathe

A note on safety: always shut power off at the disconnect before working around the outdoor unit. Keep at least two to three feet of clearance on every side and nothing over the top. Shade is not a repair. If your system is low on refrigerant, dirty, or failing, call a licensed pro.

description:

THE GAP SIZES, AND WHEN TO CLOSE THEM
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

WHAT FITS THROUGH WHAT
• Stink bug, cluster fly: 1/8 in — sealant, weatherstrip, screen repair
• House mouse: 1/4 in — copper mesh or coarse stainless wool packed tight, sealed over
• Snake: 1/4 in — same as mice; they are following the mice
• Bat: 3/8 in — check for young inside and check your local law BEFORE sealing
• Rat: 1/2 in — hardware cloth or sheet metal; they chew through foam and sealant
• Squirrel: 1 1/2 in — sheet metal or hardware cloth

THE TIMING THAT DECIDES IT
Do the sealing in LATE SUMMER, before the autumn window opens. Sealing in January
locks in what is already inside and changes nothing about next year.

WHERE TO LOOK, IN ORDER
• Every penetration through the exterior wall — hose bibs, electrical, gas, cable,
  AC lines, dryer vents
• Where the siding meets the foundation, all the way round, at ground level
• Under and behind exterior steps and the deck ledger
• Garage door bottom and side seals
• Crawl space vents and hatch — are the screens intact?
• Roofline: gable vents, soffit joins, where a roof meets a wall

THE FREE VERSION OF THE AUDIT
Walk the outside after dark with the interior lights on. Light gets out wherever

description:
Frank has kept a pre-war Milwaukee apartment building free of mice for thirty-three years. He has never signed a pest control contract. What he uses costs four dollars and takes twenty minutes to apply. The building went up in 1948. It has never once needed a second visit for the same hole.

The Federal Trade Commission has sent warning letters to more than sixty manufacturers of ultrasonic pest repellers since 2001, stating the effectiveness claims were not backed by reliable evidence. Independent tests found no measurable drop in rodent activity in rooms where the devices ran continuously. Bait stations kill the mice that find them and do nothing about the opening that keeps producing new ones. A female house mouse delivers up to ten litters a year. The exterminator gets paid to come back. The building's gaps stay exactly as open as the day it was built, regardless of how many service calls happen in the rooms on either side of them.

This video documents the three-method system Frank inherited from a superintendent named Gordon, who ran that building from 1961 to 1993: the Skull Rule — a mouse's skull is the only rigid part of its body, everything behind it compresses to follow, and a gap that passes a standard pencil passes a mouse, which means four dollars of coarse steel wool packed into every pipe penetration and foundation seam permanently closes what bait stations leave open, the Copper Curtain addressing weep holes and utility gaps that stay wet — steel wool rusts down to a soft residue a determined mouse can push through, copper does not rust and lasts as long as the building does, and the Blind Highway targeting balloon-framed pre-1950 construction where open stud bays run from basement to attic and a mouse past the exterior barrier can travel the entire building without entering a single room a pest control visit would have inspected. Plus the modification Gordon wrote on a page dated November 1988 in a spiral notebook that has lived in a dented coffee tin in that boiler room since 1961: capsaicin sealant wiped over the cured caulk line after it sets — the EPA registered capsaicin as a rodent repellent in 1962, a mouse investigates a new seal with its whiskers and mouth before gnawing, and the capsaicin makes that first contact the last one. Since Frank added it in 2011, not one sealed point has needed repacking from gnawing. It adds five minutes to the job. There is no separate product to sell alongside it. Complete system: forty dollars. Thirty-three years. Zero repeat exterminator calls.

tab_title: How Building Supers Fix Concrete Cracks Before They Destroy a Foundation — The $3 Method
description:
Gus has kept a six-story apartment building on Buffalo's West Side standing for thirty-four years. He has never once bought a tube of concrete caulk. He has watched tenants seal the same crack three winters running while the real damage crept toward the steel holding that wall together. The sections he has treated have not reopened since 1994.

Every hardware store sells the same answer: a flexible acrylic or polyurethane sealant rated for cracks under one-eighth of an inch with no active water — which excludes a large share of the cracks people are actually trying to fix. The sealant bonds only to the surface, never reaching the moisture still moving through the wall from the soil outside. And if there is rusting steel behind that crack, the sealant does nothing to stop it, because rust occupies several times the volume of the metal it replaces and that pressure keeps building beneath a perfectly sealed surface. Most foundation cracks are three problems simultaneously: the opening, the hydrostatic pressure behind it, and the corroding steel inside it. A tube of sealant addresses one while the other two keep working until a new crack appears eighteen inches away. Dry pack repair — mortar mixed almost dry and driven into a crack widened at the back so the patch locks into the wall rather than resting on it — appears in concrete manuals going back to the 1920s. Once pre-mixed compounds and caulk tubes became the standard hardware store product after the 1970s, a technique requiring hand skill stopped being taught.

This video documents the three-method system Gus has run every fall since the 1990s: the Dry Pack Key, a mechanically keyed patch that resists seasonal movement no surface sealant can survive, the Water's Detour addressing the hydrostatic pressure that is the actual source of most foundation cracks — left out of homeowner guides because regrading a yard sells nothing at the register, and the Sacrificial Coat of zinc-rich cold galvanizing compound that applies cathodic protection to exposed rebar, making treated steel the least reactive part of the wall instead of the most — sold to contractors for decades and rarely to homeowners because one twelve-dollar can lasts years. Plus the modification Gus wrote in a spiral notebook after his own work failed once: extend the Sacrificial Coat three full inches past any visible rust, because the corrosion driving a crack runs along an active zone of the rebar past what is visible, and treating only the exposed section shifts that corrosion to untreated steel beside it, opening a second crack past the first patch. No repair guide sold to homeowners mentions those extra three inches. It is not a product. It is a habit one man corrected after refusing to let his own work fail the same way twice.

tab_title: 12 Ways Your House Is Secretly Losing Heat (And How to Stop It)
description:
Is your furnace running but your house is still cold? A retired furnace man who spent most of his working life keeping furnaces going through Minnesota winters explains the 12 most common reasons a house feels cold and drafty, even when the heat is on. Most of them are simple, safe fixes that cost little or nothing.

In this video, you'll hear about Carol, a widow from church who couldn't keep her house warm. The furnace wasn't the problem. Her house was quietly giving heat away.

THE 12 COLD HOUSE MISTAKES COVERED:

BLOCKED HEAT
1. Furniture or long curtains covering heat registers, radiators or baseboard heaters
2. A dusty or blocked return air grille that chokes airflow back to the furnace

HOLES IN THE HOUSE
3. Leaving the fireplace damper open when there's no fire
4. Leaving the window air conditioner in all winter
5. Forgetting the bathroom or kitchen exhaust fan (an 80 CFM fan running for 2 hours can pull out about 9,600 cubic feet of warm air, roughly the whole inside of a 1,200 square foot house)
6. A loose, uninsulated attic hatch

LEAKY DUCTS AND DRY AIR
7. Leaky ductwork, which can lose 20 to 30 percent of your heated air, and why regular duct tape is the wrong fix (use mastic or metal-backed foil tape)
8. Very dry winter air, and why 30 to 50 percent humidity can make your home feel warmer

THE DANGEROUS ONES
9. Using a space heater the wrong way: extension cords, power strips, and heaters left on overnight
10. Using the kitchen stove or oven to heat the house (never do this)

THE FURNACE STILL SEEMS TO WORK
11. Ignoring new noises, strange smells or short cycling
12. Skipping the yearly furnace safety inspection

HIS SIMPLE RULE:
Heat has to be made safely, moved where you want it, and kept there long enough for you to feel it. Look first. Listen. Do the easy arithmetic. Fix the safe, obvious things. Then know where to stop.

These heat loss and furnace troubleshooting tips are for homeowners, retirees and anyone on a fixed income who wants to know how to keep the house warm, stop drafts, fix a furnace that isn't heating well, and stay warm and safe all winter.

Keep space heaters at least 3 feet from anything that can burn, plug them straight into a wall outlet, and turn them off when you sleep or leave the room. Never heat your home with a stove or oven. If you smell gas, leave right away and call your gas company. If a carbon monoxide alarm goes off, get everyone out and call 911 from outside. For anything inside the furnace, call a licensed HVAC technician.

tab_title: Your CO Alarm Has a Clock That Retires It
description:
Your carbon monoxide alarm has a clock inside it. On alarms that use a timer, it counts down to the lifetime the maker set, then starts an end-of-life signal, and one big maker warns its alarms then no longer detect carbon monoxide. It's also designed not to go off at a low, steady level of the gas.

This video opens one up: the electrochemical cell that makes its own tiny current, why that cell still ages, where the end-of-life signal came from, the canary it replaced, and why its timing is tuned to your blood, not the air.

tab_title: Your Electric Blanket Has a Wire Built to Melt
description:
Inside a lot of electric blankets there's a second wire, and its whole job is to fail before you get hurt. It's wrapped around the heating wire all the way down every loop, and if any part of the blanket gets too hot, the plastic between them gives way on purpose and the power goes off.

We cut one open in cross-section: the heating wire, the sensing layer that melts somewhere around 100–200 °C (about 200–400 °F), the newer designs that watch for a hot spot all night, and why folding, pins and years of washing wear it out. Then what the blinking light on your controller really means, and how to check yours before winter.

tab_title: How to Build a Root Cellar That Actually Works — Three Versions for Three Situations
description:
The most common reason a root cellar doesn't work isn't climate and it isn't location. It's one of four construction errors that are entirely preventable — if you know what they are before you build.

This is Video 2 in the Storage Series. Video 1 covered why root cellars work — the physics, the ventilation system, the honest crop-by-crop limits. This video is the construction. Three versions, three homeowner situations, real specs, real costs, real mistakes.

What's covered:

THE FOUR ERRORS (before any construction details):
1. Single vent — why one opening creates a cellar that never reaches temperature
2. Both vents at the same height — the most common misreading of two-vent design
3. Insulating the wrong walls — the basement mistake that blocks your cooling source
4. No drainage provision — why one flood loses everything

VERSION 1 — HILLSIDE IN-GROUND:
Site selection: north-facing slope, 18-inch water table clearance, the drainage test
Size: 5×8 ft = 30 bushels for most families
Excavation: hand vs compact excavator (when to rent one, cost $200-350/day)
Walls: concrete block vs pressure-treated lumber — which is right for 30 years
Roof load: why spans over 10 ft need engineer review
Waterproofing: the step most DIY builds skip (and what it costs to fix after)
Door: the weakest thermal link in any hillside cellar
Ventilation: exact placement specs for intake and exhaust
Cost: $800-3,000 DIY

VERSION 2 — BASEMENT CORNER:
Corner selection: why northeast, which walls to leave bare, which to insulate
Framing and insulation: R-13 minimum, R-20 better for interior walls and ceiling
Floor: why leaving it bare is correct
Ventilation through a window — the plywood panel method
The radon check: why this is non-negotiable before you enclose the space
Cost: $150-400 DIY

VERSION 3 — IMPROVISED SMALL-SCALE:
Buried drum (zones 4-6): specs, cost, limits
Unheated outbuilding: when it works, when it fails
Zone 7+ refrigerated alternative: external thermostat + window AC

THE BUILD SEQUENCE (applies to all three versions):
Drainage → structure → ventilation → insulation → door → shelves

I'm Silas Eli Yoder. 40 years inspecting old farmhouses and modern subdivisions. Root cellars that work and root cellars that fail have specific differences. This video is those differences.

Leave your state and your house situation in the comments — hillside, basement, or improvised — and the specific question you have going into the build.

Next video: the springhouse.

tab_title: Why Zoned HVAC Systems Go Wrong So Often (The Bypass Damper Scam)
description:
Discover why so many zoned HVAC systems end up noisier, less efficient, and more uncomfortable than the systems they replaced. In this video, we expose the hidden problems behind modern HVAC zoning systems — especially the controversial bypass damper setup that many homeowners are never warned about. What sounds like a “smart comfort upgrade” can often become a pressure-management shortcut hiding deeper design flaws.

We break down how oversized HVAC systems, poor duct design, static pressure issues, and improper airflow balancing create the perfect conditions for zoning failures. You’ll learn why bypass dampers are commonly installed, how they recirculate conditioned air back into the system, and why many building science experts argue they should never be used in properly engineered systems.

From loud vents and uneven temperatures to humidity problems, coil freeze-ups, rising energy bills, and rooms that never feel comfortable, this video explains the real physics behind bad zoning design. We also cover why some advanced HVAC manufacturers specifically discourage bypass dampers entirely, and what properly designed zoning is actually supposed to look like.

Whether you’re considering a zoning upgrade, dealing with comfort issues in your home, or simply want to understand how HVAC systems really work, this deep dive reveals the uncomfortable truth behind one of the most misunderstood “upgrades” in residential heating and cooling.

tab_title: What Can a $1,500 Power Station REALLY Power? (You'll Be Surprised)
description:
A power station will not run your house - and what it will run is not what the box implies. Here is what a $1,500 unit actually powers in a real home during a real winter outage.
The same battery runs your gas furnace for most of a night, and an electric space heater for about one hour. Same battery. Once you know why, you can look at any appliance in your house and know the answer in four seconds.

I am Dale Prosser. Twenty five years pulling furnaces and air handlers in and out of people's basements. I do not sell power stations and I do not have a link.

In this video:
The two numbers on the box, and why the big one is not the one that matters
Tank and pipe: watt hours versus watts, explained so it sticks
The third number they barely print - surge - and why it decides whether an appliance runs at all
A walk through the house with real figures: furnace, fridge, freezer, router, CPAP, sump pump
The ones that will NOT work: space heater, kettle, microwave, window AC, well pump
The rule that covers everything: makes heat = brief, moves air or water = a long time
Why cold weather costs you more than the label admits, and why most units will not charge below freezing at all
LFP versus the cheaper lithium, and how to tell which one you are buying
Three ways to recharge in an outage, ranked honestly - solar is the slowest
The October dry run that proves the whole plan before you need it
Two units or one? And when expandable batteries are right
The floating-neutral trap that stops a furnace dead even when every watt number is correct

THE HONEST PART: if you are on a well, no battery you can carry will run the pump. That is a generator and a transfer switch, and I would rather tell you now than have you find out in the dark. And if all you want is a fridge, some lights and your phones, you need far less than $1,500 - do not let anyone upsell you a whole-house solution for a lamp.

SAFETY: a battery power station is fine indoors, and that is its real advantage. Anything that burns fuel goes OUTSIDE, well away from the house, exhaust pointed away from every door and window - carbon monoxide kills more people in winter storms than the cold does. And never back feed: no cord with a plug on both ends, ever. It can kill the utility crew that came out in the storm to restore your power.

Tell me in the comments what you are actually trying to keep running, and I will tell you straight whether that unit will do it.

Next week: the flame sensor. Ten dollar part, most common no-heat call in the country, and cleaning it costs you nothing at all.

Check the sticker. Do the arithmetic. And take twenty percent off whatever the box tells you.

Don’t wrap the whole unit (trapped moisture and a mouse nest in the wiring) - cover the top only
Don’t cut the power all winter (it shuts off the crankcase heater and sets up the compressor for a rough spring startup) - leave it on for a few dollars a month

And here’s why nobody warns you: a mistake you make in the fall doesn’t make a sound. It sits quiet all winter, then hands you the bill in the spring.

Already cut the power this year? Put it back on and give it about a day before you call for cooling.

Tell me in the comments how you’ve been putting yours away: cover on or off, power on or off, and how old the unit is. I read every one and I’ll tell you straight if you’ve been setting yourself up for a rough spring.

Subscribe, there is a lot of season left.

tab_title: Turning Your Heat Up Past 70 Is NOT Warming Your House. Do This Instead
description:
If your thermostat says 70 degrees but your cold house still feels freezing, the problem might not be your furnace at all.

We are looking at the factors that actually dictate your comfort, starting with why dry air makes a room feel significantly colder than the number on your wall. We walk through the simple maintenance steps for your system, specifically how to change a humidifier pad that has likely been ignored since last winter.

Finally, we cover the importance of proper thermometer placement. Placing a gauge right next to your favorite chair can tell you more about your actual environment than the reading on your central control. It is a quick way to diagnose drafts and humidity issues before you call a professional to fix a system that isn't broken.

Tell me in the comments which state you live in, how old your furnace is, and what your gauge reads after a day. I read them, and I'd like to know how dry it gets where you are.

Subscribe so the next one finds you. Next time: the furnace itself, and the few things that decide how long it lasts.

description:
You can support this channel on Patreon! Link below    
Oh no. It’s a new version of a well-established product that trades efficiency for convenience. But this time, it’s more than just being cool. It’s about cooling.

tab_title: How To Build A DIY Retaining Wall | Complete Step-By-Step Guide
description:
👉 Free Retaining Wall Build Guide:  https://geni.us/Ii9qB8n

This DIY retaining wall turned a steep, unusable slope into a solid 11' x 15' pad we can actually use — 42 hours of labor and about $1,600 in materials.

Most "retaining wall" videos use the small tumbled blocks from the big box store. Those are flower bed blocks. In this complete step-by-step guide, I'm using a commercial-grade 75 lb block from a landscape supply yard, and I walk through the whole build: how to lay out and square your pad, how to set a 6" compacted base, how to get drainage right, and how to get that first course perfectly level — because that's the course that decides whether your wall is
still straight in 30 years.

⏱️ CHAPTERS
0:00 – The problem: a steep, unusable slope
0:45 – Roughing in the pad size and stripping organics
2:00 – Corner stakes, squaring up, checking diagonals
3:15 – Running a level string line
4:15 – Excavating down to stable soil
5:00 – Compacting subgrade + geotextile fabric
5:45 – Retaining wall blocks: what to buy and what to avoid
8:15 – Drainage: 4" perforated pipe daylighted to the ravine
9:15 – Commercial geotextile and the 6" compacted base
10:15 – Course math: how tall before you need geogrid
11:15 – String level vs laser level
12:15 – Setting the first corner block
13:30 – Leveling the first course (and knocking off the lip)
15:00 – Stepping up the grade
15:49 – Backfill and the second course
17:10 – Filling the block voids + setting top caps
18:30 – Cutting a cap with a chisel (no saw needed)
19:10 – Final surface + total cost and hours

🧱 THE BUILD — KEY SPECS
Finished pad: 11' x 15'
Wall height: 3 courses (24") + 4" top cap = 28"
Base: 6" compacted CA-6 / crusher run (also called road pack)
Drainage: 4" perforated corrugated pipe, daylighted
Backfill + final surface: 3/4" clean stone, compacted in 3–4" lifts
Fabric: commercial geotextile — NOT weed block
Block: commercial grade, ~75 lbs, 18" face Belgard Diamond Pro
Corners: construction adhesive (no lip on corner pieces)
Total: 42 hours labor · ~$1,600 in materials

Thinking about hiring this out instead? The build guide has my hours and material costs on this wall AND the larger wall I built last year, so you can price out your own project before you commit.

#RetainingWall #DIYRetainingWall #Landscaping
title: How To Build A DIY Retaining Wall | Complete Step-By-Step Guide

   • 9 BRAD NAIL MISTAKES (and how to avoid them!)  
MINI-HACKSAW—A VERY HANDY TOOL:
   • Mini Hacksaw—A Very Handy Tool!  

The Painter’s Tool isn’t just for painters. It’s a multi-use, multi-functional tool that will augment the tool collection of every person who owns one. Painters, carpenters, plumbers, electricians, homeowners and DIYers can all benefit from owning this tool.

10 USES FOR THE PAINTER’S TOOL / 5-IN-1 / 6-IN-1:

1. Cleaning Paint Rollers: The curved inner wall of the painters tool can be used for pushing excess paint out of paint rollers (which can hold more than ½ pint in the roller nap!) It works for both full-sized rollers, and mini-rollers.

2. Opening Paint Cans: The flat head on the tool is perfect for prying up paint lids with ease. It can also be inserted beneath the lid and drawn backwards like a can opener to get gunked up paint can lids unstuck.

3. Hammer Striking: Most painters tools and 5-in-1s now come with a metal butt on the end. This is great for driving paint can lids back down. It can also be used for general striking on the jobsite (though it’s not useful for driving nails!)

4. Paint Scraping: Perhaps the most common use, the beveled blade of the painter’s tool is perfect for scraping paint. It’s flat and yet sturdy, and can be wedged beneath paint chips with ease. Just be sure to wear a glove when you’re scraping paint.

5. Corner Gouging: The painters tool has a sharp pick on the other end of the head, which is great for scraping paint and grime out of corners. Just draw it down in a slashing motion to dislodge caulk and paint.

6. Spreading Putty: The flat blade of the painters tool or 5-in-1 is also perfect for spreading putty. It works as a simple trowel to fill nail holes and cracks with putty or woodfillers.

7. Nail Prying: The small teardrop shape on the body of the painters tool can be used for lightly prying up small nails.

8. Surface Protection: The Painters tool or 5-in-1 can be used in conjunction with a hammer to pry out larger fasteners. It can act as a protective surface for the head of the hammer to transfer leverage onto. This will preserve trim and walls.

9. Light Chiseling: The bevel of the painters tool or 5-in-1 is strong enough to split end grain in most wood, and also split face grain in soft woods. You can just tap it in with a hammer.

10. Prying Materials Apart: By far the most useful function of the painters tool or 5 in 1 is prying materials apart. The tool is so flat and strong, it can be driven into gaps between two materials, then gently leveraged to begin working those materials apart. It is far more gentle on surfaces than blunt demolition tools.

Thanks for watching the video! Be sure to visit us at The Honest Carpenter website:

tab_title: Why You Should Consider Heated Glass for Your Next Build
description:
Heated glass bifold doors can't go into any old frame, because the power has to run through the outer frame and down into every sash. We're fitting Glow heated glass into the bifolds on our garden room build, so we went to Premier Frames to see how a heated bifold is wired and made.

The cable runs are routed into the aluminium profile on a CNC machine and the whole door is pre-wired before it leaves the factory, with two feeds dropped into each sash. On site it installs like any other bifold, then the glass is connected and two cables come out of the frame, one to a fused spur and one to the thermostat.

Andy explains how the glass gives off radiant heat, why its surface temperature is capped, what it costs to run and what happens when you open the doors. Then it's down to the factory floor to see the profiles cut, machined and fitted with the thermal block that protects the frame's efficiency.

MENTIONED IN THIS EPISODE 👇

Glow Heated Glass https://go.skill-builder.uk/glow

Premier Frames https://go.skill-builder.uk/premierfr...

KEY TAKEAWAYS

Heated glass needs a frame with routed cable channels and access points, so the bifold has to be built for it from the start rather than glazed with heated panes later.

Each sash gets two feeds, and the frame trails two cables out of the left or right hand side: one for a fused spur and one for a thermostat you can control from your phone or Alexa.

The glass gives off radiant heat that warms people and surfaces across the room, so you feel it from the other side of the room instead of waiting for warm air to circulate.

A sensor in the pane caps the surface at radiator temperature in case a child touches it, and the heat cuts out when the doors are opened.

A tint on the outside reflects heat back into the room and also helps stop furniture fading in the sun.

Andy puts the running cost at around 9p an hour per pane, depending on your tariff, and the same Glow glass is available in tiled and living roof systems.

Robin Clevett loves a scarf joint, and in this video, he shows you how to create a strong one.
Roger & Robin also have an epic fight, see who wins this battle.

We'll soon have more woodworking tips, carpentry tutorials, and hacks.


__________________________________

A scarf joint is a woodworking technique that combines two pieces of timber end to end, creating a single, longer piece of wood. This joint is particularly valuable in carpentry when the required length of timber exceeds the available length of a single piece or when it's necessary to repair or extend an existing beam.

The scarf joint cuts the ends of the timber pieces at an angle, creating matching, sloping surfaces that are then glued or fixed together. The angle of the cut can vary, but it's typically between 30 to 60 degrees.

There are various types of scarf joints, such as the plain scarf, which is a simple, straight cut, or more complex versions like the keyed or wedged scarf, which include additional features to increase the strength and stability of the joint.

Carpenters use scarf joints because they distribute the stress more evenly along the length of the joint compared to a simple butt joint, where the ends are merely butted together. This makes the scarf joint much stronger and more durable, especially when the timber is under tension or bending forces. In structural applications, such as roofing or long beams, the strength provided by a well-made scarf joint is crucial.

Moreover, the scarf joint is often preferred for aesthetic reasons. The angled cut can be made to blend smoothly into the surrounding wood, making the joint less noticeable. This is particularly important in visible structures, where the finish and appearance are key considerations.

We analyze the Nairobi building collapse to understand the structural failures behind this 18-story apartment tragedy.

This investigation examines the root causes of the structural collapse in Nairobi, Kenya, on October 23rd, 2026. We review several eyewitness videos taken before the Nairobi building collapsed, then during the collapse, and perform frame-by-frame analysis to narrow down where the construction failure occurred. 

The investigation also uncovers documentation, including the enforcement notice citing illegal development and the notification of application approval for the building. This forensic breakdown is intended for those following urban safety standards and the legal accountability surrounding such incidents.

We provide a clear visual record of the site devastation and the documents that highlight the critical oversight in construction project management and alleged corruption in Nairobi, Kenya. Understanding these variables provides a clearer picture of the event as the official inquiry continues.

Kenyan engineers estimate 85% of all buildings in Nairobi are uninhabitable. The figure explicitly means that 85% of the buildings in Nairobi are structurally unsafe for human occupation and unfit to be lived in.

This alarming statistic comes directly from a sweeping engineering survey of 15,000 structures conducted across the city. Industry bodies—including the Institution of Engineers of Kenya (IEK), the Architectural Association of Kenya (AAK), and the Kenya Institute of Planners—warned that only 15% of Nairobi's buildings actually meet basic habitability and structural safety standards.

The technical breakdown behind why so many buildings are flagged under this 85% umbrella reveals a layered systemic crisis:
• Sidelining Professionals: Up to 80% to 87% of all active construction projects in Kenya proceed entirely without the supervision of certified engineers, architects, or qualified site consultants. Developers frequently act as their own general contractors to save money.

• Adulterated Materials: The structures are built using heavily compromised components. Testing by the Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) historically found that over 60% of commercial cement samples failed baseline strength benchmarks, while structural steel reinforcement bars are routinely watered down or thin-gauged.

• Illegal Vertical Overloading: Developers routinely secure approvals for a safe 4- or 5-storey foundation, but then illegally pile on an extra 10 to 12 floors of heavy concrete on top without modifying the base. Experts warn that even a minor, mild earthquake or tremor could trigger catastrophic, widespread collapses across these top-heavy structures.

tab_title: Fix a Toilet That Keeps Running
description:
For more home improvement tips visit https://www.homerepairtutor.com/👍🏼

This video shares several methods for fixing a toilet that keeps running. Your toilet tank has a fill valve, flush valve, and flapper. And it's these parts that ultimately lead to the toilet running. My $116 water bill could have been prevented by simply replacing the $5 flapper.

The second way a leak occurs is when the flapper chain gets stuck between the flapper and flush valve. If you encounter this just trim the chain so that it doesn't drape below the flapper. Problem solved.

Sometimes the water in the tank is too high. If this is the case it will run over the overflow pipe and cause the tank to refill. You need to lower the tank's water level to about 1 inch below the overflow pipe. Watch the video for a more in depth explanation.

A toilet that keeps running is annoying, not to mention expensive. I'm sharing my tips so that you don't suffer from a $116 water bill like me. Hopefully these tips help you with your project.

tab_title: How to remove a broken bolt in a deep hole | remove broken bolt in recessed hole
description:
It can be difficult removing a broken bolt or stud that is recessed in a deep hole as there are not many techniques to remove the bolts. Before attempting to remove any bolt, it is a good idea to shock the bolt first, then apply some heat and finally some spray penetrant (once it is cool). Drilling out the bolt is one of the few options that will work in this scenario. In this video I show two techniques that could potentially work when a bolt is broken in a deep hole or a bolt is sheared in an aluminium component.

I talk you through the 7 things that you should NOT DO when applying silicone, followed by my 12 GOLDEN RULES for achieving perfect silicone joints - applying these rules at the end of the video to new silicone joints in the tricky, hand glazed tiles in my bathroom shower area.

The Amazon links above are affiliate links. It doesn't cost you anything to click on them but I do earn a small commission if you do. 

And here's the legal bit I have to state: As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.

 MY 12 GOLDEN RULES FOR THE PERFECT SILICONE JOINT
De-grease joints first with methylated spirit or acetone
Use the right silicone for your joint - high or low modulus
Use a FUGI Silicone Profiling Tool
Look for the greatest gap & select smallest tool to cover gap + 2/3mm
Cut the silicone nozzle at 90 degrees ie straight across &
Push the silicone into the joint
Aim to cover 2 not 3 sides of the joint
Use adapter for smooth lines over transverse joints
Work in short sections
Corners - up first then right to left
Clean Fugi with paper towel when finished

WHAT NOT TO DO
Don't use tape
Don't use your finger
Don't shape silicone in a concave profile
Don't use water & detergent
Don't cut the nozzle really small or at 45 degrees
Don't pull the nozzle along the joint
Try not to cover all 3 sides of the joint

tab_title: We Sold Our Barndominium… Now We’re Building This
description:
We sold the barndominium that started this channel—and now we’re beginning our biggest build yet.  A new Homestead with a shop, office, and new Barndominium.

In this first episode, Emily and I close the door on our original barndominium, return to the abandoned motocross property we purchased more than a year ago, and reveal the complete plan for our new 64x120 post-frame shop and attached 32x32 office.

This property operated as a motocross track for more than 20 years and still has over a mile of track, river frontage and plenty of history. Since purchasing it, we have converted four 20-foot connex boxes into tool storage, dealt with serious flooding and built up the construction site well above the surrounding ground. The building location itself is outside the mapped floodplain, but last year’s flood made it very clear that preparing this site correctly mattered.

THE BUILDING PLAN:

• 64x120 main post-frame building
• Equipment and tool storage
• Canning kitchen, utility room and full bathroom
• Tool-storage loft and bow/gun shop
• 48x56 basketball court
• Workout gym
• Game loft with a bar and hangout area
• Attached 32x32 office for Emily and me
• Kitchenette, conference space and covered porch

I’ll be building most of this project myself while testing some new construction systems along the way—including the Rapid Framing System, Perma-Column Sturdi-Wall brackets, Richland glulam columns, underslab insulation and hydronic floor heat.

Throughout the series, I’ll track the retail material cost, what I actually paid and what it would likely cost to hire the work completed. I’ll also share the mistakes, weather delays, system comparisons and decisions that normally get left out of a finished-building tour.

This project will also help us develop new shop and garage plans through Back Forty Buildings, with building kits fulfilled through Burrows Post Frame Structures. My goal is to determine which products and methods genuinely make sense for DIY builders—not simply show you a polished final result.

Next up: laying out the building, drilling the pier holes and attempting to pour the foundation after more than 10 inches of rain.

Subscribe and follow the complete build from an empty pad to the finished shop, office, gym and basketball court.

tab_title: Hardie Fiber Cement  vs Vinyl Siding | Everything you need to know!
description:
The first 500 people to use my link will get a 1 month free trial of Skillshare https://skl.sh/belindacarr07241

When it comes to exterior cladding for your home, there are two popular synthetic options: Hardie fiber cement board and vinyl siding. Both are attractive and cost-effective ways to give your home an update, but how do you decide between them? Which one is right for your home? 

Mics I use: https://amzn.to/3mQ0VaQ
Shotgun mic I use: https://amzn.to/41AynAS
Camera I use: https://amzn.to/3UPqnd9
Lens I use: https://amzn.to/3mTEKR1

Please support me on Patreon if you can:   / belinda_carr  
Video scripts and citations: www.carrbuilds.com
Podcast channel:    / belindacarrpodcast   

Chapters
0:00 Introduction
0:45 Function of siding
1:21 How Hardie Fiber Cement Board is made
2:46 How Vinyl Siding is made
3:21 Appearance
3:55 Durability
4:53 DIY-ability
5:26 Eco-friendly
6:16 Sponsor
7:22 Cost differences
8:03 Conclusion

While brick and stone are popular high-end options for siding, Hardie plank and vinyl are the most popular choices on the more affordable end. Let’s first take a look at how this Hardie fiber cement board is made. Fiber cement was invented in the early 1900s by combining cement with asbestos fibers. It was reinvented in the 1970s by James Hardie, the building materials company. They replaced asbestos with wood pulp.

Vinyl Siding is primarily made from polyvinyl chloride or PVC resin, along with other additives that provide color, flexibility, strength and resistance to UV rays. 

The molten PVC mixture is forced through an extruder that shapes it into a continuous profile. While it is still warm and pliable, the siding is embossed with a textured pattern that mimics wood grain. It is then cooled and cut into 12 to 16-foot sections for ease of handling and installation. 

In terms of durability, Hardie Board is more resistant to scratches, dents, UV damage and fading. It is also resistant to water. All these characteristics contribute to a long 50 lifespan with proper maintenance. Vinyl Siding is less resistant to scratches and dents, especially in colder temperatures. It is more susceptible to fading and discoloration and it typically lasts around 20 years.

Hardie plank’s biggest advantage is its class A fire resistance. It is non-combustible and will not ignite when exposed to direct flames. Vinyl siding, on the other hand, is prone to warping or melting when exposed to heat sources, like a barbecue grill or bonfire situated too close to your exterior. After melting, it exposes your home’s internal walls and studs, allowing the fire to spread.

istorically, vinyl was significantly cheaper but since 2022, their costs are almost identical. Fiber cement siding costs $5 to $11 per square foot while vinyl costs $4 to $10 per square foot. All attributes considered, Hardie plank fiber cement siding is a better long-term investment. It offers superior durability and aesthetics and lower maintenance.  Vinyl siding is easier to install and budget-friendly and offers decent performance.

tab_title: 7 reasons why shipping container homes are a SCAM
description:
• Responding to comments: Shipping Container...  
Check out my latest follow-up video to this one where I elaborate on some of the points and address some comments

Shipping container homes are glamorized all over social media but are they everything they are marketed as? In this video, I uncover 7 reasons why you should stay away from shipping container homes.

Since the early 2000s, shipping containers have captured the imagination of designers and home builders worldwide. They fit in with the very popular tiny house movement that advocates living simpler and in smaller homes. The corrugated metal exterior of shipping containers gives it a trendy, industrial look. Thousands of shipping containers are discarded every year. So, there is a sense of being socially responsible and environmentally conscious when one rescues a shipping container from a junk yard and converts it into a home. 

First issue: the size constraints. Standard shipping containers are 20 feet and 40 feet long and 8 feet wide. Most of these containers are 8.5 feet tall but you can order custom ones that are 9.5 feet tall. 

Second issue: A metal container works as a system, the idea that every part of this box is structural is false. Every single cut that you make for plumbing, windows, doors, roof openings into its structural frame or corrugated metal siding compromises its strength so you have to reinforce it with metal or wood. 

Third issue: the thermal conductivity of steel. It’s not a good insulator, so you can expect the inside of these containers to get very hot in summer and very cold in winter.

Fourth issue: the health risks that come with buying old shipping containers. You can track the locations that the container has been to around the world, but you can’t track exactly what it has carried. It could have carried toxic chemicals such as pesticides or fumigants and the contents might have leaked into the wooden floorboards. 

Fifth issue: this type of building is not the best for all locations. It might make sense in coastal regions near port cities where a container is readily available. If you are inland, the cost to transport it all the way to your plot of land is not logical. Also, building with native materials is the most eco-friendly and cost-effective method. 

Sixth issue: the idea that you are saving the environment when you use shipping containers and that is a highly sustainable practice. Another important thing to consider is the carbon footprint of your container home. Steel construction is not as environmentally friendly as wood. 

Seventh issue: the idea that shipping containers can be the solution to the housing crisis in the world but, this crisis is not a technology problem, it’s far more complex. Purely from a financial aspect, it would be cheaper to build a homeless shelter with wood than build a complex shipping container building. This type of building can maybe be 20% cheaper, not more. The modifications that you need to make a metal box livable aren’t cheap.

description:
How much time do you lose searching for the right driver bit—or discovering that the bit you need is back in the toolbox, truck, or shop? This is the solution!

#BATTEX #MissionToolCompany #DeWalt20V #CordlessTools #PowerTools #ToolReview #DrillBits #ImpactDriver #ToolOrganization #MadeInUSA #DIYTools #DirtFarmerJay

The BATTEX Battery Attachment Extension System from Mission Tool Company adds a slim accessory-mounting rail between the battery and a compatible cordless tool. You can then attach bits, bit holders, and a belt hook directly to the tool and swap them as the work requires.

In this episode, we unbox and install the DeWalt 20V MAX version, provision it with the accessories we commonly use, and put it to work for our initial evaluation. We’ll examine:

• What comes in the BATTEX set
• How it installs between the tool and battery
• How the locking rail and spring-ball detents work
• Why each accessory must be fully seated in its detent
• The horizontal and vertical magnetic bit holders
• The removable Easy-In belt hook
• Added size, weight, balance, and handling
• Battery fit and removal
• Stability and vibration during actual use
• Situations where having several bits on the tool could save time

BATTEX maintains the electrical connection between the battery and tool while adding a sturdy, Picatinny-inspired mounting system for accessories. The holders use powerful N52 magnets, while a 35-newton spring-ball detent helps keep each accessory locked onto the rail.

The snug fit is intentional. It minimizes movement and vibration, but it also means installation and accessory changes require deliberate pressure and attention to ensure everything is fully seated.

Mission Tool Company provided four DeWalt-compatible BATTEX sets for our independent evaluation. We will place two with regular tool users for an extended field test. After about a year of real-world use, we plan to report on durability, accessory retention, battery connections, ease of use, and whether the system continued to earn its place on the tools.

BATTEX is engineered and manufactured in the USA and is currently offered for DeWalt 20V MAX and Milwaukee M18 battery platforms. Mission Tool Company backs it with a lifetime warranty against defects in materials and workmanship.

tab_title: How to Resurface a Driveway
description:
Learn how to repair and resurface an asphalt driveway from home improvement expert Ron Hazelton. For more projects, visit Ron Hazelton's website: http://www.ronhazelton.com/

*The Dupot Re-Surfacer Ron uses in this video is no longer available. You can use this product in its place MACMAT-AR 5-Gal. Asphalt Re-Surfacer, Model # X9510.

Transcript:

I've been noticing that my driveway is in pretty rough shape, there are spots like this that are badly eroded, cracks pretty much everywhere and you know with winter coming on, it's just going to get worse.  Water will enter places like this, freeze and expand and by next spring, I'm going to have a real mess here.  So I want to do something about it now.
 
Sealing a driveway is a job that at first I thought I'd have a professional come in and do but then I came across a relatively new product from Dupont that I think is going to be easy enough to apply that I believe I'll do it myself
 
Before anything can go on my driveway some things have to come off; dirt and debris, algae and weeds.  

I'll start with the weeds.  I'm always amazed at how well these guys can do in a pavement crack.
 
Next I loosen the debris that's collected in the wider cracks using a wire brush.
 
Then it's time for the big sweep. Now I could use a broom, but my leaf blower will do a great job of cleaning out the cracks, then clearing everything off the surface quickly.
 
To get rid of the algae, I pour a gallon of household bleach into four gallons of water, dip a scrub brush in the solution and apply the bleach and water mixture.  A heavy scrubbing is really not necessary here, I'd rather let the chemicals do the work.  I let the solution set for about 10 minutes, then rinse with fresh water.  Well, I've got the hose out. I use the nozzle to flush out any material in the cracks that the blower left behind.
 
The final cleaning I do with a pressure washer, you might consider this option, but this machine does a terrific job of removing dirt and the way I see it, The cleaner, the surface, the better anything I put on top will stick.
 
Well, the surface is clean and the algae is gone, but before I can put any kind of sealer on this driveway, I'm going to have to deal with these damaged areas.  The erosion right here and all of those cracks,
 
Narrower cracks, up to a half inch wide or so can be most easily filled using a liquid elastomeric filler like this one.  I like to cut the tapered nozzle about a quarter inch wide.  The idea here is to move backward, away from the tip, slightly overfilling the crack. You may have to speed up or slow down, depending on how deep or wide the crack becomes.  Once the filler is in place I like to take a two inch putty knife and flatten the bead, spreading the material over the adjacent surface.
 
The eroded areas need to be filled using a paste like trowel grade filler.  I find that it's easier and less messy to use a wide putty knife to remove the material from the bucket and distribute it on the surface.  Then I switched to a trowel to smooth the filler and blend it at the edges.  The trowel grade filler also works well on sunken in areas like this and larger cracks up to one inch wide.
 
No, I'm not trying to emulate a Jackson Pollock painting, I'm applying a bonding agent and sealer on top of what had been an oil stain.  I washed the surface area first with a degreaser, now I'm spreading the sealer evenly over the surface.  It will dry clear.
 
Now, this is the sealer or resurfacing that I'm going to be using today, it's by Dupont and it's asphalt with polymers added.  Now that combination will ensure that it sticks well to the old surface, it remains flexible, reducing the likelihood of cracking, resistant to the ultraviolet sun rays and it will also be highly resistant to gas and oil spills.  On top of that, it has sand added to it.  That will give me better traction here on the driveway.
 
The resurfacer needs to be mixed thoroughly before using.  Now I could do this by hand, but a paddle mixer and a cordless electric drill is much faster, easier and less messy.  My first application tool will be a four inch wide paint brush.  With this, I'll apply the material around the edge of the driveway, being careful to keep it off the cobblestone border.
 
Now here is where a second person helps a lot.  Teela Keller, a friend of mine, has agreed to lend me a hand on this next phase.  She's pouring the resurfacer on the driveway ahead of me while I follow behind with a wide squeegee spreading it out evenly.  Now, there is definitely a technique here.  The idea is to move in a continuous back and forth pattern, always working with a wet edge.
title: How to Resurface a Driveway

tab_title: How We Made Our Chicken Coop Run!
description:
As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.

Please leave a comment, thumbs up the video, and don't forget to subscribe if you enjoy our videos! Thank you!

💜 Our channel is family-friendly. 💜
♦-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------♦

Material List:

Kennel panel with gate and five 1" conduit straps to hook it to the run. 

We used all pressure treated lumber: 

two 2x6x10's
three 2x6x12's
three 2x4x10's
two 2x4x12's
three 2x4x8's
two 4x4x10's 

25 foot roll of 1/2" hardwire cloth 3 feet wide. 

50 foot roll 2 inch by 4 inch welded wire 4 feet wide. 

3" inch screws for outdoor use/pressure treated wood. 

And we used 2x4 joist hangers for the ceiling, but you can just angle screw the boards, which is probably easier. 

The run measures 5' by 12'. 

We dug two post holes and attached the other two corners to the garage. The posts were back-filled with the dirt that was removed. No concrete was used, which we feel is better. To prevent splitting, we pre-drilled all screw holes. We used rolled metal wire mesh on the three sides and roof (smaller mesh on bottom half). And we used a black dog kennel panel with a gate so we didn't have to make a door. 

We decided to build the coop part in the garage for many reasons:

1) We wouldn't need to dig any post holes for it since it would be out of the wind. 

2) We wouldn't need to build a leak proof roof. 

3) It will be much better to come out in the winter to tend to them and be out of the cold wind.

4) It will be out of the elements, so it won't rot!

♦-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------♦

tab_title: How to Flush & Descale a Tankless Water Heater (Complete Step-By-Step)
description:
Learn how to flush and descale a tankless water heater, start to finish, with no guesswork using a kit from Chromex. Scale and sediment build up on the heat exchanger over time, and that quietly costs you efficiency, hot water, and years of appliance life. This walkthrough covers the tools and supplies you need, what comes in the flush kit versus buying the pieces separately, taking a baseline pH reading, isolating the heater and shutting off the heat source, cleaning the inlet filter, mixing and circulating descaling solution with a sump pump for 30 minutes, rinsing until the pH is back to baseline, disposing of the used solution safely, and putting the heater back in service without trapped air in the lines. A plumber charges roughly $150 to $300 for this, and you only buy the equipment once. Manufacturers want it done annually, or every six months on hard water.

description:
Promotion: Navimow X4 now starts at $2,099 through July 8!
Amazon Store: 👉 https://z.navimow.com/4xKWSfk
Official Store: 👉  https://z.navimow.com/4oIybwe

We’ve now used the Segway Navimow X450 robot mower for more than 60 days on approximately 1.5 acres of Tennessee lawn—and the results genuinely surprised us.

In this video, we share an honest two-month update on how well our robot mower, “Lawnie,” has maintained the property during peak grass-growing season. We show the areas it handled well, the weeds and patches it missed, what regular maintenance looks like, and whether a robot mower can truly replace a traditional lawn mower or tractor.

We also replace the cutting blades, test the mower’s all-wheel-drive capabilities across rough terrain, and—against our better judgment—send it into tall pasture grass to see whether it can act like a miniature brush hog. The result was not what we expected!

According to the Navimow app, Lawnie has already mowed approximately 1.1 million square feet and potentially saved us 195 hours of mowing time. We also discuss the mower garage, manual-control mode, cellular and Wi-Fi connectivity, battery-life considerations, ongoing costs, and whether an expensive robotic mower can be worth the investment.

Stay until the end for an update about the five wool sheep coming to our homestead and our plans for their future pasture, fencing, and barn.

description:
For a toilet tank that is leaking, you will need a toilet tank repair kit. This will repair a leak from the bolts that hold the tank to the bowl and the gasket that joins the 2 pieces.

Most toilet tanks are held onto the bowl with 2 bolts. But there are some that have 3 bolts. Look at your toilet before going to the hardware store, you may need to purchase an extra set of bolts and washers.

You should be able to replace the bolts by using a large slotted screwdriver, an adjustable wrench and pliers. If the bolts are rusted in place, you will need a hack saw blade and locking pliers.

In most cases this is a pretty easy project. Be careful of the porcelain, it can be cracked if you tighten down too hard on the bolts.

tab_title: How to Wash Your Car Engine the Safe Way (Before & After)
description:
How do you safely wash your car's engine bay? In this DIY video I clean a wicked dirty engine bay full of sand and grime using Super Clean degreaser and a regular garden hose with a sprinkler head, with no pressure washer. I show how I prep the engine (cold and dry), protect the oil fill opening, spray the degreaser, let it soak, start the car before rinsing so the heat helps dry everything out, and rinse any overspray off the paint. The before and after is night and day.

Disclosure: The folks at Super Clean sent me this degreaser. I've been using their product for 20 to 30 years.

🔗 Super Clean on Amazon:https://link.amazon/B0erSVU9P

⏱️ TIMESTAMPS
0:00 Intro: dirty engine bay & Super Clean degreaser
0:45 Before you start: cold, dry engine (no carb or chrome)
1:21 Protect the carb & make sure the oil fill cap is on
1:40 Spray degreaser over the engine bay
2:23 Let it soak, then start the engine
2:56 Rinse with a garden hose (no pressure washer)
3:52 Rinse residue off the paint
4:13 The result: clean engine bay
4:40 Let it run to dry it out
4:54 Wrap-up

🧰 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
Super Clean cleaner-degreaser (spray bottle)
Garden hose with a sprinkler head nozzle
Plastic bag (only if your engine has a carburetor)

❓ FAQ
Q: Should the engine be hot or cold when you wash it?
A: Start with a cold, dry engine that hasn't been running for a while. Super Clean's own directions also say to spray it on a cool engine.

Q: Can I use a pressure washer on my engine?
A: I don't. Modern cars have a lot of electronics under the hood, so I use a regular garden hose with a sprinkler head and go in gently.

Q: What should I cover before washing an engine?
A: If your engine has a carburetor, put a plastic bag over it so water doesn't get in. Make sure the oil fill cap on the valve cover is on so no water gets down in through the oil fill.

Q: Is degreaser safe on chrome and paint?
A: Any degreaser can risk dulling or discoloring chrome, so this method is for engines with plastic covers and no chrome. Don't let it sit on your paint. Rinse off any overspray right away.

Q: Why start the engine before rinsing?
A: Running it builds some heat so the leftover water evaporates and moisture gets out of the wires. A little steam coming off afterward is just water evaporating. I let it run 5 to 10 minutes after rinsing, then close the hood.

Q: Any safety tips for using Super Clean?
A: Read the label first. The manufacturer's safety sheet lists it as a skin and eye irritant and recommends gloves and eye protection.
