tab_title: 15 Cheap Walmart Items the Amish Say Are Worth Gold When Your Furnace Dies
description:
🔗 The Complete Winter Library — The One Warm Room Plan (which room, how to set it up in one Saturday, the bed for January, and the whole night the furnace dies, hour by hour), The Amish Winter Bed and The Winter Ledger:
https://eliyodersecrets.com/warm/?v=w...

🔗 The Warm Room Letter — one job a week, in the order the winter comes (for members):
https://eliyodersecrets.com/letter/?v...

Watch next — 9 Heating Items the Amish Buy in Bulk — All Under $5 at Dollar Tree:
   • 9 Heating Items the Amish Buy in Bulk — Al...  

The furnace quits after midnight and the house goes cold room by room. The repair company says three days. In this video, the fifteen cheap things from Walmart that an Amish neighbor carried across the yard in a plastic bag the night that happened to the older couple next door, and that kept two people warm for four days with the furnace dead. Most are under ten dollars. Prices checked on walmart.com this week.

The thing in the picture is real and it is item one: an emergency Mylar blanket (about $8 for a pack of four) laid over the quilt, shiny side down, so the heat your own body makes stays in the bed. It will not heat a house. It keeps the heat you still have where you are lying. Later in the video the same blanket goes across a doorway to keep one room warm.

In this video, in order:
1. Mylar blankets in the doorway, behind the chair and over the window
2. Bubble wrap on the glass, with water and no tape
3. Foam weatherstrip tape, the attic hatch, and a rolled towel under the door
4. Painter's plastic and blue tape across the big openings and the stairs
5. Air-activated hand and body warmers, and where on the body they go
6. The rubber hot water bottle, hot not boiling
7. A vacuum thermos filled before dark
8. A knit cap and wool socks ("cotton kills")
9. Fleece throws, under you before over you, and where the chair goes
10. A cold-rated sleeping bag, with something underneath it
11. A small tent indoors: the room inside the room
12. Foam pipe insulation, the dripping faucet and the ribbon on the shutoff
13. A battery LED lantern instead of candles
14. The 36-hour emergency candle in a tin, used as a lamp only
15. The battery carbon monoxide alarm: the one item that warms nothing and is worth the most
Plus: the four things to check before you call the repairman, and when to leave the house.

Safety first. Never heat your home with the oven, a grill, a camp stove, a generator or a propane heater that is not rated for indoor use; carbon monoxide has no smell. Keep a working battery carbon monoxide alarm in the room you live in, and if everyone has a headache or feels sleepy, get out first and call 911 second. Mylar blankets and painter's plastic melt and burn: keep them three feet from any flame or heater, and never across the only way out of a room. Candles are a lamp, not a heater: on a plate, nothing above them, never in a tent or a bedroom, and out before you sleep. Hand warmers never on bare skin, never under you in bed, and not in your shoes if you have diabetes or numb feet. Hot water bottles: hot tap water, never boiling, and never sleep lying on one. A rolled towel on the floor is a trip hazard: push it against the door, out of the walkway. The National Institute on Aging says an older person's home should stay at 68 to 70°F; a house at 60 to 65°F can already bring on hypothermia in someone over 65. Watch for slurred speech, confusion, sleepiness, stiffness or clumsiness, and call 911. If the warm room will not stay above 65, go to family, a neighbor or a warming center; dial 211 to find one.

Source for the storm figures: Texas Department of State Health Services, final report of January 2022 on the February 2021 winter storm (246 deaths, close to two-thirds from hypothermia, at least 19 from carbon monoxide).

Tell me in the comments: furnace, boiler or wood, and your state. "Furnace, Ohio." And if your mother had a trick for a cold night that did not make this list, put it down there too.

description:
When the power goes out, the internet disappears, and modern appliances stop working, the simplest tools in the house can suddenly become the most useful. Before every household depended on electricity and battery-powered gadgets, Grandma had a collection of reliable everyday tools that helped her repair, prepare, clean, and manage a home with fewer conveniences. Many of those tools still have a place in a well-prepared household today.

In this episode, we uncover 25 forgotten home tools Grandma used that can still prove useful during a power outage. From manual kitchen gadgets and hand-powered tools to simple cleaning equipment, traditional household essentials, and practical repair items, these are the dependable tools that don’t need a wall outlet to do their job.

You’ll discover how old-fashioned household tools fit into modern off-grid preparedness, emergency home supplies, power outage planning, and self-reliance. We’ll also explore why keeping a few manual alternatives on hand can make everyday tasks easier when electricity is unavailable—whether you're dealing with a winter storm, a temporary blackout, or a disruption to normal services.

The smartest emergency kit isn’t necessarily the most expensive one. Sometimes, it starts with a hand-operated tool you already own, know how to use, and can maintain without complicated parts or charging cables. Check your cupboards, basement, garage, and old toolboxes before buying anything new.

This is a world first. A unique FPS simulator that turns gaming into reality as you move, aim, fire and get shot within a 360-degree immersive environment.
 
Using a pre-release copy of Battlefield 3 and a team of top technology experts from across Europe we've built a truly one of a kind simulator.

Centred on the world's first, portable omni-directional treadmill (designed by Swedish company MSE Weibull) the simulator lets you control the movements of a Battlefield 3 character with your own body. Other key technology employed includes: an Igloo Vision projection dome; 12 paintball markers that allow the player, in real time, to feel the enemy gunfire experienced in the game; a wireless gun system; ambient LED lighting; and an Xbox Kinect camera hack.

description:
🔗 Save Money The Hillbilly Way — Learn The Forgotten Tricks Families Used To Make Every Dollar Stretch
👉 https://thehillbillyway.com/v/wonders

A generation of women kept modest houses looking polished and prosperous using techniques that never made it onto a store shelf, and almost none of it was ever written down. This video uncovers twenty-five of those forgotten grandmother cleaning tricks, from rubbing a square of wax paper on chrome faucets to stop water spots before they form, to using a half lemon dipped in salt to polish brass, to laying a brown paper bag under a warm iron to lift candle wax from a tablecloth. You'll learn why a clear-water rinse is the real reason floors stay shiny, how cornstarch pulls a grease stain out of upholstery without spreading it, why washing soda dissolves the sticky film on top of your kitchen cabinets, and how liquid bluing makes twelve-year-old sheets look brand new. These are practical, cheap methods using vinegar, baking soda, cornstarch, wax paper and paste wax that the cleaning product industry had every reason to let you forget.

tab_title: The One Thing Every Aluminum Boat Owner Should Do | Alaska
description:
I hadn't been down to the boat in almost a month. When a buddy needed a load of building materials hauled across Kachemak Bay, it was the perfect excuse to get back on the water and check everything over.
First thing — fire up the heater, because it's October in Alaska. Then I opened up the voids below deck. If you own an aluminum boat, this part's for you. My boat is starting to show some corrosion in the bottom plating, and I learned something I didn't know before: the anodes on the outside of your hull only protect the outside. Water that sits inside a void — mostly from condensation — becomes its own electrolyte, and nothing is protecting it. The fix that's working for me is simple: keep it bone dry with bentonite clay desiccant bags, and check them regularly.
Then we loaded up on a rising tide and headed across the bay. Our tides here are huge — at Kilcher Beach the difference between high and low can be half a mile of sticky mud — so timing your loading and unloading matters a lot. We also met a sea otter who did not like my selfie stick, and landed at McDonald Spit, a place with thousands of years of history: Sugpiaq and Aleut summer camps, fox farms, fish traps, and eventually homesteaders like my family.

On the run over to Halibut Cove I gave an update on the engines (about 275 hours in and running flawless), showed off the one-lever throttle, and told the story of the day near Kodiak I got thrown out of a skiff before I'd clipped in my kill cord — and the fishing boat that saved my bacon. Wear the kill cord.

Then we finally found Dad, up in the excavator, storm-proofing the isthmus at Halibut Cove for another season.

It started as another chore on the list. It turned into one of those days that resets your perspective. Thanks for riding along.

tab_title: How to Build a Mason Bee House | Easy Cedar Woodworking Project
description:
Build a practical mason bee house that helps support native pollinators while adding a useful woodworking project to your garden.

Mason bees are gentle, solitary bees and remarkably effective pollinators. Unlike honeybees, they do not live in large colonies or produce honey. Instead, female mason bees lay their eggs inside narrow tubes, separating each egg with a small wall made from mud.

In this video, I explain how my cedar mason bee box works and walk through the important design features, including:

• Removable and cleanable plastic nesting trays
• A sheltered compartment for overwintering mason bee cocoons
• A removable roof held in place with wooden dowels
• Weatherproof glue and stainless-steel fasteners
• Proper mounting in a garden or orchard
• Optional routed edges for a more finished appearance

The box can be built largely from ordinary 1x6 cedar fence-board material, making it an approachable project for a small home woodworking shop. The nesting trays should be purchased before construction so the wooden housing can be fitted accurately around them.

A well-maintained mason bee house can encourage more pollinating activity around fruit trees, berry plants, flowers and vegetable gardens. Since installing ours, we have noticed considerably more mason bee activity and excellent fruit set in our raspberries.

There is one aisle at Walmart where everything comes in a little bag instead of a jar, and most people walk right past it on the way to the spice wall, where the same things cost three and four times as much in glass. Seven dry goods from the Hispanic aisle, every one under $2 at my Walmart this week, what each one is, the ten-minute supper or drink it makes, and the honest comparison to the American shelf, including the two places the Mexican aisle is not cheaper. And the one thing I left off because it was twelve cents over.

📖 My mother's whole way of running a house is written down in one book, The Old Mexican Way: https://oldmexicanway.com

None of this is your fault. Nobody taught you to read a bag with no English on the front.

The 7:
7. Fideo, about 57¢ (the ten-minute sopa de fideo; fry it gold first)
6. Mexican oregano, about $1.48 (not the plant in the jar; a pinch is a pot)
5. Whole cloves, about $1.63 (the bag is the spice, the jar is the furniture)
4. Maizena atole packet, about $1.08 (four mugs of hot breakfast in five minutes)
3. Knorr caldo de pollo, the small jar, about $1.78 (this or the salt shaker, never both)
2. Bay leaves, about $1.25 (a year of pots, and the flour bin)

Said plainly: your store differs. Pour the bag into a jar with a lid, the name folded inside, the month on tape. Out of the light. The clove on a tooth is for the way to the dentist, not instead of it, and never for a child. Not medical advice.

tab_title: Put Hydrogen Peroxide on Your Feet and Watch What Happens (6 Uses Mexican Mothers Swear By)
description:
Fill a basin with warm water tonight. Pour in the brown bottle. Put your feet in, and watch. In about thirty seconds the water starts to fizz around your toes, and that fizz is showing you, honestly, where the trouble is. Your feet are telling on themselves.

And before anybody feels bad about their feet: it is not because you are dirty and it is not because you are lazy. Feet are the part of the body we are told to hide, so we hide them, in shoes, in the dark and the warm and the damp, which is exactly where every one of these problems grows. My mother kept the feet of seven children and a husband in boots with one basin, one brown bottle, one file and a jar of cream. Six uses today.

1. The soak itself: three parts warm water to one part 3% peroxide, 10 to 15 minutes, dry, then the foot file (la lima) on the hard skin, then the cream
2. The smell and pie de atleta: same soak, toes spread, and the step everybody skips, drying between every toe
3. The thick yellow nails: slow, weeks, it helps, and I correct my own "half and half" from the peroxide video, three to one for anything you repeat
4. Cracked heels: soak, file the rim only, cream, old cotton socks overnight. NEVER on an open or bleeding crack
5. Whitening stained nails: a spoon of bicarbonato and peroxide, a thin paste, five minutes, an old toothbrush
6. The shoes. The truth item: the fungus does not live on your foot, it lives in the insole. Spray, sun, once a week, and the tools too

THE FOUR RULES, so nobody gets hurt:
· The 3% brown bottle only. Never the strong one from the beauty supply.
· Never mixed with vinegar in the same basin. Together they make an acid that burns skin.
· Never on an open crack, cut or bleeding heel. Peroxide was never good for cuts.
· Never every day. Once or twice a week, then the cream, always the cream. Peroxide dries the skin.
⚠️ If you have diabetes, numb feet, or poor circulation, do not soak your feet in anything without your doctor saying yes first. I am not a doctor. I am a mother with a basin, and a mother knows when to send you to the doctor. A nail that is painful, lifting or spreading is a doctor, not a basin.
title: Put Hydrogen Peroxide on Your Feet and Watch What Happens (6 Uses Mexican Mothers Swear By)

tab_title: Savory Low-Carb Smoked Pork Butt Roast (No-Sugar BBQ Rub!)
description:
Today we're smoking a delicious, savory Pork Butt Roast on the Masterbuilt cabinet smoker! 

Most traditional BBQ rubs are loaded with brown sugar that can burn easily and add unwanted carbs. This recipe drops the heavy sugars for an herb-forward blend of coarse kosher salt, garlic powder, onion powder, and dried herbs. We also use a hard cider and apple cider vinegar braise to keep the meat juicy, tender, and packed with flavor—making it completely low-carb and keto-friendly!

💬 Have you ever tried smoking a pork roast without sugar in the rub? Let me know in the comments below!

If you enjoyed this video, please LIKE, COMMENT, and SUBSCRIBE to Robinson Homestead for more equipment mods, repairs, and practical homesteading projects!

Step-by-StepRecipe
Step 1: The Rub (Savory & Herb-Forward)
​Skip heavy brown-sugar-loaded rubs (which caramelize and burn more easily in a smoke) and go for a savory, aromatic crust that pairs well with non-sweet finishes.
​Ingredients:
​2 tbsp coarse kosher salt
​1 tbsp freshly cracked black pepper
​1 tbsp garlic powder
​1 tbsp onion powder
​1 tsp smoked paprika (just for color)
​1 tsp dried thyme
​1 tsp dried rosemary (crushed finely)
​Optional binder: A thin coat of yellow mustard or olive oil to help the rub stick.
​Method: Coat the pork shoulder evenly all over. Let it sit at room temperature for 30 minutes while your smoker comes up to temp.
​Step 2: The Smoke
​Temperature: Set your smoker to 225°F to 250°F.
​Wood Choice: Fruitwoods like apple, cherry, or pecan pair exceptionally well with savory herb rubs and avoid the heavy bite of hickory or mesquite.
​The Cook: Smoke the pork shoulder uncovered until it reaches an internal temperature of about 160°F to 175°F and has developed a deep, dark bark (usually around 5 to 6 hours).
​Step 3: The Wrap & Braising Liquid (Where the Magic Happens)
​Instead of just wrapping it in foil dry or with apple juice, use an aromatic braising liquid that will infuse the meat and create a fantastic finishing jus.
​The Wrap: Place the pork shoulder in heavy-duty aluminum foil or a foil pan with a lid.
​The Braising Liquid (Pour this into the foil/pan before sealing):
​1 cup hard apple cider (or unfiltered apple juice)
​1/4 cup apple cider vinegar
​3 cloves of smashed garlic
​1 small onion, sliced thin
​2 sprigs of fresh rosemary or thyme
​Finish the Cook: Seal the foil tightly and put it back in the smoker (or oven) until the internal temperature reaches 203°F and the probe slides in like butter (usually another 2 to 4 hours).
​Step 4: Shredding & The Natural Jus
​Rest the wrapped pork for at least 30 to 45 minutes.
​Carefully open the foil and pull the bone out (if it has one—it should slide right out).
​Shred the meat.
​Make the finishing sauce: Strain the remaining liquid from the foil/pan. Let it sit for a minute so the fat rises to the top, skim off the excess grease, and pour the warm, seasoned apple-herb juices back over the shredded pork.
​This gives you meat that is incredibly juicy, packed with smoky flavor, and dripping with a savory, tangy, aromatic pan-jus instead of heavy, sticky barbecue sauce.

An eggshell is about 95 percent calcium carbonate, the same mineral as limestone, and limestone is what cement is made from. Burned hot, shell becomes lime, the same lime the tabby builders of coastal Georgia made from oyster shells in 1736.

Safety: wear waterproof gloves, safety glasses and an N95 mask with cement, lime and shell dust. Wet cement and lime are caustic; if any gets in your eye, rinse with clean water for 15 minutes and get medical care right away. Quicklime (burned shell) can boil water, burn skin and eyes and start fires: never burn shells in a kitchen oven, and never slake quicklime indoors. Wash your hands after handling raw eggshells. Garden projects only: no foundations, footings, structural walls, chimneys, everyday entry steps or driveways. Keep children and pets away.

Two metals. No electricity. No filter cartridge. No subscription.

The ancient Egyptians knew about this 4,000 years ago. Greek sailors survived months at sea because of it. A piece of copper. A piece of zinc. Twisted together and dropped into contaminated water. Within hours, chlorine is neutralized, heavy metals are trapped, and bacteria are destroyed — silently, chemically, without a single watt of power.

tab_title: Why Do Heat Pumps Exist?
description:
If gas boilers already work, why do heat pumps exist? And why are we suddenly being encouraged to install them in our homes?

The answer has surprisingly little to do with carbon emissions — and a lot more to do with physics, efficiency and the future of home heating.

For hundreds of thousands of years, humans have heated their homes by burning something. 

From wood and coal to oil and modern gas boilers, we've spent centuries finding better ways to generate heat.

But around 170 years ago, something changed.

Scientists discovered that instead of generating heat by burning fuel, we could move heat from one place to another using a fraction of the energy.

And that's exactly what a heat pump does.

While a modern gas boiler typically converts around 85% of the energy in its fuel into useful heat over a heating season, a well-designed heat pump can deliver three, four or even five units of heat for every unit of electricity it consumes.

That's a fundamental shift in how we heat our homes.

And the technology isn't new. It's already in our fridges, freezers, air conditioning systems and even electric cars.

So why are heat pumps becoming such a big part of the conversation now?

In this video, Adam explains:

Why humans have spent thousands of years burning fuel to generate heat
How Lord Kelvin helped establish the science behind heat pump technology
Why moving heat is so much more efficient than generating it
How heat pumps can deliver several times more heat energy than the electricity they consume
Why you've probably been using heat pump technology your entire life without realising it
What's changed to make heat pumps more practical for UK homes
How heat pumps could help homeowners reduce their heating bills
Why government grants are helping make heat pump installations more affordable
How solar panels and batteries can work alongside heat pumps
Why the quality of your heat pump installation matters just as much as the technology itself

Heat pumps aren't a new invention, and gas boilers haven't suddenly stopped working.

We've simply reached a point where moving heat can make more sense than burning fuel to create it.

But there's one important detail: a heat pump is only as good as the heating system it's part of.

Correct system design, suitable radiators, pipework and an experienced installer all play a crucial role in getting the efficiency and comfort you expect.

Because the future of home heating isn't just about choosing a different piece of equipment.

It's about heating our homes more intelligently.

description:
This video explores the surprising story behind one of the oldest and cheapest building materials on Earth. Thousands of years ago people built homes using simple adobe bricks made from clay sand and straw. Some of these houses are still standing today lasting longer than many modern buildings while costing only a few hundred dollars in materials. Even more incredible these thick earthen walls naturally regulate temperature keeping homes cool in summer and warm in winter without heating or air conditioning.

But if adobe works so well why is it difficult or even illegal to build this way in most places today. In this video you will discover the history of how building codes industry interests and financial systems slowly pushed natural construction methods out of the mainstream. The story reveals how a material that once housed entire civilizations became almost impossible to use in modern construction even though the science behind it is simple and proven.

You will also learn how thermal mass works and why thick earthen walls can store heat during the day and release it at night creating a natural temperature balance inside the home. Studies comparing adobe structures with conventional houses show that these buildings can maintain comfortable indoor temperatures with far less energy. In many climates they can even eliminate the need for mechanical cooling entirely. 

The video also explores the people who tried to bring this ancient knowledge back. Architects engineers and builders around the world have demonstrated that earth construction can provide durable affordable housing using materials that already exist beneath our feet. Their work challenges the modern assumption that building a home must require massive loans expensive materials and complex technology.

Finally you will discover the remarkable story of a woman in Texas who found a legal loophole and used it to help hundreds of families build their own adobe homes. These homes cost a fraction of conventional houses require almost no energy to heat or cool and allow families to live without mortgages or energy bills. Her work proves that the knowledge has never disappeared and that people can still build strong comfortable homes using techniques that humanity has known for thousands of years.

🔬 Scientific Facts & Reference Sources:
Oxidizing Action & Decomposition (H₂O₂ ➔ H₂O + O₂):

Mechanism: Hydrogen peroxide produces hydroxyl free radicals that oxidize and break down bacterial cell membranes and extracellular polymeric substances (biofilm). It cleanly breaks down into water and oxygen gas.
Source Reference: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) – Guideline for Disinfection and Sterilization in Healthcare Facilities (Chemical Disinfectants: Hydrogen Peroxide).
Biofilm & Organic Clog Breakdown:

Mechanism: Standard drain sluggishness is frequently driven by bacterial biofilm mixed with soap residue and keratin. The bubbling action mechanically loosens organic matter while oxidizing the slime layer.
Source Reference: National Institutes of Health (NIH / NCBI) – Mechanisms of Biofilm Disruption via Oxidative Agents.
Mineral & Metal Oxidation (Toilet Rings):

Mechanism: Red/orange/brown toilet rings are caused by dissolved iron and manganese oxidation. Peroxide reacts directly with iron compounds, shifting their oxidation state to facilitate dissolution and removal.
Source Reference: U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) – Water Science School: Iron and Manganese in Groundwater.
Mold & Mildew Eradication (Washers & Dishwashers):

Mechanism: 3% topical hydrogen peroxide acts as an effective fungicidal agent against common household mold species (Aspergillus, Cladosporium) without corrosive fumes.
Source Reference: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) – Pesticide Registration & Fungicidal Efficacy of Hydrogen Peroxide Solutions.
⚠️ Important Safety Precautions:
Use Only 3% Concentration: Never use industrial or food-grade 35% peroxide—it causes severe chemical burns.
Never Mix With Bleach: Mixing hydrogen peroxide and chlorine bleach creates rapid oxygen gas release and potential chemical splashing.
Never Mix With Vinegar In The Same Container: Combining peroxide and acetic acid forms peracetic acid, a corrosive substance that irritates the eyes, respiratory tract, and skin.
Storage: Store in its opaque brown bottle in a cool, dark location. Light and heat degrade H₂O₂ into plain water.
Know When to Call a Professional: These tips are strictly preventive maintenance for minor organic issues. Major backups, main sewer line blockages, or collapsed pipes require a licensed plumber.

tab_title: This $150 Tractor Supply Alternator Powers a Whole Cabin All Winter — No Generator, No Grid
description:
�  The Energy Trap — Full Off-Grid Manual:
https://energy-trap-vol1.netlify.app

The Complete Winter Power Library → https://energy-trap-vol1.netlify.app/...

An old farm design: a small engine, a belt, a one-wire tractor alternator and two deep-cycle batteries. Farms made their own power this way before the lines reached them. In this video you see every part with its price, every wire terminal by terminal, and the meter readings that tell you it works.

In this video:
• Why a one-wire tractor alternator (Delco 10SI style, 63 amps, regulator inside) is the simplest alternator ever made
• The one number that decides everything: the speed a one-wire alternator needs before it "wakes up" and starts charging
• What it really runs, in blackout order: refrigerator, freezer, LED lights, box fan, well pump (with a straight yes or no on starting surge)
• The sum, out loud: about 16 hours of a full-size fridge and four LED lights on half of a two-battery bank (an estimate from spec sheets, in mild weather)
• The pulley math: a 5-inch engine pulley, a narrow alternator pulley, and why both must take the same belt
• The direction it turns: why the Predator 212 needs a counterclockwise alternator
• The full wiring: BAT stud, fuses next to every battery post, the negative return on a wooden bench, batteries in parallel, inverter cables and chassis ground
• Is it worth it? The honest comparison against the grid and a store-bought inverter generator
• The full build, step by step: parts list with prices, layout, bolting, belt tension, the meter test and the blackout load test
• The daily winter rhythm: how many engine hours a day, the notebook to keep, and how long food stays safe (USDA)
• Three budgets: under $50, about $200 and about $500+
• From Delco-Light farm plants (1916) and Winchargers to Amish shops today
• What it will NOT run: electric heat, electric stove, water heater, central air
• What it really costs: about $150-$190 for the alternator and close to $700 for the full bench, before wire and fuses

Safety notes:
• Carbon monoxide kills. The engine always runs OUTSIDE, at least 20 feet from doors, windows and vents, never in a garage (even with the door open), shed, barn or enclosed porch. Put a battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm in your home and test it.
• Store gasoline in an approved can outside, away from the cabin and from a hot engine. Never refuel a running or hot engine.
• Never connect batteries or an inverter to your home's electrical panel yourself. House circuits need a transfer switch installed by a licensed electrician. Never use a cord with two male ends: it backfeeds the grid and can kill utility line workers.
• Fuse every positive cable close to its battery post, sized to protect the cable. Follow your inverter's manual for fuse size and chassis grounding.
• Lead-acid batteries give off hydrogen while charging: vented box, no sparks or flames, eye protection. Most lithium batteries must not be charged below freezing.
• A running belt and pulleys can injure in a second. Guard the belt before starting, set tension with the engine off, and keep children and grandchildren away.
• If you rely on a medical device, check its power needs with your supplier and test before you need it.
• This is a homemade build, not a certified design. Runtimes and charging times are estimates from spec sheets, not measurements of this bench. Measure your own setup before you rely on it.

Get the full written record here: https://energy-trap-vol1.netlify.app/...

The presenter in this video is a digital presenter. Prices were checked in October 2026 and change by store and season. Not affiliated with Tractor Supply, Harbor Freight, Predator, Renogy, Walmart, EverStart, Delco Remy or DB Electrical.

tab_title: This $60 AutoZone Alternator Powers a Whole Cabin All Winter — No Generator, No Grid
description:
📘 Get The Alternator Power Manual: https://manual.eliyodersecrets.com
(Read chapter 1 free before you buy) 

https://energy-trap-vol1.netlify.app

   • This $15 Sand Battery Heats Any Cabin All ...  


Before World War Two, American families powered entire homes with spinning generators and battery banks in the cellar. A sixty-dollar alternator from AutoZone can do it today. A retired rancher in Holmes County, Ohio does exactly that — lights, freezer, well pump, and furnace blower all running through winter on battery power alone. No grid connection. No generator noise. None of it is new. All of it disappeared after 1945, not because it stopped working, but because utility companies decided you should be a customer instead of a producer.

A standard automotive alternator produces over a thousand watts of raw electrical power. The auto industry builds them by the tens of millions, which is precisely why they cost fifty to eighty dollars instead of three or four hundred. You're riding on an economy of scale designed by accident to hand you the cheapest reliable generator ever built.

The history gets uncomfortable fast. In 1916, Delco-Light plants were installed in hundreds of thousands of American farmhouses. By the 1920s, rural children did homework under electric lights a full decade before city kids saw their first power lines. Farm families wired for thirty-two volts, bought thirty-two-volt refrigerators and washing machines, lived completely independent — and then the system vanished from public memory.

Here's exactly how it works, what the numbers actually mean, and why this forgotten piece of American ingenuity changes everything about how you think about that alternator sitting in your engine bay.

There was no need to send a sample of water off to a lab like a lot of reviewers do on YT.  Funny how so many do this. That doesn't come close to what an authorized certifier, like IAPMO, does when testing and certifying a filter to NSF standards. See below:

Standard 42 (Aesthetic Effects): Says that the filter reduces non health related contaminants such as chlorine, taste, odor and particulates.   Actual NSF Certificate:  https://myplc.iapmo.org/certificate#/...

Standard 53 (Health Effects): Says that the filter reduces specific health related contaminants that cause illness , such as lead, VOC.s, asbestos, and cysts.  Actual NSF Certificate:  https://myplc.iapmo.org/certificate#/...

Standard 58 (Reverse Osmosis): This is for Reverse Osmosis (RO) systems for the reduction of total dissolved solids TDS, arsenic, lead and nitrates. Actual NSF Certificate:  https://myplc.iapmo.org/certificate#/...

Standard 372 (Material Safety/Lead-Free): Verified that the plumbing materials and components in contact with drinking water contain no more that .25% lead by weight. 
Actual NSF Certificate:  https://myplc.iapmo.org/certificate#/...

Standard 401 (Emerging Contaminants): Says the filter reduces emerging compounds and incidental contaminants not yet fully regulated by the EPS such as Pharmaceuticals, prescription drugs, herbicides and BPA. Actual NSF Certificate: https://myplc.iapmo.org/certificate#/...

description:
Can a portable power station under $500 keep your refrigerator running through a power outage—and still make your morning coffee? I put the GEYOTO N1000 through real-world home backup power tests to find out.

In this GEYOTO N1000 review, I test refrigerator battery backup, run multiple devices together, and push its 1800W inverter with a toaster oven. I also briefly showcase the smaller GEYOTO N300 for portable charging, camping, travel, and everyday use.

▶ GEYOTO N1000 — specifications and current pricing:
https://visionstarmkt.com/LZRIMPDZ

Prices and promotions can change. The under-$500 pricing discussed in this video reflects the price at the time of filming.

REAL-WORLD REFRIGERATOR BACKUP TEST

The N1000 powered my full-size inverter refrigerator overnight. After 11 hours and 49 minutes, the power station still showed 32% battery remaining. Based on that battery usage, I estimated roughly 17 hours of total refrigerator runtime.

That is an estimated total—not a completed run-to-empty result. Your refrigerator’s energy consumption, room temperature, settings, and how often you open the doors will affect runtime. Adding other devices also uses battery capacity.

But keeping the fridge running is only part of the story. During an actual blackout, you may also want to charge your phone, use a tablet, or make a cup of coffee. So I tested the N1000 with several loads running together:

• Refrigerator + coffee maker + iPad charging
• Refrigerator + toaster oven + iPad charging
• A displayed combined load of approximately 1,832W during the toaster oven demonstration
• Switching from wall power to battery power while the refrigerator was running

These tests show what this portable battery backup system handled in my setup, including brief high-power kitchen appliance use while keeping the refrigerator connected.

GEYOTO N1000 FEATURES COVERED

• 1024Wh LiFePO4 battery capacity
• 1800W pure sine wave AC inverter
• Four AC outlets
• Four USB-C ports, including two rated up to 140W
• Two USB-A ports and a 12V car outlet
• Adjustable magnetic wireless phone charging pad
• Built-in LED light and recessed carry handles
• Fast and slow AC charging selected directly on the unit
• Solar and vehicle charging connections
• Pass-through power and battery backup operation

I demonstrate AC charging in this video and show the solar charging connections. Solar charging performance is not tested here.

N1000 VS. N300: DIFFERENT JOBS, DIFFERENT SIZES

I also show why I enjoy using the smaller GEYOTO N300. With its 256Wh battery and 300W AC inverter, it is a convenient option for charging phones, tablets, and laptops, powering a small lamp, and bringing portable power to a campsite, vacation rental, or desk.

You’ll see the N300 charging my MacBook while the N1000 handles the larger household loads. This is primarily an N1000 review, with a brief N300 comparison and demonstration.

AFFORDABLE BACKUP POWER FOR ESSENTIALS

If you’re researching a portable power station for refrigerator backup, a battery generator for power outages, or a solar-compatible emergency power system, this video shows a practical approach to keeping essential devices running.

A battery power station lets you power connected appliances indoors without gasoline, exhaust, or engine maintenance. Battery capacity determines how long your devices can run, while inverter output determines which appliances it can handle.

For emergency preparedness, short blackouts, overnight refrigerator backup, camping, and portable charging, choosing a system starts with understanding what you actually need to power.

description:
Part 3 of my DIY geothermal AC project is finally here.

In this video, I take a free *14,000 BTU LG Dual Inverter window air conditioner* that I pulled out of a dumpster and turn it into a homemade ground-source cooling system.

Catch up on the video series here.
Part 1 -       • DIY Geothermal Gives Me FREE Air Condition...  
Part 2 -       • Will my DIY geothermal AC system work?

▶️ Full DIY Geothermal Playlist:      • DIY Geothermal Gives Me FREE Air Condition...  

I cleaned the unit up, removed the condenser fan, rotated the condenser without opening the refrigerant circuit, built a water jacket around it, and tied it into my 2,000 feet of buried PEX ground loop.

The idea is simple: instead of dumping heat into hot outside air, the AC rejects that heat into circulating ground-loop water.

By the end of the test, I was seeing  very cold air making it upstairs into the main living space.

This project has changed a lot since the beginning, and a big part of that has come from your comments, suggestions, questions, and ideas. Thank you to everyone who has followed along and helped me improve the system.

tab_title: Zombie Outbreak Ep.6: Day 501 - Noor's Final Hours
description:
Zombie Outbreak Ep.6: Noor's Final Hours. It's 9 at night, you're holding Noor's bitten hand, and the dead are 300 yards out, walking in. Noor is the nurse who's kept you alive for 500 days, and nothing in the freezer matches her blood. Lena pulls her off the line and gives her fourteen hours.

Eleven doses sit in the freezer, all type O, and type O plasma can attack Noor's type A blood. Then a voice answers on the radio: a bitten woman at a grain elevator nine miles east. 100 of the dead stand between you and her, so Ravi floors it, drives straight through them, picks up Ada and her sister Ruth, and drives back through them again.

This survival story runs on real science. You'll learn why you wash a bite for 15 minutes, what low titer type O blood is, how thinning plasma to half, a quarter, then an eighth measures its antibodies, why type A B plasma can go to anyone, why whole blood is spun down to plasma first, the warning signs of a reaction to even the weakest bag, and why a siren loses about 6 decibels every time the distance doubles.

Tell us in the comments: would you have waited for Ada's blood, or taken the weakest bag like Noor?

CHAPTERS
0:00 Day 501: Fourteen Hours
0:29 Kill The Near Bell
0:53 The Fence Bows
1:11 Eleven Doses, All Type O
1:47 Low Titer
2:08 The Slide Test
2:29 A Voice On The Radio
3:11 The Weakest Bag
3:52 Out The Back Gate
4:22 Through 100 At The Crossroads
4:50 The Grain Elevator
5:09 Type A B
5:36 One Pint
6:07 Ada And Ruth Come Too
6:18 Noor's Blood Breaks
6:52 Through Them Again
7:13 Spin The Pint
7:46 Hour 14

WHAT IS REAL IN THIS STORY
• After a bite, wash the wound with soap and water for at least 15 minutes. It cleans the wound; it cures nothing.
https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sh...
• Low titer type O whole blood has weak anti A and anti B antibodies and is given in major bleeding before the patient's type is known.
https://profedu.blood.ca/en/transfusi...
• Antibody strength (titer) is measured by thinning plasma to half strength, then a quarter, then an eighth and on, until red cells stop clumping. Labs set their own cutoff.
https://nhsbtdbe.blob.core.windows.ne...
• Type O plasma carries antibodies that attack type A cells. Type A B plasma carries neither, so it can go to any blood type. About 4 in 100 Americans are type A B.
https://www.lifeblood.com.au/health-p...
https://www.redcrossblood.org/donate-...
• Blood type comes from both parents, so two sisters can have different types.
https://www.redcrossblood.org/donate-...
• A whole blood donation is about a pint and takes about 10 minutes. A little over half of it, about 55 percent, is plasma.
https://www.redcrossblood.org/donate-...
https://www.redcrossblood.org/donate-...
• Spin a bag of whole blood in a centrifuge and the red cells pack to the bottom while the straw colored plasma rises on top, so the plasma can be drawn off.
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles...
• Frozen plasma is thawed at about body temperature; too much heat damages its proteins.
https://www.jpac.org.uk/guidelines/re...
• Chills, back pain, fever and dark urine are warning signs of a hemolytic transfusion reaction.
https://www.lifeblood.com.au/health-p...
• For people with diabetes, being sick can push blood sugar up even when they aren't eating.
https://www.cdc.gov/diabetes/living-w...
• In open air, sound from a point source drops about 6 decibels each time the distance doubles.
https://www.osha.gov/otm/section-3-he...
• A full freezer with the door kept shut holds its temperature for about 48 hours in a power outage.
https://www.fda.gov/food/buy-store-se...

This is a fictional animated story. The zombies and the cure are made up; the survival science is real. Never try a blood test or a transfusion outside a hospital.

description:
STOP spending $10,000 on expensive home battery systems before you discover this forgotten energy storage technology! What if ordinary bricks could store massive amounts of heat and release it hours later, without lithium batteries or complicated electronics?

While modern home energy systems rely on expensive lithium-ion batteries, an older technology uses something surprisingly simple: BRICKS.

It's called thermal energy storage, and the science behind it has been around for generations. By heating specially designed bricks or other thermal storage materials, energy can be stored as heat and released gradually when needed.

In this video, we explore how brick-based thermal batteries work, why high-temperature materials can store useful amounts of thermal energy, and how this technology compares with modern home battery systems like the Tesla Powerwall.

You'll discover how thermal mass absorbs heat, why insulation matters, how stored heat can be released over time, and why engineers are exploring thermal batteries as an alternative for certain heating applications.

But here's the surprising part: unlike lithium batteries, brick-based systems don't need to store energy through chemical reactions. Instead, they rely on the ability of solid materials to absorb and retain heat.

Could this century-old concept help reduce heating costs during winter? And why are researchers and companies bringing thermal storage technology back into the spotlight?

Watch until the end to discover the science, potential benefits, costs, and limitations of storing energy in ordinary-looking bricks.

How old brick thermal storage technology works

Storing energy without lithium batteries
How bricks absorb and release heat
Thermal mass and heat retention
Modern applications of ancient heating principles

tab_title: Better Than Honey. Produces For 60 Years. Grows On A Bush — Why Don't You Know It?
description:
Better Than Honey. Produces For 60 Years. Grows On A Bush — Why Don't You Know It?

#Jujube #HoneyDate #FoodIndependence #Permaculture #ForgottenFruit #GrowYourOwn

There is a fruit so sweet that when it dries on the branch, it tastes like honey caramel.

Not from a hive.
Not from a bee.
Not from a $600 startup kit.

It grows on a bush.

In dirt.
In heat.
In neglect.

It’s called the Ziziphus jujuba — known across Asia for over 5,000 years as the “honey date.”

And in most of America, almost nobody knows it exists.

🍯 WHAT MAKES IT DIFFERENT?

When fully dried on the tree, jujube fruit:

• Concentrates its sugars naturally
• Develops a dense, chewy, caramel-honey flavor
• Stores for months without refrigeration
• Requires zero chemical spraying in most U.S. climates
• Survives extreme heat and drought

Fresh jujube tastes like a crisp apple.
Dried jujube tastes like honeyed caramel dates.

Two completely different experiences — same fruit.

🌱 WHAT THE JUJUBE ACTUALLY DOES

Let’s be clear:

Jujube is not a perfect honey substitute in every kitchen use.
It does not pour like liquid honey.
It must be dried or processed for maximum sweetness.

But it offers something rare:

• Long-lived perennial production (often decades)
• Minimal pest pressure in North America
• Strong drought tolerance
• High natural sugar concentration
• Documented traditional medicinal use

Research has identified bioactive compounds in jujube studied for:

• Sleep support
• Immune modulation
• Antioxidant activity

(Links to research discussed in the video.)

🌞 GROWING BASICS

Best in USDA zones 6–10
Needs full sun and long hot summers
Benefits from planting two varieties for cross-pollination
Extremely drought tolerant once established

Popular varieties for U.S. growers:

• Li
• Lang

Fruit begins in 2–3 years.
Full production typically in 4–7 years depending on climate.

⚖️ THIS VIDEO IS NOT ANTI-BEE

Bees are essential pollinators.
Honey has antimicrobial and culinary value.
This is not about replacing beekeeping.

It’s about expanding food resilience.

About knowing your options.

About planting something permanent.

Frank Meyer believed this fruit could transform American agriculture.

Over a century later, the trees are still here.

Still fruiting.

Still waiting.

If this story matters to you, subscribe and share it with someone who believes food independence starts with planting.

Next episode drops soon. 🌳🍯
title: Better Than Honey. Produces For 60 Years. Grows On A Bush — Why Don't You Know It?

The Twelve Dollar Antenna That Cools a Room Without a Compressor, a Refrigerant, or a Permit

What if the technology to cool your home already existed, sitting quietly in the public record for over a century, blocked from your walls not by physics but by paperwork? In this investigation, we walk from a modest workshop in eighteen thirty four Paris, to a wooden laboratory outside Colorado Springs in nineteen oh one, into a Raytheon lab in nineteen sixty four, and finally onto a workbench where a twelve dollar antenna and a forty dollar chip pull ambient radio frequency energy out of thin air and turn it into measurable cooling. We trace the forgotten discoveries, the buried patents, the modern validations, and the specific regulatory mechanisms that keep this technology out of American homes. Names, dates, patents, and measurements. Nothing invented. Everything recovered.

The science rests on two pillars that never met in the mainstream. The first is the thermoelectric effect discovered by Jean Charles Athanase Peltier in eighteen thirty four, where direct current passing across a junction of dissimilar semiconductors moves heat from one face to the other with no moving parts and no working fluid. The second is radio frequency energy harvesting, the practice of capturing ambient electromagnetic waves from cellular, Wi-Fi, and broadcast sources through a rectifying antenna, or rectenna, and converting them into usable direct current. Modern bismuth telluride modules and inkjet printed rectennas have closed the efficiency gap that stood open for more than a century. The physics is settled. The engineering is documented. The application is what has been withheld.

Beneath your home lies a temperature that never changes. Summer heat waves and winter freezes mean nothing six feet underground where the earth holds steady at fifty five degrees year round. They stored ice through desert summers and maintained comfortable temperatures in brutal heat using nothing but buried passages and patient engineering. Ground temperature stability results from thermal mass and the slow rate of heat transfer through soil. tab_title: The $600 Tank That Beats a $10,000 Powerwall
description:

What if you could store more usable energy for your home without spending $10,000 on a lithium battery?

In this video, we explore underground thermal energy storage — a simple system that uses a large insulated water tank to store heat for later use. Instead of storing electricity in expensive batteries, the idea is to store the energy your home actually needs for heating and hot water.

We break down how a $600–$2,000 thermal storage system can work, how much energy a 1,000-gallon tank can theoretically store, why water is such an effective thermal battery, and how insulation and thermal stratification help keep that heat available.

We'll also look at real-world examples of seasonal thermal energy storage, including the Drake Landing Solar Community in Alberta, and explain how similar principles can be adapted for individual homes.

In this video you'll learn:

How underground thermal energy storage works
• Why water can store huge amounts of thermal energy
• How thermal storage compares with lithium battery storage
• How solar thermal collectors can charge a storage tank
• Why insulation is critical
• How thermal stratification improves performance
• Where this system makes the most sense
• The major limitations you need to understand
• What a basic system could potentially cost
Important: Thermal energy is not the same as electrical energy. A thermal storage tank cannot replace a Powerwall for running appliances, electronics, or other electrical loads. Its advantage is storing heat for space heating and hot water.
The goal of this video isn't to tell you that batteries are useless. It's to ask a different question:
Are we spending thousands of dollars storing electricity when a large part of our home's energy demand is actually heat?

description:
The skills that kept families alive before the grid existed are disappearing faster than anyone is writing them down. Fire, food, water, shelter, weather, medicine — Lost Survival Knowledge digs up how our great-grandparents actually handled it, and why those methods worked.

💬 Did your own family pass any of this down? Tell us in the comments — the best ones end up in future episodes.

Subscribe to Lost Survival Knowledge and take back the practical genius our great-grandparents took for granted. 🪓🔥 👉   / @lostsurvivalknowledge  

Lost Survival Knowledge — Creative Process Disclosure
Our Mission: Lost Survival Knowledge exists to document and teach the self-reliance skills of early American homesteads, trail camps, and backcountry farms. What a settler family knew about food, fire, shelter, water, and weather wasn't trivia — it was the difference between a hard winter and a fatal one. We treat that knowledge as something worth keeping alive, not just remembering.

Research & Writing: Every episode begins with source work, not a search bar. Our videos are built from period manuals, farm and homestead ledgers, county histories, agricultural bulletins, patent records, and firsthand accounts from the 1700s and 1800s. Scripts are 100% original to this channel, and we aim past the surface-level "life hack" version of history to explain why a method worked, what it cost the people using it, and why it fell out of use.

Visual Production: Each video is assembled by hand. We source and license archival photography and footage, then restore it — repairing damage, stabilizing motion, and color-grading period imagery for modern screens. Editing is done in professional suites, with original motion graphics built to show how a technique actually functioned step by step, and a documentary pacing meant to hold you for the whole runtime.

Narration: Every episode is narrated by Joe, recorded for this channel. No synthetic, cloned, or AI-generated voices are used anywhere on Lost Survival Knowledge — a real human read is what carries the weight of these stories, and the commentary and delivery are his throughout.

tab_title: Don’t Buy an Air Purifier Before Watching This
description:
This is the top-of-market option I actually trust - JASPR has the metrics that matter, none of the wifi & other nonsense, just serious filtration 👉 Code 'HEALTHYHOMES' for $400 off jaspr.co/healthyhomes

--- --- --- --- --- 

Is your air purifier secretly failing you, even if it was top-of-the-line? 

After owning more than ten different models, I've learned that the most expensive mistake isn't choosing the wrong brand, but falling for one critical assumption about how they clean your home's air. 

So this isn't just about decoding specs like H13 HEPA or the right CADR for your rooms – though I'll explain why these are non-negotiable if you want to actually trap those invisible lung irritants. 

It's about the strategy that ensures the air in your most vital spaces, like your bedroom, truly gets purified. I'm sharing what I wish I'd known years ago to save you from the frustration of a noisy, ineffective machine, the shock of hidden filter costs, and help you finally achieve that peace of mind that comes with genuinely cleaner air.

--- --- --- --- --- 

These are the air purifiers I would actually consider buying, I've used and trust.

1) Top of the market option is JASPR - commercial-grade power, shows you real-time air quality, lifetime warranty. This is what's in my living room. It's expensive at $1,199 but genuinely 3x more powerful than anything else I've tested (CADR 614 vs most units at 200-300). 

But I also got them to give me a code so use 'HEALTHYHOMES' for 20% off → jaspr.co/healthyhomes

Now, JASPR is honestly overkill unless you have serious allergies, deal with wildfire smoke, or just want the absolute best. 

For everyone else, here are the other purifier brands I've used & recommend this strategy: start with an entry-level unit like Levoit (or go for Winix) to build confidence in the products and then if/when you hit frustrations then just level up from there

2) Entry & budget: Levoit — We had the Core 300, it's a great budget option. Our first purifier. But it developed a metallic whirr. Also, take the filter out of plastic first, tiktok is full of people buying one & never removing the plastic. There's also a model called Levoit HEPA I think that I've heard good things about. They're all generally decent entry options, but they're not the most powerful ones. And I don't like the wifi and all the bells & whistles.

3) Good middle ground: Winix — Winix 5500-2 is great, you can switch off the ionizer, but not as effective ultimately as some of the more upscale ones, and I don't like that the filters are separate I always forget to change the carbon filters.

4) More upscale: Coway — Only problem I've had is with both the Airmega 150s where they created this vibration that we had to stick lambskins underneath it. The 250 that we have is also decent but sometimes makes a noise until I slightly shake it and then it stops. Otherwise great! If I had the budget and went for a Coway I'd take the Storm. 

5) Bonus wildcard: Ikea — Never used it but people in the comment section of a viral video we had on TikTok were raving about it and constantly bringing it up. But honestly, still, I'm not sure. But others say it's great for $60.

tab_title: MIT Just Confirmed This $0 Fog Fence Pulls Gallons of Water From Morning Air Daily.Why Is It Banned?
description:
A mesh fence the size of a kitchen table produces seventeen gallons of clean drinking water every morning — and the American building code still pretends it doesn't exist.
On a mountain in southern Morocco, a community of women fills water jugs every morning from a mesh panel stretched between two steel poles. No pump. No filter. No electricity. No bill. This video traces the full story: from a UC California research ridgeline where a reporter watched fog turn into clean water in real time, to a seventy-year suppression written into state constitutions, water rights law, and building code committees stacked with industry representatives. The technology works. The numbers are verified. And by the end you will know exactly how to build one yourself for under a hundred and fifty dollars.
The Science
Fog is not humidity. It is liquid water already suspended in the air as droplets typically five to forty microns in diameter — already past the phase change that makes conventional water collection energy-intensive. Wind pushes those droplets into a vertical mesh. The fibers intercept them, surface tension causes them to merge into larger drops, and gravity pulls them into a gutter below. No electricity. No pumping. No treatment. In 2013, MIT researchers demonstrated that by optimizing mesh openness, fiber diameter, and surface coating simultaneously, fog collection efficiency increases by five hundred percent over standard passive mesh. A 2018 follow-up showed that standard passive mesh captures only one to three percent of passing droplets — meaning the gap between current performance and theoretical maximum is still enormous, and largely unexplored in residential building science.

tab_title: This $500 Tower Makes 25 Gallons From Air Daily. Why Is It Banned in the U.S.?
description:
A $500 Bamboo Tower Pulls Drinking Water From Thin Air — And They Don't Want You To Build One

There are three quadrillion gallons of freshwater floating above your head right now. A desert beetle cracked the code to harvesting it millions of years ago. An Italian architect turned that code into a thirty-foot bamboo tower that produces up to twenty-five gallons of clean drinking water per day — no electricity, no pipes, no permits. It costs less than a weekend grocery run. Ancient civilizations on every continent built versions of this technology for thousands of years. Then the modern world buried it. This video breaks down exactly how it works, why building codes and water rights laws block it, who profits from your dependence on centralized water systems, and how you can build one yourself.

The science is deceptively simple. When air cools below its dew point, water vapor condenses on any available surface. The Namib Desert beetle exploits this principle using a shell covered in hydrophilic bumps and hydrophobic channels that collect fog and funnel droplets directly into its mouth. Researchers at MIT replicated this surface geometry on synthetic materials and found condensation efficiency increased by up to forty percent. Fog collectors in peer-reviewed field studies yield three to ten liters per square meter of mesh per day. Dew collectors add another fraction overnight. The Warka Water Tower combines these principles into a passive vertical structure using polyester mesh with eighty square meters of condensation surface. University testing confirmed it collects rain, fog, and dew simultaneously. The water meets WHO guidelines for safe drinking in unpolluted environments.

What if the power grid failed tomorrow? Would your home still have the basics needed to get through the first few days?

Japan has developed a strong culture of household disaster preparedness, and official Japanese guidance recommends keeping essential supplies ready before electricity, water, gas, or other infrastructure is disrupted. Tokyo's current stockpiling guidance recommends maintaining household supplies for several days, while other Japanese disaster-preparedness guidance recommends preparing for at least three days and, when possible, about a week.

Japan's Cabinet Office specifically advises households to prepare for situations where refrigerators, microwaves, air conditioning, heating, water pumps, and other electrically powered systems may stop working.

Tokyo's preparedness guidance also recommends maintaining several days of food and supplies, while Tokyo Electric Power highlights flashlights, radios, backup batteries, emergency bags, food, and water as useful preparations for extended outages.

The bigger lesson is simple: you don't need a bunker or an expensive generator to begin preparing. A few carefully chosen essentials, stored before an emergency, can make a major difference when normal services suddenly disappear.

description:
How we've heated our house on 1 cord a year for the last 34 years: Tips and tricks for burning firewood in a fireplace or wood stove to efficiently heat your house. If you cut your own wood it's a cheap way to heat.  But it's important to burn a CLEAN EFFICIENT FIRE, for more heat and less pollution.  Burning wood creates 400 times more fine particle air pollution than oil or gas.

If you have a wood stove with a metal stovepipe, using a Heat Reclaimer can increase your heat output by 30%, such as this: https://amzn.to/3adjgTA
This lower cost Heat Reclaimer is best used with a fan: https://amzn.to/3bpcsSY 

The glass doors I found on Amazon are NOT air tight, and say to leave the doors open when burning the fire, which defeats the purpose if you want to heat your house.  You might be able to find air tight glass doors at a fireplace shop, or have them custom made, but if you can afford to buy and install it, an insert is much better.

A certified wood burning fireplace insert is more efficient than glass doors.
You'll also need a chimney liner kit which comes in many sizes:  https://amzn.to/31Lapo6
Measure your fireplace opening width, height and depth, and be sure to order an insert that will fit. 

Our house came with an open fireplace. For $300 in the 1980's we had custom airtight Pyrex glass doors made, greatly increasing the heat output. Plus we added double mylar to the windows in our house, which made a huge difference.
Video includes:  Creating an outside air intake directly into the firebox,  drying firewood,  lighting a fire,  keeping it burning well, keeping smoke out of your house when you open the doors, and using fans to extract heat and circulate it into the house.

5. Osage orange, the heaviest firewood in North America, and the rules for burning it.

Harlan Sawyer. Sawyer Ridge, Pocahontas County, West Virginia. Forty-two years in the timber, 1969 to
2011. Heft the split. The tree is lying.

Stack it dry, friend. It keeps.

A note before anybody writes in: every heat number here assumes seasoned wood; burn at 20 percent
moisture or less on a fresh split face (EPA Burn Wise). Osage orange, black locust and mulberry throw
sparks: never burn them in an open fireplace without a screen, and keep the stove door shut. Dense woods
can overfire an older stove: mix one dense split in three and use a stovepipe thermometer. Trees over a
roof or near power lines are a job for a professional. Have your chimney inspected every year (CSIA).
title: 5 Woods That Burn Longer Than Oak. Number 2 Is Probably Growing in Your Yard.

tab_title: 5 Woodpile Dangers That Can Put You in the Hospital. Number 3 Grows on Half of America's Firewood
description:
Tomorrow morning you'll carry an armload in with your gloves still in your back pocket. There are
five things in an ordinary American woodpile that put people in hospital beds every winter, and
four of them you can find in ninety seconds with a flashlight.

In 1977 my saw partner Manny cleared a fence line, piled the vines with the deadwood, and burned
it. He stood in that smoke about twenty minutes. Two days later they took him to Elkins with his
face swollen shut and his throat closing. He never touched a leaf.

I'm Harlan Sawyer. Forty-two years in the timber, 1969 to 2011.

The five:
pressure treated lumber and how to spot it by the rows of slits (arsenic until the end of 2003) -
what lives in the bottom two rows, and the eight-dollar fix - the hairy vine, which is poison ivy
on a dead log, still active for years, and what burning it does to your throat - the white bloom
on wood stored indoors - and the ash bucket, which isn't in the pile at all, and is the one the
fire departments write up every January.

Number three is on about half the cords I've split in the last ten years, on my own ridge, on
trees I cut myself. You cannot see it once the bark is off.

Tell me your state and whether you've ever found a hairy vine on your own firewood. I think most
of us have burned one without knowing.

Stack it dry, friend. It keeps.

Sources mentioned: EPA (never burn treated, painted or stained wood; CCA removed from residential
use at the end of 2003), CDC (never burn poison ivy; urushiol stays active on dead wood for
years). Ash: metal can with a metal lid, outdoors on dirt or concrete, four days minimum, and a
carbon monoxide detector in the sleeping hall. I'm not a doctor. A darkening bite, a reaction to
smoke, or a chest that won't clear is a doctor's business, not mine.

tab_title: How Gravity Fed Pellet Stoves Work (Designing a DIY/wiseway) (Easy Woodstove to pellet conversion)
description:
For several years now I've been heating my house with a DIY gravity fed pellet stove made out of a woodstove. The only part thats different is the door so it can be easily converted back. Here I explain the concept behind gravity fed pellet stoves and their short comings.
How do they work? 
Basically the hopper feeds into a angled shoot. At the bottom of the shoot is a wire mesh basket that holds the pellets as they burn. when the embers and ash are soft enough they fall through the baskets mesh and fresh pellets slide down into the basket due to gravity and the cycle repeats, the fire doesn't go up the feed tube because air comes from a separate tube and meets the pellets on a angled burner plate. After hours of running a ridge of ash can form right on top of the burner plate. this can start to obstruct the pellets, so it needs cleaning occasionally.

Thanks for watching, like and subscribe and make sure to check out my other videos on this project:

description:
👇 Get the 3-book bundle here 👇
eliforgottenways.com

Why Did We Stop Using Ammonia To Cool Our Homes?

Before electricity reached most American farms, a simple device cooled food using nothing but the heat of a small flame. No compressor, no motor, no monthly power bill. It worked beautifully for decades, and in some cases it is still working today. So why did it vanish from our homes almost entirely? That is the question this video sets out to answer, and the answer has very little to do with science.

This is the story of absorption refrigeration, of the Crosley Icyball, the silent gas-powered Servel refrigerator, and the patents that Albert Einstein and Leó Szilárd filed in 1930 trying to build a cooling machine with nothing inside to break. It is also the story of how a synthetic chemical called Freon, owned by a partnership between General Motors and DuPont, quietly outspent and out-marketed a technology that nature made freely available to everyone.

Understanding this history means understanding something most people never learn: that heat can move a refrigerant just as well as an electric motor can, and that a machine with no moving parts can outlive the person who bought it. The physics never changed. What changed was who stood to profit, and how much they were willing to spend to make sure you never thought about the alternative.

tab_title: Why Did America Rip Out the Only Furnace That Works Without Electricity? (It's Not What You Think)
description:
Picture a freezing January night a century ago: a severe winter storm knocks out the local power lines, yet inside the house, every room remains comfortably warm. That home relied on a heating system that did not care whether the electrical grid was alive: the gravity furnace, affectionately known as "the octopus." With its massive central body and sprawling sheet-metal arms stretching across the basement ceiling, this marvel of passive engineering heated entire houses without a single motor, blower fan, or circuit board. Today, nearly all of them have vanished from American basements—and the real reason why has almost nothing to do with danger or mechanical failure.

Operating strictly on natural thermodynamics, the gravity furnace worked because warm air expands, becomes less dense, and naturally rises up through wide ducts while cooler air sinks back down to be reheated. However, this non-electric independence came with honest trade-offs. Early models required shoveling coal and hauling out ash pits, their ductwork was heavily insulated with asbestos, and their gentle airflow sent roughly half their heat straight up the chimney, resulting in an efficiency rating near fifty percent. As heating fuels grew expensive, the high operating costs became difficult to defend.

Yet the disappearance of the octopus was also accelerated by high-pressure sales tactics and a fundamental shift in American comfort. In the 1950s, door-to-door salesmen from the infamous Holland Furnace Company dismantled functioning basement furnaces under the guise of safety inspections, falsely condemning units to coerce homeowners into buying modern replacements—a predatory scheme that eventually landed the company's CEO in prison for contempt of court. But the ultimate blow came from the opposite season: the rise of central air conditioning. Because cold air sinks and cannot rise through gravity ducts, homes needed powered blower fans to cool rooms in July. Once houses installed ductwork and fans for summer AC, it made economic sense to push winter heat through that very same fan, leaving the electricity-free octopus behind.

This video explores the history, thermodynamics, hidden sales controversies, and modern emergency heating lessons of the gravity furnace—and why a machine that could heat a house through a total blackout was ultimately defeated by summer cooling.

If you love exploring forgotten technology, historic homes, and vintage engineering, please like the video and subscribe for more deep dives into how our world used to work! This documentary explains the whole-house fan — the giant ceiling fan that cooled American homes for pennies a night before air conditioning — why it disappeared from our ceilings, exactly where it still beats the AC today (and where it fails), and the $30 box-fan version 1950s handbooks taught, which anyone can test in one evening.

A whole-house fan doesn't make cold air. It waits for evening, then swaps every cubic foot of air in the house for cooler outdoor air every three to four minutes, using a few hundred watts instead of an air conditioner's thousands. In dry-summer and cool-night regions it can replace most AC run-time; in the humid Gulf South it genuinely doesn't work — this video gives the honest climate map, the real installed prices, and the one safety rule (windows open first — negative pressure can backdraft gas appliances) that every sponsored video skips.

What's covered:

Why your AC bill is so high — the 3,500-watt compressor vs the 300–700-watt fan, at typical mid-2026 electric rates.

How the whole-house fan works: the 3–4 minute full-house air exchange, and why it flushes the 140°F attic on the way out.

The history: cupola cooling at Mount Vernon, the 1930s–1950s golden age when almost every block had one, and the sound of summer a generation remembers.

Why America ripped them out: cheap window AC, sealed-house energy codes, and the plain margin economics of a $12,000 system quote vs a $400 fan — incentives, not conspiracy.

The honest climate map: where whole-house fans win (dry West, mountain states, high plains, cool-night Midwest and North) and where they lose (Gulf South humidity, 90°+ desert nights) — answering the #1 objection in every fan video's comments.

The real limits: negative pressure, combustion backdrafting and radon, pollen season, security, noise, and true running cost.

The $30 fix: the 1950s box-fan whole-house method — exhaust high on the hot side, one shaded intake window, dusk-to-bedtime — proven in a 1.2-million-view modern test.

The evening ritual: open and run at dusk, seal and shade at morning, and the hybrid pattern that lets the fan do the cheap 90% while the AC only touches up.

Honest prices: ~$30 box-fan test; ~$250–$450 installed for a basic modern whole-house fan at typical mid-2026 prices; quiet insulated-door models higher.

Sources referenced: U.S. Department of Energy (Energy Saver) on whole-house fans and ventilation cooling; industry sizing standards (2–3 CFM/sq ft); building-science guidance on depressurization, backdrafting and radon; historic ventilation practice documented at Mount Vernon; documented DIY whole-house box-fan demonstrations.

Safety note: a whole-house fan run with windows closed depressurizes the home and can pull combustion gases backward from gas appliances and radon from crawlspaces. Windows open before the fan, always. Homes with gas appliances should have working carbon-monoxide alarms.

tab_title: Paul Spence: What’s Wrong With Heat Pump Installations?
description:
What does a qualification actually tell you about the person installing your heat pump? Paul Spence has been in heating since 1980, and his answer is blunt: not much.

Paul started as an apprentice at Leeds Building College, spent five years as a marine engineer in the Royal Navy working on screw compressor chillers and ships' cooling systems, then went self-employed through the combi boiler boom of the 1990s. He now runs the Heat Pumps UK Facebook group, with 33,000 members, and has spent years rectifying heat pump systems that were signed off as compliant and still didn't work.

In this episode we talk about what an apprenticeship used to involve versus a three-day course, why City & Guilds gave way to NVQs, how gas certification quietly let people into wet heating work they weren't trained for, and why the same problem has reappeared in heat pumps. Paul explains why he thinks MCS, MCS 3005D and BS 12831 have made installers' lives harder without improving standards, what the Boiler Upgrade Scheme's future means for certification bodies, and what a genuine apprenticeship route for the next generation of heat pump installers would look like.

If you've had a heat pump installed and it isn't performing, or you're an engineer fed up with the paperwork, this one is for you.

description:
What temperature should your gas boiler run at — and how much does turning it down actually save?

Lowering your boiler flow temperature is one of the easiest free ways to improve heating efficiency and save money on heating bills. In this video I explain what flow temperature really means, why return temperature matters for a condensing boiler, and how much the difference between 80%, 85%, 90% and 95% efficiency changes the annual cost of heating — using a simple 10,000 kWh of heat example.

I also share what I did in my own home before fitting a heat pump: starting at around 75°C and gradually testing 70, 65, 60, 55 down to around 45°C. You'll see which rooms struggled first, why lukewarm radiators aren't necessarily a problem, and why longer, steadier heating often works better than short blasts of very hot water.

I cover:
• Flow temperature vs return temperature
• Why a 90% efficiency badge doesn't mean 90% all the time
• How to start your own boiler experiment safely
• Why to test when it's properly cold outside
• Weather compensation and boiler controls
• Combi boiler hot-water temperature
• Using lower flow temperatures as a simple heat-pump readiness test

This isn't based on estimates — it's based on real data from my own home and heating system.

A five-gallon bucket of saltwater can give back around 800 BTUs as it cools overnight — and this video gives you the honest, complete picture of what that actually means for heating your home. The salt bucket concept is rooted in real physics called thermal mass and specific heat capacity, the same principles behind stone farmhouses, adobe walls, and passive solar design. But this video also explains what the viral versions leave out: a single bucket equals about ten minutes of a space heater and costs you roughly five cents of electricity equivalent per night. The salt itself is not there to improve heat storage — it lowers the freezing point of water, protecting unheated spaces like pump houses and greenhouses without the container bursting. You'll also learn how much salt to use, where to place the bucket for maximum effect, why flat black paint matters, and how to actually measure whether your setup is working with a min-max thermometer. The video also covers the history of Glauber's salt solar heating experiments at MIT, the real truth about electric space heater efficiency claims, and what genuinely keeps a room warmer overnight at zero cost.

tab_title: You Only Need These 6 Canned Foods to Survive Hard Times — And How Alaskans Store Them
description:
🔗 Everything 66 Alaska Winters Taught Me, Written Down:
https://dickcolter.com/winterproof

If an ice storm shuts the road to your grocery store for a week, the cans in the cupboard are all you've got. Here are the only six canned foods you need, what each one does for an older body in a cold house, and how Alaskans store them so they're still good when you open them. The state's emergency office calls two weeks of food the best grade. This is how you build to it.

I was born in Fairbanks, Alaska, and I spent 66 winters there, most of them fixing oil furnaces. I'm not a doctor.

The six, counting down:
6. Canned fruit packed in its own juice, your vitamin C and the shortest clock on the shelf
5. Canned sweet potatoes, soft fuel you can eat cold, with a full day's vitamin A in a cup
4. A hearty soup that's ready to eat, never condensed, never in the garage
3. Canned beans, the tallest stack you own, every can checked
2. Alaska pink salmon, the traditional kind, with the soft bones mashed in
1. Evaporated milk, the can that turns the rest into meals

Safety, said plainly: keep your cans inside the heated part of the house, above 34 degrees and below 85. A can that froze gets a look at the seams: bulging, or a broken seam once it's thawed, goes in the trash. A deep dent, any dent on the rim, rust that won't wipe off, a bulging or leaking can: out, no exceptions. Never use a camp stove or a grill inside your home. With no refrigerator, an opened can is perishable: food that sits above 40 degrees for two hours or more gets thrown away, so open only what you'll eat at one meal. Don't confuse evaporated milk with sweetened condensed milk. If you're watching your blood sugar, your salt or your blood pressure, your own doctor decides what goes in your body. Keep the shelf between your hip and your shoulder, and keep a manual can opener right next to the cans.

Which of these six is already on your shelf right now? Drop the number in the comments. I read them.
