tab_title: 10 Dollar Tree Items Alaskan Households Buy Before Winter (And 5 They Never Touch)
description:
When the shelves go bare before a winter storm, the cheap things go first. Here are the 10 plain Dollar Tree items that get a house ready before the cold, the 5 on the same shelves that people up north leave alone, and what each one means for an older body. There isn't a single Dollar Tree in Alaska, so up there folks buy these same things wherever they can, and the State of Alaska puts almost all of them on its own emergency kit list.

I was born in Fairbanks, Alaska, and I spent 66 winters there, most of them fixing oil furnaces. I'm not a doctor.

The 10, counting down:
10. Quart freezer bags, for your papers and a list of your pills
9. Long kitchen matches, for the stove burner and never for heat
8. A manual can opener you've tried on a real can
7. An LED flashlight in every room, with alkaline batteries in it
6. Emergency blankets, shiny side in, under your real quilt
5. Wool socks, and toe warmers if your doctor says yes
4. A foam cover on every outside faucet, hose off first
3. Foam weather stripping tape around the doors
2. A window insulation kit for the rooms you'll live in
1. Plain clay cat litter by the back door, the kind that doesn't clump

The 5 they never touch: chafing fuel as a heater, tea lights under a flower pot, a thin extension cord for a space heater, Super Heavy Duty batteries in a flashlight, and cotton socks and gloves.

Safety, said plainly: never use a gas range or oven to heat your home. Light only the top burners by hand, and only if your owner's manual says your model allows it; never the oven. Use flashlights, not candles, when the power is out, and keep any candle at least 12 inches from anything that can burn. Camping stoves, chafing fuel and heaters made for outdoors never come inside, and a cracked window is not enough. Plug a space heater straight into the wall, never into an extension cord or power strip, and keep it at least 3 feet from anything that can burn. Toe warmers never go to bed with you; if you're diabetic or have poor circulation, ask your own doctor first. Put a carbon monoxide alarm near every place people sleep and on every level of the house. Do the outside work on a dry October afternoon, sitting on a stool for the low parts.

Which of these is already sitting in your house right now? Drop the number in the comments. I read them.

tab_title: 9 Things in Your House That Turn Dangerous in Winter (I Threw Out #1 at 74)
description:
The furnace runs its first long winter night, and the little alarm on your ceiling stays quiet. You take that quiet to mean you're safe. Turn it over. The date on the back may say it quit years ago, right when winter leans on it the hardest.

I'm June, forty-seven years a lineman's wife, and these are the nine things in a house that turn dangerous once the snow comes, counted down to the one I threw out at seventy-four. Every one of them has a cheap fix, and a few of them start with a plain old broom.

Chapters
0:00 The alarm that stays quiet
0:42 9. The two white furnace pipes

2:19 7. Your gas furnace in a blackout

4:56 4. The tailpipe in the drift
5:48 3. The space heater's cord
6:38 2. Rock salt below 15 degrees
7:29 1. The alarm I threw out at 74
8:20 Before the next snow

Why these matter (the numbers I kept out of the video):
· More than 400 Americans die each year from carbon monoxide poisoning not linked to fires, and more than 100,000 visit an emergency department (CDC).
· From 2012 to 2022, about 750 people died from carbon monoxide poisoning linked to portable generators alone (CPSC).
· Portable space heaters are involved in an average of 1,600 fires and 70 deaths a year (CPSC, 2020-2022).
· In the January 1996 blizzard, 25 people in Philadelphia and New York City were poisoned in idling cars with snow-blocked tailpipes, most of them children and older people (CDC, MMWR).
· One in four adults 65 and older reports a fall every year, and falls are the leading cause of injury death at that age (CDC).
· Adults 65 to 74 are about twice as likely to die in a home fire as the general population (U.S. Fire Administration, 2023).

The short rules: clear outside vents and the gas meter by hand or broom, from the ground; ice on the meter or a gas smell means call the gas company from outside. Generator outdoors only, 20+ feet from windows, doors and vents, never into a wall outlet. Space heater straight into the wall. Check the tailpipe before you start the car. Sand below 15 degrees. Smoke alarms out at 10 years, CO alarms by their label.

Tell me in the comments: what did your father or your husband check after the first big snow? I read them all.

Stay warm, stay safe, and check on your neighbor.

description:
/ @homeguard  
Before you pay $400 for a dryer repair, check these six things.
If your dryer suddenly needs two cycles, leaves clothes damp, runs without producing heat, or has become unusually loud, the problem may not be inside the machine at all. The dryer may simply be losing airflow, power, or proper ventilation.
My name is Walt Harden. I’ve spent forty years deciding when a repair bill was legitimate and when it was not. In this video, I’ll show you how to separate a simple homeowner check from a real appliance repair.
The six checks include:
• Confirming the dryer is receiving the full 240 volts it needs

• Testing the lint screen for invisible fabric-softener buildup

• Cleaning lint from the housing below the lint screen

• Inspecting the flexible exhaust connection behind the dryer

• Checking the outside vent for weak airflow, lint, shrubs, grills, or bird nests

• Understanding what two-cycle drying actually reveals about restricted venting
You’ll also learn what common internal problems may look like, including a failed thermal fuse, gas-dryer ignition problems, a defective door switch, motor overheating, worn drum rollers, and an unbalanced blower wheel.
A dryer that produces hot clothes that are still damp usually has an airflow problem—not necessarily a failed heating element. Before authorizing a repair, check the vent path and exterior exhaust first. A blocked dryer vent wastes energy, extends drying times, and creates a serious fire hazard.
If you smell burning, notice unusually high heat, or find that clothes are coming out dangerously hot, stop using the dryer until the vent system has been inspected and cleared.

They heated entire villas with a single fire. No ducts. No electricity. No monthly bill. Two thousand years ago, Roman engineers built floors that turned the ground itself into a radiator—and then we stopped using it.

This is the hypocaust system. Stone floors raised on small pillars. A furnace outside the room pushing hot air and smoke underneath, circulating through hollow spaces and up wall flues. The heat didn’t blast—it soaked. Floors stayed warm for hours. Rooms heated evenly. Bathhouses, villas, even military forts ran on it across the empire.

It wasn’t just Rome. In Korea, the ondol system used a similar idea—routing heat under stone floors to warm entire homes. Different continents. Same solution. Radiant heat, built into the structure itself.

So why don’t we use it now?

Modern building codes strictly prohibit routing combustion exhaust under living spaces. Carbon monoxide risk. Fire risk. Liability. Instead, we rely on sealed systems—forced air, gas furnaces, electric heating—expensive to install, expensive to run, and dependent on constant energy input.

The Romans managed airflow with flues and draft design. They burned wood, controlled the draw, and kept living spaces separated from direct smoke. It worked for centuries. But one failure in a modern home isn’t just discomfort—it’s deadly. And today’s standards are written around that risk.

The idea wasn’t forgotten. It was replaced.

Modern radiant floor heating still exists—but powered by hot water pipes or electric coils, sealed, regulated, and far from the open-fire systems of the ancient world. The principle survived. The method didn’t.

The question isn’t whether it worked. It did. The question is whether we could ever build something like it again—and make it safe.
title: FREE Heat All Winter From a $300 “Ancient” Floor. Why Did the HVAC Industry Bury It?

tab_title: FREE Heating and Cooling From a Roof That Costs Almost Nothing. Why Did the Energy Industry Bury It?
description:
No furnace. No air conditioner. No ducts, no refrigerant, no utility contract. Just water on a roof — and the simple, relentless physics of heat moving toward cold.

Harold Hay's Skytherm system is almost insulting in its elegance. Shallow bags of water sit on a flat metal ceiling. In winter, you slide the insulation panels open during the day and let the sun heat the water. Close them at night, and that stored warmth radiates downward through the metal ceiling into the house for hours. In summer, you reverse the cycle — open at night to bleed the heat out into the cold sky, close during the day to let the cool water absorb the house's heat from below. The roof becomes the entire HVAC system.

Hay built a working demonstration home in 1967. It maintained comfortable temperatures year-round in the Atascadero desert with zero mechanical heating or cooling. The data was clean. The concept was proven. Government researchers studied it and confirmed it worked.

Then nothing happened.

No manufacturer picked it up. No building code was updated to accommodate it. No developer standardized it into a housing tract. The American construction industry looked at a system that permanently replaced two of its most profitable product categories — the furnace and the air conditioner — and found no compelling reason to adopt it.

Harold Hay spent the rest of his life trying to give the idea away. The problem was never the roof. The problem was that a bag of water and a sliding panel don't generate a service call.
title: FREE Heating and Cooling From a Roof That Costs Almost Nothing. Why Did the Energy Industry Bury It?

tab_title: Why Old Houses Didn’t Rot (Modern Homes Are Built to Trap Moisture)
description:
Most people think old houses survived because they were built “better.”

That’s wrong.

Old houses lasted because they followed rules modern construction forgot.

They weren’t sealed boxes.
They weren’t wrapped in plastic.
They weren’t designed to trap moisture.

They were built to shed water, breathe, and dry — and that’s why many of them are still standing a century later.

🏠 THE FORGOTTEN HOUSE-BUILDING SYSTEM:
→ Walls designed to dry, not stay sealed
→ Ventilation that removed moisture naturally
→ Roofs and overhangs that shed water away from structures
→ Materials that tolerate moisture instead of failing from it
→ Air gaps that prevent rot before it starts
→ Simple physics, not chemicals or machines

🔥 THE CRITICAL BUILDING PRINCIPLE:
Houses don’t rot because water gets in.
They rot because water can’t get out.

Modern homes try to block moisture completely.
Old homes assumed moisture was inevitable — and designed around that reality.

When water is allowed to drain, evaporate, and move:
– Wood lasts longer
– Mold struggles to grow
– Structures stay dry
– Repairs are minimal
– Houses age slowly instead of failing suddenly

Miss this principle, and no material or technology can save the building.

🏚️ TESTED OVER CENTURIES:
These ideas aren’t theory.
They come from traditional homes that survived without plastic barriers, dehumidifiers, or HVAC systems.

No hype.
No “modern solutions.”
Just construction logic that worked long before machines existed.

tab_title: 3 Volts Turn Sand Into Stone | Could Cement Be Replaced? #BuildingMaterials #ScienceExplained
description:
In 2024, researchers at Northwestern University showed that a tiny electrical current (2–4 volts) can turn seawater-soaked sand into solid stone in minutes. No cement. No high-temperature kilns. Just electricity and minerals already dissolved in the ocean.

The process causes calcium and magnesium minerals to crystallize between sand grains, locking them together like natural rock. Even more surprising, the material can be reversed back into sand by flipping the electrical polarity.

The idea actually dates back to 1976, when architect Wolf Hilbertz discovered that electricity in seawater could grow limestone structures — a method later known as Biorock. Over the following decades, hundreds of these mineral-grown reefs were built in more than 40 countries.

This matters because the material we currently rely on — cement — produces about 8% of global CO₂ emissions every year.

If sand can be turned into stone with just a few volts of electricity, it raises a fascinating question: could the future of construction grow from the ocean instead of being burned in a kiln?

tab_title: Old Plumbers Trick for How To Boost Shower Pressure. ($0)
description:
If your shower’s so weak the shampoo won’t rinse out, odds are your pipes are fine. There’s a little plastic disc behind your showerhead choking the water, and pulling it is the easiest DIY plumbing fix there is. No new showerhead, no plumber, no money. Just an old trick for low water pressure in the shower that most folks never got shown.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
MY BOOK
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Get my book here: https://eliasmercer.com/

Fifty-plus years of what I know, in over eighty chapters. Walt the plumber took most of his tricks to the grave with him. I wrote mine down so they don’t go the same way.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
In this one I’ll show you how to tell if it’s really your shower head flow restrictor or a bigger problem, how to get the head off without chewing up the chrome, where that disc hides on different heads, the one part you must never pull out, my grandmother Ida’s vinegar trick for clogged holes, and the bucket test that tells you for certain it worked. This is home repair on a budget, done the way my people always did it: fix what you’ve got.


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
A WORD ON SAFETY
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

On a handheld wand, leave the spring-loaded one-way valve alone. It’s a check valve that keeps dirty water from being pulled back into the lines you drink from. If it springs back when you press it, it stays in.
If you’ve got a tub-and-shower combo and the pull-up knob won’t stay up after you pull the disc, put the disc back.
If every tap in the house is weak, this won’t fix it. Call a plumber or your water company.
Vinegar can dull brass, nickel, and gold-colored finishes. Keep those soaks to half an hour.
More flow means more water and hot water used. On a weak well, a tight meter, or in a drought, keep the disc in.
Flow limits on new fixtures vary by state. Know your county.
I’m not a licensed plumber. Do this on your own fixtures at your own risk.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
WHAT I USED
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Getting the head off

Adjustable wrench
Shop rags (to protect the finish)

Pulling the disc

Long-reach needle-nose pliers
Pick set
Small flathead screwdriver set

Putting it back

Thread seal tape (PTFE / plumber’s tape)
Replacement showerhead washers

Clearing the holes

White distilled vinegar
Heavy zip-top bags and rubber bands
Old toothbrush or detail brush

Testing it

One-gallon bucket with markings
Simple stopwatch

If you’d rather save water

High-efficiency (WaterSense) showerhead with strong spray

tab_title: 3 Easiest Ways To Remove a Tree Stump Without Breaking Your Back
description:
That tree-service quote was never the cost of the work. It was the cost of not knowing the three old methods that pull a stump without a grinder.

The stump you see is the small part. Underground the root ball can outweigh the trunk you cut, and it keeps sending up sprouts while a rotting one draws termites and carpenter ants toward your shed. Rented grinders stop at the soil line, store-bought stump killer soaks off into the dirt, and dynamite is a fast way to lose a hand. The mountain folks skipped all of it, working on one principle: soften the wood first, then let it let go.

We walk through all three. Salt or Epsom salt packed into deep drilled holes and capped under a tarp rots the wood through a season. Saltpeter soaked into a drilled grid turns the stump into a slow, self-feeding smolder that hollows it below the soil line. And the lever, an undercut root ball, a firewood fulcrum, a long pole, and soaked ground, pops the whole thing loose in an afternoon. Along the way you get the mistakes that turn each one back into a backache, and a simple way to pick the method that fits the stump in your yard.
title: 3 Easiest Ways To Remove a Tree Stump Without Breaking Your Back

tab_title: How to Get Rid of Spiders Naturally — And Stop Them From Coming Back
description:
There is a web in the corner of your ceiling again.

You took one down last week. You swept it away, cleaned the corner, and thought the problem was handled. Now there is another web in the same place, a smaller one above the window, and another behind the bin near the stairs.

So you buy a spider spray.

But here is the part most people miss: the spider may not be the real problem.

A spider is a hunter. It builds its web where it can find food. If you remove the web but leave the insects that attracted the spider in the first place, another spider may simply move into the same spot.

In this video, you'll learn:

• A simple homemade spray and what each ingredient actually does
• Where to spray—and where spraying is completely unnecessary
• Why the mixture needs to be shaken before use
• How often to make a fresh batch
• What the spray can realistically accomplish—and what it cannot
• How to read spider webs and figure out what may be attracting them
• Why a vacuum cleaner works better than a broom for removing webs
• The simple daylight test that can reveal gaps and entry points around your home
• One inexpensive change that can make a surprisingly big difference
• What you should move away from exterior walls
• Two common spiders worth learning to identify
• Why most spiders you find indoors are not something you need to panic about

Safety

Essential oils such as peppermint and lavender can be harmful to cats, so use extra caution if you have pets. Keep pets away from treated areas until everything is completely dry, and avoid spraying areas where they sleep or spend time.

Always test homemade sprays on a small, hidden area first. Oils can stain or damage certain paints, wood finishes, and other surfaces.

Wear gloves when reaching into woodpiles, moving old boards, or cleaning dark, undisturbed areas.

There are shelves full of spider sprays in stores, but most products focus entirely on killing the spider.

They don't address the bigger picture: why are spiders appearing there in the first place?

Look at the lights around your home after dark. Stand outside for a minute and watch what gathers around them.

Those insects are part of the reason spiders may be nearby.

Instead of only removing the spider, look at what is attracting it.

Tell me in the comments what you found around your home. Are your webs concentrated near doors, windows, lights, or other areas? And what kind of house do you live in?

In the next video, we'll look at another common household problem: keeping mice out before they become a bigger issue.

Because sometimes the thing you notice first isn't the actual problem. It's the warning sign.

tab_title: The $0 Shed Heater Farm Families Made Out of Trash
description:
A tin can candle heater costs nothing, plugs into nothing, and has been used in cold sheds, workshops and root cellars across the north for well over a century. This is how it actually works, what it genuinely does, and — just as important — what it will not do, no matter what the internet tells you.

Put a tin can over a candle flame and three things change at once. The can shields the flame from draft, so it burns steady instead of guttering and wasting wax. The metal itself warms and becomes a small radiator, throwing heat out in every direction instead of straight up at the ceiling. And the air trapped between flame and metal becomes a pocket of warmth the room can borrow from gradually. No motor, no electricity, no moving parts.

Here's where most videos on this lose the plot: a candle heater will NOT heat a room. A single candle puts out roughly the heat of a bright incandescent bulb, and no arrangement of tin and air multiplies that, because energy doesn't come from nowhere. The can doesn't make more heat — it makes better use of the heat already there. There's a world of difference between those two sentences.

What it genuinely does, in a shed, a hunting blind, an ice fishing hut, or the cab of a parked truck: takes the raw edge off, holds a small space above freezing, and keeps your hands working at a bench for an hour.

In this video: the physics of why the can beats an open flame, the build (one hole punched low for draft, and why that hole is not optional), the ten minutes of patience most people skip before deciding it doesn't work, the safety rules that are not negotiable — fireproof surface, never unattended, never while asleep, and crack a window because a flame in a sealed room burns your oxygen and produces carbon monoxide — and why something this cheap and this old is never sold in a store.

Have you ever run one? Tell me in the comments what it actually did in the space you actually put it in. Not what a video promised — what it did.

tab_title: Why Don’t Seniors Put $40 of Bricks Behind Their Wood Stove? It Holds the Heat Till Morning
description:
Forty dollars of plain red brick, stacked behind a wood stove, can still be warm under your hand hours after the fire dies. My grandfather never believed it. He packed his stove full every night, shut the air down, and swore it would last till morning. The Environmental Protection Agency says that habit does little for heating. So what does keep a house warm after the fire’s out? And can forty dollars of brick do it?

The heat was never the problem, losing it was. This guide shows you the old-school fix for that.
Get it here: https://halthebricklayer.com

I’m Hal. I laid brick for forty years, and I’ve stood in a lot of cold kitchens at five in the morning next to a stove that roared at ten and was cold iron by dawn.

In this video I show you why a steel wood stove loses its heat so fast once the fire dies, and how a simple stack of solid red brick behind or beside your stove can hold that heat well into a winter night with no gas and no power. It’s the same idea behind the old masonry heaters of Europe, the German kachelofen and the Russian and Finnish fireplaces, which store the heat of one hot fire in tons of masonry and give it back for twelve to twenty-four hours. I run the honest numbers on what fifty bricks can and can’t do, so you know exactly what to expect before you buy a single one.

What you’ll learn:
🔥 Why packing the stove full and shutting the air down at bedtime wastes wood and heat
🪵 The 20 percent moisture rule for firewood, and how to check it with a cheap meter
🧱 How to stack bricks on the hearth so they soak up heat safely
⚠️ Why bricks don’t let you move your stove closer to the wall, and why concrete block is a no
🛏️ The one wrapped brick that carries the warmth to your bed until morning

Stick around to the end, because the part that actually gets you to morning isn’t the stack at all. It’s a single brick, and our grandparents knew exactly what to do with it.

I’m Hal. On Shelved Science, an old bricklayer takes a trade fix down off the shelf every week and checks it honestly against the numbers, before you pay a contractor for the expensive version. Subscribe if that’s worth something to you.

Tell me in the comments: did anyone in your house ever warm a bed with a brick? Who was it, and what did they wrap it in? I read every one.

⏱️ CHAPTERS
0:00 Can $40 of brick keep your house warm?
1:16 Understanding the thermal flywheel
7:36 Three steps to better heating
12:49 The trick to staying warm all night
15:57 Putting the thermal flywheel to work

⚠️ SAFETY
Bricks do not reduce your stove’s required clearances. Follow your stove’s manual and your installer. Use solid clay brick only, never concrete or cinder block. Keep the stack off the stove body and clear of its air openings, and keep combustibles at least 3 feet away. Never put a bare or scorching brick in a bed. Test it on the back of your hand, wrap it thick, and take extra care if you have reduced feeling in your feet. Install carbon monoxide alarms on every level and outside sleeping areas, and test them monthly.

Sources mentioned: EPA Burn Wise, Masonry Heater Association of North America, Consumer Product Safety Commission, Museum of English Rural Life, Children’s Museum of Indianapolis. This video is for general information only. Always follow local fire and building codes.

tab_title: 12 Foods That Can Sit on Your Shelf for YEARS and Still Save You in an Emergency
description:
🥫 What foods can last for years on the shelf and still be useful when stores close, deliveries stop, or the power goes out?

In this video, Mason Reed breaks down 12 long shelf life foods for emergency preparedness — including pantry staples, canned foods, shelf-stable protein, ready-to-eat meals, and long-term storage options that can help keep your household fed when refrigeration and normal shopping are unavailable.

A strong emergency pantry is not just about the longest expiration date. The best emergency foods store well, fit your household, use realistic amounts of water and cooking fuel, and are foods you will actually eat under stress.

🥫 12 LONG-LASTING FOODS FOR EMERGENCY STORAGE

🍚 1. Granulated Sugar — Stores extremely well when kept dry and sealed. Useful for calories, drinks, and improving basic stored foods.

🍯 2. Honey — A ready-to-eat source of energy with excellent long-term storage potential when stored properly.

🥛 3. Nonfat Dry Milk — Shelf-stable protein and calcium, but it requires safe water.

🍝 4. Dried Pasta — Affordable, familiar, compact, and easy to rotate, although it requires water and fuel.

🫘 5. Dried Beans & Lentils — Provide protein, fiber, carbohydrates, and minerals. Lentils and split peas can be especially useful when fuel is limited.

🍚 6. White Rice — A practical long-term grain because it is calorie-dense, versatile, and stores far better than brown rice when properly packaged.

🌾 7. Whole Wheat Berries — Can store for many years under good conditions, especially for households that know how to use them.

🍑 8. Commercially Canned Fruit — Ready to eat, requires no cooking, adds variety, and provides useful moisture.

🥕 9. Commercially Canned Vegetables — Shelf-stable, hydrated, and easy to use during a blackout.

🐟 10. Commercially Canned Meat, Poultry & Fish — Provides valuable shelf-stable protein without refrigeration before opening.

🍲 11. Retort Meals & MRE-Style Foods — Useful when cooking, refrigeration, or extra water may be limited.

🥘 12. Professionally Packaged Freeze-Dried Foods — Some products can remain usable for decades when stored according to manufacturer instructions.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🏠 BUILD A PRACTICAL EMERGENCY PANTRY

Long shelf life alone does not make a food a good survival food.

A balanced emergency food supply should include:

🥫 Ready-to-eat foods
🍚 Long-term grains and staples
🐟 Shelf-stable protein
💧 Foods that do not consume excessive water
🔥 Foods that do not require large amounts of cooking fuel
🍎 Foods your household already eats

Rice, pasta, dry milk, wheat, beans, and freeze-dried meals can store well, but many still depend on safe water and fuel. A good emergency pantry combines no-cook foods with longer-term storage foods.

🌡️ STORAGE CONDITIONS MATTER

Heat, moisture, oxygen, light, insects, rodents, and damaged packaging can shorten food storage life.

✅ Keep food cool, dry, and dark
✅ Protect dry foods from moisture and pests
✅ Use food-safe containers and proven storage methods
✅ Inspect canned food before eating it
✅ Rotate older food forward and use it first

Never eat from cans that are bulging, leaking, badly rusted, or severely damaged.

🔄 ROTATION BEATS HOARDING

The strongest emergency pantry is not a museum.

Eat from it. Replace what you use. Keep newer food behind older food. Learn what your family likes before an emergency forces you to depend on it.

Rotation can expose problems early: too much fuel or water required, food nobody likes, meals that do not fit dietary needs, or packaging that is difficult to open.

💧 DON’T FORGET WATER

Emergency food storage and emergency water storage must work together.

Rice, pasta, dry milk, wheat, dried beans, and many freeze-dried meals require water. A long-term food supply is far less useful if every meal depends on water you never stored.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🧭 ABOUT MASON REED

Mason Reed focuses on practical emergency preparedness for real homes and families, including emergency food storage, emergency water, blackout preparedness, grid-down readiness, winter emergencies, home safety, affordable prepping, and everyday self-reliance.

You do not need to buy years of survival food in one weekend. Start with several days of foods you already use, store them correctly, rotate them, and gradually build a more resilient pantry.

💬 QUESTION FOR YOU:

If you had to live for seven days only on the food already in your pantry, what would run out first — protein, bread, milk, coffee, or something else?

Share your answer in the comments. It may reveal the next gap worth fixing in your emergency food supply.

Stay ready. Stay practical. Stay prepared.

— Mason Reed

tab_title: Before You Seal the Windows, Do This (Or Pay for It by January)
description:
Before the plastic goes on your windows this week, leave the kit in the bag one more night.
There's a check that comes first. It has six parts and takes about twenty minutes, and most of it costs nothing.

Most of us put the film up first and find the trouble after Christmas. By then the tape has let go, and the sill under it is still wet. A sill that stays wet goes soft, and that's how people end up pricing new windows. New windows start around four hundred dollars a window and run up from there. Here are the six checks that come before all that, in the order I'd do them:

The way out. In every bedroom, the window you'd climb out of opens by hand, with no tools. Plastic goes on the inside of the glass only. On that window, use plastic that peels off by hand, or leave the window bare. Free.
The meter. A hygrometer runs about $10 to 14. Read it morning and evening for three or four days. If it reads over sixty percent, the plastic waits until you find what's feeding the moisture.
Fan and dryer. Hold a tissue to the bath fan grille, then go outside and find where the fan comes out. Make sure the dryer duct goes outside, stays clear, and the flap swings. Free.
Dry the sill. Wipe it tonight, look at it tomorrow in daylight, and press a thumbnail into the corners. Small mildew spots on hard paint get soap and water, then dry the sill all the way. Anything bigger, soft or inside the wall goes to a professional. Soft, dark wood is rot, and that's carpentry. Free.
Clean the frame. Wipe it with rubbing alcohol, about $2, then test it with a scrap of painter's tape. If the tape pulls off easy, wipe it again. Kits are made to go on metal, painted wood or vinyl.
The tissue. On a cold evening, with the heat running, tape a strip of tissue to a pencil and look for holes. Mark each one with painter's tape. Tissue only. No candle, match or lighter.
Then you seal. Rope caulk is about $6 a roll. A film kit is about twelve dollars and does two or three windows. Keep the film and curtains clear of a baseboard heater by the distance on its label. Shrink the film with a hair dryer the way the kit's sheet says: a hand's width off, kept moving, never touching the film. No heat gun. Twenty minutes and a roll of tape, once the checking's done. I can't tell you what any of this takes off your bill. Yours is yours.

Renting? Everything here peels off in April. If a bedroom window won't open, or the bath fan or dryer doesn't vent outside, tell your landlord in writing the same week.

Cheap first. Then expensive, if you still need it.

One rule when you seal or change anything: you seal around things, never over them. Dryer vents, bath fans, and flues stay open. Anything that burns fuel needs air and an alarm: air coming in, exhaust going out, and a carbon monoxide alarm on every level of the house and outside the bedrooms.

description:
Why Is the Graf Spee Still Sitting in an Estuary 

The Nazi Warship That Destroyed Itself — and the Truth Berlin Never Explained
In December 1939, one of the most powerful warships in the German Navy blew itself apart in shallow water — not by enemy fire, but on the orders of its own captain. The Graf Spee had hunted Allied shipping across two oceans, sinking nine merchant vessels and killing 72 civilian sailors. Then, cornered in neutral Montevideo, she was scuttled, and her captain took his own life three days later.
But the real story isn't how the Graf Spee sank. It's why — and who's responsible.
In this video, we dig into the Battle of the River Plate, the British deception operation that may have changed the outcome, and the troubling gaps in the German naval communications record that have never been officially explained. We examine Captain Langsdorff's impossible position, the contradictory orders from Berlin that gave him responsibility while preserving command's plausible deniability, and the choice he made that historians still debate.
The wreck still sits in ten meters of water in the Río de la Plata. Germany claims ownership, blocks salvage, and has never published the complete signals exchanged with Langsdorff during his final 72 hours. The men he killed have no museum. The ship that killed them does.

This video counts down twenty tricks Pennsylvania farmers used to keep a stable above freezing on a bitter night, starting with the long forebay, the overhang that sheltered the stall doors and yard below. From there it moves through the south-facing stable, the hillside bank that let wagons drive onto the upper floor while livestock sat beneath, and the hay stored above the animals. It also covers the evergreen windbreak on the north and west sides, which cuts wind speed and the heat it strips from walls, and the cattle themselves, which give off heat and moisture all winter.

Along the way the video explains why the old barns lost out, from the Rural Electrification Administration of 1935 to 1953, when more than 90 percent of farms had power. It also shows why modern builders keep rediscovering the same ideas, from the Saskatchewan Conservation House in Regina in 1977 to the first Passivhaus row houses in Darmstadt, Germany in 1991.

Number one is the idea underneath every other trick, and it is simpler than any machine. Stay to the end for the principle that ties all twenty together.

How did farmers keep livestock warm through blizzards before heat lamps and tank heaters? This countdown covers 20 forgotten barn tricks from American farms, and every one follows the same idea. An old barn never made heat. It kept the heat its animals made from blowing away.

It opens with an argument. In 1881 army officer James Brisbin promised that cattle on the plains would winter safely with almost no shelter, and in 1883 livestock editor Elliott Stewart answered that shelter cost less than feed. The winter that began in 1886 settled it, when Granville Stuart's Montana outfit lost two thirds of its herd.

From there you will see the hayloft used as insulation, the low stable Franklin Hiram King measured in Wisconsin and his ventilation flues, prairie shelterbelts and straw sheds, the beaverslide hay stacker patented in 1910, the curtain front hen house from a 1909 Department of Agriculture bulletin, the sunshine hog house from a 1911 one, and Plumb's feeding test in Indiana. description:
25 Forgotten Appalachian Power Tricks That Make $3,000 Power Stations Look Useless

A $315 home-built power station that does the work of a $3,000 box — plus 24 cheaper tricks. 25 old mountain ways to keep the lights on cheap.

Wade Caudill lays out how a portable power station is just a deep-cycle battery, an inverter, a charge controller, and a solar panel, and how to build one for $315. Plus solar path lights, power banks, 12-volt LED strip, a hay box cooker, zeer pot fridge, root cellar, solar oven, rocket stove, golf-cart battery bank, and micro hydro for real blackout power.

THE $315 BUILD Let me run the build by you one more time, slow, so you can write it down. One twelve-volt deep-cycle battery, about a hundred amp-hours, the size of a car battery and near about sixty pounds.

One hundred dollars. One pure sine wave inverter, about five hundred watts, the size of a hardback book. Sixty dollars. One two-hundred-watt solar panel, close to five feet long and two feet wide. One hundred dollars. 

One twenty-amp charge controller, the size of a paperback. Thirty dollars. Ten-gauge wire from the panel to the controller, a fuse within a foot of the battery on every positive wire, and the short heavy cables that come in the box with the inverter. 

Twenty-five dollars. Now the order. Wire the controller to the battery first. Then the panel to the controller. Then the inverter straight to the battery, through its fuse. Face the panel south, tilted up about thirty-seven degrees here in Kentucky, about the pitch of a steep roof, and set the battery in a vented box outside the rooms you live in. 

That is three hundred and fifteen dollars all in, one afternoon at the bench, and every part of it can be swapped on its own for as long as you own it.


Method:
Wire the charge controller to the battery (27:14)
Wire the solar panel to the controller (27:14)
Wire the inverter to the battery through its fuse (27:14)
Face the panel south at about 37 degrees (27:14)

tab_title: This $5 Candle-Powered Heater Keeps My Room Warm All Winter
description:
📕 The Plain Heat Library, a warm house all winter for less, written down: https://elisplainheat.netlify.app/?b=bundl...

My English neighbor built the famous clay pot candle heater from a video, set it in the middle of her living room, and called me two hours later to say it was a fraud. On the same night, the same kind of pot was keeping me warm in my reading chair. Here is why hers failed and mine worked, what the pot really does and does not do, and exactly how I set mine up. Four candles cannot heat a room, and I say so plainly. The five dollars is what I paid for the pot and my first bag of tea lights; the candles you burn after that are extra, and I show you how to figure them.

In this video:
• How much heat a tea light really gives (and why a pot does not add any)
• Why the pot failed in a big room and worked beside one chair
• My grandmother's foot stove, and the old rule: warm the person, not the house
• What the TV reports warned about, and what they got right
• Using it in a regular house with a furnace, without turning the heat down too far
• The seven steps I follow, every time
• What a month of evenings costs in candles

Figures and advice come from the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA), the U.S. Fire Administration, the U.S. Department of Energy, the National Institute on Aging and FOX television reporting (January 2026). Results depend on your room, your house and your weather.

Safety first (this is an open flame inside your home):
• Never leave it burning unattended. Blow the candles out when you leave the room, before you sleep or if you start to get drowsy. Never in a bedroom overnight.
• Set it only on something that cannot burn: brick, stone, ceramic tile or a metal tray on a hard floor. Never on carpet, rugs, wood floors or wooden furniture.
• Keep it at least 12 inches from anything that can burn: curtains, blankets, chairs, papers.
• Use a dry, unglazed, unpainted clay pot with no cracks. A damp pot can crack when heated.
• No more than four tea lights, spaced apart so they never touch. Leave a gap under the pot for air.
• The pot gets hot enough to burn. Never move it while lit or warm; let it cool and use gloves.
• Keep it away from children and pets. Never use candles where anyone uses medical oxygen.
• Smoke alarms, and carbon monoxide alarms with working batteries on every floor and near the bedrooms. If an alarm sounds, get everyone outside and call 911.
• If the wax catches fire, get everyone out and call 911 from outside. Never pour water on burning wax.
• Candles are not a way to heat your home. Keep your home at 68°F or warmer (National Institute on Aging). If the heat goes out or the bill is more than you can carry, call 211.
This video is general information, not professional advice.

tab_title: 9 Ways I Keep My Bed Warm All Winter With No Heat (The Cold Comes From Underneath)
description:
📕 The Plain Heat Library, a warm house all winter for less and a warm room when the heat goes out, written down: https://elisplainheat.netlify.app/?b=bundl...

Five quilts on top, a thin sheet underneath, and at three in the morning your back is cold. My English neighbor Walter slept that way all winter, while my grandchildren slept warm in an upstairs room with no furnace at all. In this video I follow how I found out why, and the nine plain ways I keep my own bed warm all winter with no heat. The biggest one is not on top of you. The cold comes from underneath.

In this video:
• Why a cold body in a cold bed stays cold
• Nose out, cap on, and wool socks
• The hot water bottle, the careful way
• Flannel sheets, and which one matters most
• The right order for your quilts, and tucking the bed like an envelope
• Moving the bed off the cold wall and away from the window
• Making the bedroom small, and turning the thermostat back at night
• What camping stores measure, and why it explains a cold back
• The wool blanket under the sheet, and quilts hung around the bed

Figures come from the British Medical Journal (2008), the journal Nature (1999), the NFPA, the U.S. Department of Energy, the CDC, the CPSC, ASTM and REI.

Safety first:
• Hot water bottles: hot water, never boiling, no more than two-thirds full, always in a cover, never against bare skin. Take it out before you sleep, and never use one with an electric blanket switched on.
• Never put heated stones or bricks in a bed.
• Keep candles out of the bedroom. Use a battery lantern or flashlight.
• Hand warmer packs: not on bare skin and not while you sleep.
• Plug electric space heaters straight into a wall outlet, never an extension cord or power strip, keep them 3 feet from the bed, curtains and anything that can burn, and turn them off before you sleep.
• Electric blankets: follow the label, keep them flat, never fold or tuck them in, check the cord, and retire old ones without automatic shut-off.
• Never heat a room with a grill, a camp stove, a generator, or the kitchen oven or stovetop.
• Keep working carbon monoxide alarms on every level and outside the bedrooms. If one sounds, get everyone outside and call 911.
• Ask for help moving heavy furniture. Hang quilts clear of lamps and heaters, with a generous opening for air.
• If your home will not hold heat, call 211 and ask about a warming center.

tab_title: Stop Buying Peppermint Oil and Plug-In Repellers for Rats — This $20 Roll of Wire Is What Works
description:
My name is Wade Corbin. My house is the last one on the line, so I have had to work most of this out myself.

Every fall somebody says a rat came up through their toilet, and somebody else says it's a myth. It's real. King County Public Health says rats make their way into toilets via sewer pipes. The University of Nebraska says a rat can jump three feet straight up, drop fifty feet without serious injury, and swim half a mile. And this month a lot of them are moving indoors. But if you're on septic, the toilet is the one door you can almost forget. Here are the ones you can't.

In this video:
Why October: rodents move into buildings as it cools, and a female Norway rat has four to six litters a year (UC IPM, University of Nebraska)
Norway rats come in low, roof rats come in high
What doesn't work: peppermint oil (EPA doesn't review minimum-risk products; UC and NC State say repellents fade fast), plug-in ultrasonic repellers (the FTC's 2001 warning letters), expanding foam and chicken wire
Where they get in: a half-inch gap under a door, and UC's rule to seal anything bigger than a quarter inch. What they chew through, including soft metals like copper
The roll of hardware cloth, about $20–25 for 3 by 10 feet, and why it isn't "rat-proof" (Nebraska's rat spec is 19-gauge)
Copper mesh or steel wool, always with caulk over it
Outside: limbs back six feet, firewood off the ground and off the wall, no pet food out overnight
The toilet: lid down on city sewer; on septic, check your cleanout caps
Poison: why the strongest baits are off the consumer shelf (EPA), and the rat that dies inside your wall
Traps done right: rat traps not mouse traps, baited end to the wall, a pea-sized bait
The first-night mistake: rats fear anything new, so pre-bait the traps unset, then set them all at once
Cleanup the CDC way, without sweeping or vacuuming

Have you had rats in the house, the barn or the garage this year? Tell me in the comments, yes or no. I read every one of them.

Subscribe so you do not miss the next one.

Stay warm. Stay dry. And remember, the people who had to work these things out for themselves usually got closer to the truth than the people selling you the answer.

I am not an exterminator. Keep every bait and trap away from children and pets. Mix bleach only with water, 1½ cups to a gallon, and never with ammonia or any other cleaner.

tab_title: EMERGENCY HEAT, Light & Cooking for 4 Months? The Crisco Candle With a Million Views, Checked
description:
My name is Wade Corbin. My house is the last one on the line. The power goes out about ten times a winter out here, the nearest hardware store is forty minutes, and nobody is coming to sort it out for me.

There is a video going round with more than a million views. A big catering can filled with five pounds of white shortening, six wicks, all six burning, a pan of steak sizzling on top, and the words burns for four months across the picture. Light, heat and cooking, all in one can that sits on a pantry shelf until the power goes out.

I went through it properly — what it is, how it is made, what the claims are, and what the people whose job is house fires and carbon monoxide say about every part of it.

Part of it is genuinely useful. As a backup light, one wick at a time, behind a flashlight for every person in the house, it earns its place on the shelf. The fire service's own advice in a power cut is flashlights first, and I tell you exactly why.

Part of it is how a family ends up in an ambulance. A clay pot over a flame makes no heat of its own — it only gives back the heat the flame already made. And every flame burned indoors makes carbon monoxide. The CDC says people who are asleep can die from it before they ever have a symptom. This can is not a heater, and I say so plainly.

The cooking is real, outdoors, with the lid beside it. Five pounds of shortening is five pounds of cooking fat, so I go through what the Fire Administration says to do if it catches — and the one thing you never do.

And I am straight with you about the four months: I could not find a burn rate I trust from any source, so I do not give you one.

tab_title: Why Do Americans Eat Tilapia But Avoid Carp?
description:
In 1882 the U.S. government sent about 260,000 live carp out by rail, free, to nearly every congressional district in the country. Today most Americans walk past that same fish to a bag of tilapia in the freezer. It was never only about taste: five things turned a country against the carp — a giveaway, a flood, a name, mud and bones, and a freezer case. This is the story of the fish Washington said ranked with the trout, the fish nobody could name a generation ago, and why your hand goes to one and not the other.

Key figures & facts referenced:
Spencer F. Baird — head of the U.S. Fish Commission; wrote in 1880 that the better kinds of carp "ranked in Europe with the trout"

tab_title: One Stove Heated the Whole House — and Its Pipe Could Burn It Down
description:
A January night in the 1860s. One iron stove glows downstairs, and its pipe climbs through a hole cut in the ceiling, straight across the children's bedroom, before it ever reaches the chimney.

That pipe was the only heater upstairs. It was also the most dangerous thing in the house: iron hot enough to warm a room could slowly char a wooden joist for months — and set it alight on an ordinary evening, with nobody awake to smell the smoke.

What you'll see:
· Why a sealed cast-iron stove beat the open fireplace — and pushed heat into the whole house
· The stovepipe detour: routed through the bedroom above on purpose

· Frost on the inside of the windows, and which child got the warm side of the room
· The thimble: the small metal collar that stood between a family and a house fire
· Banking the stove at night — and how the octopus furnace grew out of all this

description:
Betty is eighty, and she called me embarrassed. Her 1954 ranch house in Englewood smelled like fish. She'd cleaned the refrigerator twice and had the windows open for three days. It took me four minutes to find it behind her recliner: an outlet with a brown stain the color of weak tea. But what really worried me was something she said about the smell, and I'll tell you why before the end.

I'm Walt Harmon. I inspected houses around Dayton, Ohio for 38 years. These are the 7 house smells I never ignore, and which of three boxes each one goes in: open a window, call someone today, or leave the house now.

In this video:
• Burnt dust the first time the heat comes on, and when it isn't dust anymore

• A fishy or hot-plastic smell: what an overheating outlet looks like

Three things to do this week:
1. Do a smell walk. Come in from outside, where your nose is fresh, and walk the whole house slowly: basement, furnace, water heater, laundry, every bathroom. Take somebody younger with you if you can.

3. Put the emergency number from your gas bill in your phone, and check that you have a carbon monoxide alarm on every level and outside the bedrooms, with a working battery.

tab_title: Before You Buy Window Film or Bubble Wrap This Winter, Know These 12 Numbers (What Each One Saves)
description:
One old single-pane window in a gas-heated house near Chicago lets about $35 of heat out every winter, through the glass alone. A film kit covers it for about $1.50; a new window costs about $2,200. Here is what each fix in between saves, with the math so you can redo it for your own house.

The twelve: 30% of a home's heating energy goes out the windows; about 1 home in 3 still has single-pane glass; about $35 a winter for one old window on gas ($96 on electric heat); half a tube of caulk per window; a hidden 1/4 to 1/2 inch gap behind the trim; bubble wrap on the glass cut a window's heat loss about 15% in a lab test, not half; shrink film about a third in a real house; closed curtains up to 10%; tight cellular shades 40%; a low-E storm window takes an old window from a U-factor of 0.88 to 0.36; a new window takes about 80 years to pay for itself on gas; and the 5.7 square feet of opening every bedroom window has to keep.

The per-window dollars are my arithmetic: U-factor times area times heating degree days times 24 hours, priced with 2025 EIA averages. The popular line that bubble wrap "cuts the heat loss in half" goes back to an estimate on a do-it-yourself website, not a measurement.

Safety: every bedroom needs a window that opens for escape. Don't caulk, nail, screw or paint a bedroom sash shut, and if you film or wrap a bedroom window, make sure everyone who sleeps there knows it pulls right off. In a home built before 1978, old window paint may contain lead: mist it with water before you scrape and clean up with wet cloths, as the EPA advises. Keep space heaters at least three feet from curtains, and keep candles away from them.

tab_title: How To Install Your Battery-Powered Nest Doorbell Wire-Free
description:
Keep an eye on what’s going on at your front door with the #NestDoorbell (battery). It has a built-in rechargeable battery which means it can be installed in any type of home and is easy to set up yourself.

To set up the Nest Doorbell at your front door:

1. Charge your Nest Doorbell with the power cord provided.
2. Add your Nest Doorbell in the Google Home app and scan the QR code on the back of your device. Make sure the battery option is turned on.
3. Connect your device to your home Wi-Fi and bring outside. The Nest Doorbell will light up green when it connects. You’ll want to make sure you have a strong connection where you’re installing the device.
4. Install the base plate to the wall using a drill and the screws provided.
5. Clip Nest Doorbell into the base plate. You will hear a click when it’s secure.
6. Once it is secured, finish setting up your Nest Doorbell by following the steps in the Google Home app.

September Description Update: Nest Doorbell (battery) requires the Google Home app and a Google Account – it’s not compatible with the Nest app or the home.nest.com site.

tab_title: Stop Lost-Time Injuries: PPE, Van Checks & Driving
description:
Field safety starts long before you open the panel. In this HVAC School safety meeting, we lay out the everyday habits that keep technicians on the job and out of the hospital. We cover vehicle inspections, the right gloves, and staying alert behind the wheel. One theme runs through all of it: routine work becomes high-risk the moment you stop paying attention. The goal is to stop injuries before they turn into stitches, an OSHA recordable, or lost time away from work.

We open with a real story from the turnpike. A service van with low tire tread hydroplaned during a simple lane change, spun a full 360, and hit the wall. Luckily, nobody else was nearby. That near miss is why weekly van checks matter. Walk around your vehicle before you get in, check tire tread depth, have a coworker confirm your brake lights work, and report new noises right away through the QR code system. Dropping your van off for weekend maintenance catches worn brakes, leaks, and bald tires before they leave you stranded or worse.

Next, we talk about PPE, especially gloves. One of our techs had a hand sliced by sheet metal dangerously close to a main artery. Since then, we’ve challenged every technician to make gloves part of the daily routine. Skipping gloves for weeks without a problem tricks your brain into thinking it’s safe, until the day it isn’t. Today’s high-dexterity gloves let you feel screws, valves, and spade terminals, and welding sleeves protect your arms during brazing. Keep a spare pair clipped to your bag or belt so a rooftop gust of wind never catches you bare-handed.

We also cover driving. Distracted drivers, pedestrians glued to their phones, and electric scooters crossing intersections make every trip a risk. Use the Smith System, look left-right-left before crossing a crosswalk, and remember that dash cameras protect you if something goes wrong.

In the second half, we get into ladder safety, which is part of your van checks too. Secure ladders to the racks and racks to the vehicle, and replace sun-damaged straps. Never stand a short ladder on top of the van to reach a roof. When climbing, stay aware of anything bulky you’re carrying, like a backpack that can snag at the top or a drill that can fall on the person holding the ladder.

tab_title: How to Evacuate an AC system, Full Vacuum Procedure
description:
Bryan goes deep into how to evacuate an AC system, covering the full vacuum procedure. He explains how to connect vacuum pumps, micron gauges, remove cores, and much more to show you start to finish how to pull a deep vacuum on any air conditioner or refrigeration equipment.

This video is a collaboration with Paul from The Engineering Mindset channel. Check out Paul's video on how a vacuum pump works here:    • Vacuum Pumps Explained - Basic working pri...  

The goal of a deep vacuum is to get EVERYTHING out of the system, including non-condensable gases, oxygen, water vapor, and other contaminants in the air. There isn't really such a thing as a true "vacuum," which is the absence of molecules; however, the vacuum pump creates negative pressure, which forces molecules to move towards the area of lower pressure. We measure vacuum in tiny units called microns; one micron is equivalent to one-MILLIONTH of a meter of mercury column. Atmospheric pressure is equivalent to 762,000 microns, and the vacuum pump should pull below 500 microns.

Before we even hook up a vacuum pump, we need to make sure we have a clean, dry, and tight system that's free of solid and liquid contaminants. To do that, make sure your copper is sealed and that you are purging with nitrogen and flowing it while brazing. The system also needs to be leak-free before you connect the vacuum pump, and you can verify that a system is leak-free with a pressure test and a bubble test at joints. Eventually, the decay test will reveal microscopic leaks, which is normal.

For best results, use a modern two-stage vacuum pump, large-diameter vacuum hoses (greater than 1/4" and not a manifold or refrigerant hose), a core remover tool, and a high-quality vacuum gauge that reads in the micron scale. You also need to check the vacuum pump oil level and quality; change the oil if it's opaque or the level is low. Then, connect the micron gauge to the pump and pull below 50 microns to confirm that the pump is working. It's also a good idea to utilize the gas ballast when you're working on a potentially wet system. A system that's known to have water in it can benefit from the use of a heat gun to speed up the boiling process under low pressure.

To connect to the system, make sure there's no pressure on the system. Use the core removal tools to remove the cores from the system. From there, you can use a one-hose setup or two-hose setup to attach the pump. If you're pulling a vacuum on the evaporator and line set, a one-hose setup will suffice. However, a two-hose setup is ideal if you're pulling a vacuum on the entire system. After you remove the core from the side you're pulling the vacuum from, remove the end of the tool and connect the hose. Connect the hose back to the vacuum pump and attach your micron gauge to the system (as far away from the pump as possible); you can use a brass adapter with a core depressor to attach the micron gauge.

Then, you pull the system below 500 microns and isolate the system by shutting off the core remover tool. You will then do your decay test, where you make sure the system pressure doesn't rise. In general, pulling below 500 microns, isolating for 10 minutes, and making sure the pressure doesn't rise above 1000 microns will suffice; we pull below 300 microns and make sure the pressure doesn't exceed 500 microns in 10 minutes. However, the sensor in the micron gauge can be affected by refrigerant and can give strange numbers. (You can break the vacuum with nitrogen to stop that.)

There are some myths about pulling fast, deep vacuums. One myth is that you'll freeze water in the system, and the other is that you'll damage the oil by pulling too deep. POE oil actually requires a very deep vacuum, and you won't damage the oil unless you pull below 1 micron. You CAN freeze water in a vacuum, but there is usually enough heat in the HVAC system to prevent that from happening.

tab_title: How to Cut Rafters FAST
description:
If you've never seen production roof cutting (gang cutting) please check out Will Holladay's website http://theroofcutter.blogspot.com/.  I read Will's book as soon as it came out and was blown away by his techniques for increasing production.  With some practice this gets fast and is very accurate. 

If you decide to try gang cutting, use a good sharp chisel tooth chain and the Headcutter from Big Foot Tools (http://www.bigfootsaws.com/bigfootpro....  

The 2 most common knee jerk responses to this are:
1) Chainsaws aren't accurate enough.  This is totally false.  My rebuttal is cut a batch of rafters 1 at a time and then rack them and notice the differences.

2) It takes longer to set up than to just cut 1 at a time.  "False"-Dwight Shrute  As you can see the rafters only get handled to rack them, and even cutting the tails and stacking them off to the side is faster than handling a pattern and marking that pattern times the number of rafters.  The more rafters you need to cut, the more time is saved.

Production comes from economy of movement and sometimes speed of movement.

Thanks for watching. 

Please remember, I’m not showing the best way of doing something, just what works well for us.

EIGHT brand-new Crown boilers. ONE $30,000 mistake. And a New York master plumber who traveled across America to help save them from the scrap yard!

tab_title: The #1 Fireplace Remodeling Mistake
description:
Planning a fireplace remodel in the Phoenix area? The Fire Place by Magic Touch designs, installs, finishes, services, and repairs complete fireplace projects. 

Visit FireAndAirAZ.com or TheFirePlaceAZ.com to learn more or schedule a private showroom consultation in Mesa, Arizona.

The biggest fireplace remodeling mistake happens before the new fireplace is ever installed: designing and building the wall before choosing the fireplace and understanding its installation requirements.

In this video, I explain why the fireplace, venting, framing, clearances, gas supply, electrical requirements, finish materials, TV placement, and future service access all need to be considered as one complete system.

This is especially important when replacing or relocating a gas fireplace.
Homeowners—and sometimes experienced remodelers—often assume an existing fireplace can simply be moved a foot or two, that a couple of vent elbows can be added, or that a new direct-vent system can be routed through existing fireplace venting.

Fireplace venting doesn't work like HVAC ductwork.
If it physically fits, that does not mean it is listed and approved.

In the video, I explain:
• Why you should choose the fireplace before framing the remodel
• Why gas fireplace venting can determine whether a design is possible
• Why direct-vent fireplace components cannot simply be fabricated or modified in the field
• What can happen when an older fireplace's listed vent components are discontinued
• Why moving a gas fireplace only a few feet can require redesigning the entire vent system
• Whether existing fireplace venting can be reused
• Why framing and combustible-clearance requirements matter
• Why electric fireplaces provide considerably more remodeling flexibility
• Gas vs. electric fireplace remodeling considerations
• Why an NFI Certified Hearth Design Specialist should be involved early in the project
• Why future fireplace service access needs to be designed in from the beginning
• The advantage of having one company responsible for the fireplace, construction, installation, finishes, service, and warranty support
One of the biggest differences between gas and electric fireplace remodeling is venting.

Electric fireplaces eliminate the combustion vent system entirely, which can make relocation and modern media-wall designs substantially easier. Gas fireplaces can provide a real flame and significant heat, but the fireplace and its approved vent system need to be planned together from the beginning.

I'm not suggesting that gas fireplaces are the wrong choice—we install, remodel, repair, and service gas fireplaces every day. The important thing is understanding the complete scope of the project before demolition and construction begin.

Why Work With a Fireplace Specialist?
At The Fire Place by Magic Touch, fireplaces aren't an add-on to kitchen and bathroom remodeling. They're our specialty.

Our team can handle the complete project, including fireplace selection, hearth design, demolition, framing, gas work, electrical work, venting, fireplace installation, tile and finish work, startup, warranty assistance, and future fireplace service.

I'm also an NFI Certified Hearth Design Specialist, and our experience extends beyond making the finished wall look good. We design around the appliance manufacturer's installation requirements and think about how that fireplace will be maintained and serviced years from now.

If you're considering a fireplace remodel in Mesa, Gilbert, Chandler, Scottsdale, Phoenix, Tempe, Queen Creek, Apache Junction, Gold Canyon, or the surrounding Phoenix metro area, visit:

See the fireplaces operating in our Mesa showroom, compare gas and electric models side-by-side, explore finish options, and talk through the entire project before anyone starts tearing your house apart.

Fireplace sales and installation (through our sister brand, The Fire Place)

Very quiet operation indoors and outdoors (comparable to a microwave hum)

⚠️ Cons of the Gree Livo

A professionally installed garage mini split (unit, electrical, refrigerant lines, warranty, etc.) typically costs $5,500 and up

description:

I show you how to cut your cooling costs down using water mist
Here's the link to my Window Air Conditioner video    • DIY How to Cut Electric Bill in Half: Part...  

Evaporative cooling is great. It's how our bodies keep cool when it's hot. We sweat. The sweat evaporates and that phase change carries heat away from our bodies because it takes heat to turn liquid water into water vapor.

When you spray a mist of liquid water into the air, the tiny droplets of liquid can evaporate into individual water vapor molecules. Again, it takes heat to do that, and in this case the heat comes from the air. The result is cooler air. If you live in a dry climate, you may even use this principle to cool the air in your home with a device called a swamp cooler.

Now, let's take that principle and apply it to your air conditioner. I've explained how air conditioners work in a previous article, collecting heat from inside the house and dumping it to the air outside the house. Because the outdoor air is hot, the compressor has to make the refrigerant that carries that heat even hotter than the outdoor air because heat always flows from hot to cold, or in this case, hotter to hot.

If you can evaporate water into the air right before it gets pulled into the condensing unit, you can decrease the temperature of the air and thus increase the capacity and efficiency of your air conditioner. Then, instead of dumping that heat from hotter to hot, you're dumping it from hotter to not-quite-as-hot, and that's easier to do.

tab_title: HVAC: BAC Cooling Tower With a CRACKED Drain Valve! Emergency Drain Valve Replacement & Repair!
description:
How Cooling Towers work - A cooling tower is a specialized heat exchanger in HVAC systems that removes waste heat from water by evaporating a small portion of it into the atmosphere. It cools hot water returning from chillers (used in large buildings or industrial processes) by spraying it over internal fill materials while fans pull air across it, dissipating heat before sending the cooled water back to the system. 

How a Cooling Tower Works:

-Hot Water Inlet: Warm condenser water from a chiller (approx. 95°F) is pumped into the top of the tower.
-Distribution & Spray: The water is sprayed through nozzles onto "fill" materials, maximizing surface area and creating a thin film of water.
-Air Movement: A fan pulls or pushes outside air through the fill material, moving in the opposite direction of the water.
-Evaporation & Cooling: As air meets the water, a small percentage of the water evaporates. This evaporation consumes heat (latent heat of vaporization), significantly cooling the remaining water.
-Collection: The cooled water (approx. 85°F) collects in the basin at the bottom.
-Recirculation: The cooled water is pumped back to the chiller to absorb more heat, repeating the cycle. 

Key Components & Types:

-Fill Material: Increases contact time between air and water.
-Drift Eliminator: Captures water droplets from the outgoing air to minimize water loss.

Types:
-Mechanical Draft: Uses high-powered fans to move air.
-Natural Draft: Uses large chimneys (often seen at power plants) to move air. 

Common Applications:
-Cooling towers are essential in large buildings, such as high-rises, hospitals, and data centers, as well as industrial facilities like power plants and factories. 

A cooling tower is a heat removal device that uses water to transfer process waste heat into the atmosphere. Likewise, an industrial cooling tower operates on the principle of removing heat from water by evaporating a small portion of water that is recirculated through the unit.

The mixing of warm water and cooler air releases latent heat of vaporization, causing the water to cool. If you are ever looking down from a high-rise building, you might notice a square unit, with fans on top of it, on the buildings below. That's a water cooling tower.

No one wants to stay in a building with bad air conditioning—at least not for too long. On the other hand, buildings with excellent cooling make you want to return, even if it’s just to enjoy the air. That’s thanks, in large part, to the continued modernization and innovation of the commercial cooling tower system.

What is the purpose of a Cooling Tower?
-A water cooling tower is used to cool water and is a huge heat exchanger, expelling building heat into the atmosphere and returning colder water to the chiller. A water cooling tower receives warm water from a chiller.

-This warm water is known as condenser water because it gets heat in the condenser of the chiller. The chiller is typically at a lower level, like in a basement. The cooling tower’s role is to cool down the water, so it can return to the chiller to pick up more heat.

How Does a Cooling Tower work?
-Air conditioning equipment and industrial processes can generate heat in the form of tons of hot water that needs to be cooled down. That’s where an industrial cooling tower comes in. Overheated water flows through the cooling tower where it’s recirculated and exposed to cool, dry air. Heat leaves the recirculating cooling tower water through evaporation.

-This is called evaporative cooling. The colder water then reenters the air conditioning equipment or process to cool that equipment down, and the cooling cycle repeats over and over again.  When the warm condenser goes into the cooling tower, the water is passed through some nozzles which spray the water into small droplets across the fill, which increases the surface area of water and allows for better heat loss thru greater evaporation.

-The purpose of the fan on top of the water cooling tower is to bring in air from the bottom of the tower and move it up and out in the opposite direction of the warm condenser water at the top of the unit. The air will carry the heat by evaporating water from the cooling tower into the atmosphere.
title: HVAC: BAC Cooling Tower With a CRACKED Drain Valve! Emergency Drain Valve Replacement & Repair!

tab_title: Refrigeration Cycle | Vapor Compression Cycle | Animation | #Refrigerationcycle #HVAC
description:
The refrigeration cycle is a thermodynamic process that is used in refrigeration and air conditioning systems to transfer heat from a low-temperature region (typically the conditioned space) to a high-temperature region (typically the surroundings). The purpose of the refrigeration cycle is to maintain a lower temperature in a controlled environment by removing heat from that space.

The refrigeration cycle consists of four main components: the compressor, condenser, expansion valve (or throttle valve), and evaporator. These components work together to circulate a refrigerant, which is a fluid with desirable thermodynamic properties for heat transfer.

Here is a brief overview of the four stages of the refrigeration cycle:

Compression: The refrigerant enters the compressor as a low-pressure vapor and is compressed, increasing its temperature and pressure.

Condensation: The high-pressure, high-temperature refrigerant then flows into the condenser, where it releases heat to the surroundings. As a result, the refrigerant condenses into a high-pressure liquid.

Expansion: The high-pressure liquid refrigerant passes through the expansion valve, which reduces its pressure and temperature. This causes the refrigerant to partially vaporize, entering the next stage as a low-pressure mixture of liquid and vapor.

Evaporation: The low-pressure refrigerant mixture enters the evaporator, where it absorbs heat from the conditioned space, causing the remaining liquid to vaporize. The vaporized refrigerant is then drawn back into the compressor, and the cycle repeats.

By continuously circulating the refrigerant through these stages, the refrigeration cycle removes heat from the conditioned space, keeping it cool, while releasing the absorbed heat to the surroundings.

It's important to note that the refrigeration cycle can be modified and optimized for various applications, such as domestic refrigerators, air conditioners, industrial cooling systems, and more. Different refrigerants and system configurations can be utilized based on specific requirements and environmental considerations.

tab_title: INDOOR INSTALLATION 2ND TYPE.|| HOW TO INSTALL SPLIT AC INDOOR WITH FLIER INSIDE THE ROOM,
description:
A mini-split system has two main components: an indoor evaporator, which cools the air, and an outdoor condenser, which dissipates heat.
They’re connected by a line set, tubing that passes through a baseball-size hole in the wall, carrying hot refrigerant outside and cold refrigerant in.
Our line set also included cable to power the evaporator and a drain line to carry condensation outside.
Mount the evaporator inside the room on an exterior wall away from direct sunlight, doorways and sources of dust.
Make sure this area of the wall is free of wires, pipes and ducts that would interfere with making a hole for the line set.
Mark the stud locations and fasten the bracket to them with screws.
The line set hole must slope slightly downward to the outside so condensate from the evaporator can drain outside.
Begin by drilling a pilot hole from inside to outside.
Then go outside and make sure no trim or other obstructions will complicate drilling the full-size hole.
Cut with a hole saw from inside, move aside any insulation and inspect the wall cavity for obstructions.
Finish the hole by drilling from the outside.
Carefully uncoil the line set from the back of the evaporator.
With an assistant outside, feed the line set through the hole.
As it emerges, the assistant should gently bend the line set downward and to the side as needed to reach the condenser.
Keep the rigid plastic collar surrounding the line set at the end that connects to the condenser.
The drain line is shorter and goes through last, below the other lines.
Add the drain extension and wrap the joint with electrical tape to keep it secure.
Wrap the foam sleeve around the section of line set within the hole and replace any insulation in the wall cavity that was disturbed.
Then hang the evaporator on the mounting bracket.
Pro tip: Your helper may need to feed a few more inches of the line set outside as you do this.
On the outside, insert the two-piece plastic trim into the hole to prevent any rough edges from damaging the line set.
Set the condenser on a pad on the ground or mount it on a wall bracket so that the refrigerant lines can reach it easily.
Route the line set so it stays tight to the building exterior and doesn’t leapfrog any obstructions. This makes it easier to install a cover.
Ensure the condenser has the recommended clearance from walls and bushes.
Avoid placement where ice or packed snow could fall on it or where other appliances vent.
A location on the east or north side of the structure maximizes cooling efficiency.\
This step varies by manufacturer.
With this system, a locking lever presses the line connections together.
Before powering up, inspect the refrigerant lines for kinks and verify the electrical connections.
Then go inside and set the temperature using the handheld controller.
Insulate and seal the hole in the outside wall, then cover the line set using sections of plastic or metal channel cut to length.
Place the back half of the channel behind the line set, plumb it and anchor it to the wall with self-tapping screws.
Our line set travels horizontally to the compressor, so when we added the channel corner, we drilled a hole in it to allow the drain line to exit straight down. Jabirwaqas.com

description:
OEM or aftermarket — it's one of the most debated questions in the boiler room. Brian Grindstaff has 24 years in boiler parts and a clear answer on when each one is the right call.

Ritchie Ware sits down with Brian Grindstaff, the man behind BoilerWAREhouse, to break down the OEM vs. aftermarket parts decision. They cover form-fit-function rules, when codes and UL listings change the equation, safety device considerations, and how to know when to call an expert.

Making the wrong call on a part substitution can mean code violations, insurance issues, or a dangerous failure. Knowing where the line is — and who to call when you're not sure — can save a tech from a serious mistake in the field.

Brian Grindstaff leads the parts operation at BoilerWAREhouse.com, where the team fields these exact calls daily and can help techs identify the right part — OEM or aftermarket — for their specific application.

Need a part or not sure if a substitution is safe? Talk to the team at boilerwarehouse.com — real parts experts, not a chatbot.
