Related search terms:
OEM vs aftermarket boiler parts, can I substitute boiler parts, boiler OEM parts replacement, aftermarket boiler controls, low water cutoff vs level control, boiler relief valve selection, UL listed boiler parts, boiler parts expert advice, when to use OEM boiler parts, boiler tech parts decisions

Related Search Q&A:

Can I substitute an aftermarket part for an OEM boiler part?

It depends on the part. For fittings, hoses, gaskets, and valves, if form, fit, and function match and pressure/temperature ratings are met, substitution is often acceptable. For safety devices, controls, and highly engineered components like blower wheels, you need to verify UL listings, code compliance, and manufacturer specs first.

What is the difference between OEM and aftermarket boiler parts?

OEM parts carry the original equipment manufacturer's part number. Aftermarket parts may come from the same factory but are sold under a different brand or part number, often at a lower price point.

When should I always use OEM boiler parts?

For highly engineered components like burner blower wheels, and for safety-critical devices where the specific UL listing, ASME stamp, or insurance approval is tied to the original part, go back to the OEM.

How do I know if a relief valve substitution is safe?

Verify the set pressure, capacity, and whether it carries the proper ASME stamp for your application — for steam boilers, confirm it has the Section I 'V' stamp, not a Section VIII stamp.

Where can I get help choosing the right boiler part?

BoilerWAREhouse.com has a team experienced in UL standards, NFPA, CSD-1, and ASME requirements who can walk you through OEM and aftermarket options for your specific application.

tab_title: Screw Compressor Noise: What Most Techs Blame On Bearings
description:
The screw compressor sounds like a bag of rocks, and everything points to bearings. Sometimes the bearings are perfectly fine. A weak IGBT in the VFD sends a dirty output to the motor, and the vibration it causes sounds just like a bearing failure. That same IGBT can still pass a diode test on your meter.

In this one I walk through the diode test on an IGBT module: where to land your leads, the readings I want to see, and why a pass only means it's safe to power up. The module on the bench passes every check. It came out of a screw machine that sounded like it had failed bearings. New module in, and the bearing noise was gone.

Would love for you to join me for more chiller training here: https://chilleracademy.com/p/intro-to...

What's covered:

Setting your meter to diode mode and finding the input side, output side, and terminal polarity
Why you test on the termination pad and not the threads inside the bolt hole
Why it doesn't matter which output terminal you test
Testing the DC bus side: OL one direction, a voltage reading when you flip the leads, same idea as an SCR check
The 0.3 to 0.4 VDC most manufacturers call for, and why I want to see 0.34 to 0.38
Running the full test across every terminal pair
What a pass actually tells you: no internal short and safe to power up, not proof the module is good
Static test versus load test, and why your meter can't see a module that is going weak
The module that passed on the bench and still made a screw compressor sound like it had failed bearings
Why this applies to any motor on a drive, not just screw compressors
Overcurrent and phase faults as other signs the module is going weak
Heat, run time, and heat sink cooling: what wears an IGBT down
How a weak IGBT's dirty output puts vibration into the rotor that sounds like a bearing failure
Why catching it early means a module swap, and letting it run means bearings too

More chiller training: https://chilleracademy.com

0:00 Setting Up a Diode Test on an IGBT Module
1:01 Testing the Output and DC Bus Terminals
1:55 The Readings to Expect: 0.3 to 0.4 VDC
2:55 Running the Full Test on Every Terminal
4:05 A Pass Means Safe to Power Up, Not Good
5:10 The Bearing Noise That Was Really the IGBT
6:14 Overcurrent, Phase Faults, and What Wears IGBTs Down
6:47 Why a Dirty Output Sounds Like Bad Bearings
7:43 Catch It Early or Lose the Bearings
title: Screw Compressor Noise: What Most Techs Blame On Bearings

tab_title: Heat Pump Refrigeration Cycle for Beginners + 4 Rules That Never Change
description:
Learn how the heat pump refrigeration cycle works in heating mode by understanding four fundamental rules that remain the same whether a heat pump is heating or cooling.

In this HVAC training lesson, we'll follow the flow of refrigerant through an air-source heat pump and explain how the reversing valve changes the direction of refrigerant flow to provide heating instead of cooling.

We'll cover:

The 4 fundamental rules of the refrigeration cycle

How the reversing valve directs hot refrigerant vapor

Why the indoor coil becomes the condenser in heating mode

How a heat pump absorbs heat from cold outdoor air

How expansion devices and check valve bypasses work

Why refrigerant pressure and temperature drop through a metering device

How the outdoor coil acts as the evaporator

The purpose of the suction accumulator and how it protects the compressor

Whether you're new to HVAC, attending trade school, or learning the fundamentals of heat pump operation, this lesson will help you understand the refrigeration cycle without getting overwhelmed by unnecessary complexity.

Understanding these four rules will make it easier to follow refrigerant flow in both heating and cooling modes.

Understanding the air source heat pump refrigeration cycle is essential for mastering heating mode diagnostics.

This lesson breaks down the heating cycle into four distinct stages. We track how refrigerant moves through the compressor, coils, and expansion devices to transfer heat effectively. By focusing on the physical state changes within the system, you will gain a clearer picture of how thermal energy moves from the outdoor environment into the conditioned space.

Whether you are an HVAC technician or a student, grasping these mechanics is vital for troubleshooting modern equipment. We look at how the refrigeration cycle functions when the system is in heating mode rather than cooling. You will learn to identify the role of each component, ensuring you can accurately diagnose issues related to refrigerant flow and heat transfer efficiency.

0:00 The 4 Rules That Never Change
2:29 How the Reversing Valve Works
3:27 Heating Mode – The Indoor Condenser
4:05 Expansion Valves and Check Valve Bypasses
4:47 Pressure Drop and Flash Gas
5:18 How Heat Is Absorbed From Cold Outdoor Air
6:16 The Suction Accumulator
title: Heat Pump Refrigeration Cycle for Beginners + 4 Rules That Never Change

description:
Learn more: https://www.rcwindowfilms.com/

How to Tint Your Home Windows: A Comprehensive Guide

Tinting your home windows not only elevates the aesthetic appeal of your residence but also brings a plethora of functional benefits. From heat rejection to UV protection, the advantages are substantial. This article delves into the step-by-step process, as detailed by Max from RC Window Films, emphasizing the key aspects of DIY window tinting.

Benefits of Window Tinting
-Heat Rejection: One of the primary benefits of window tinting is its ability to significantly reduce the heat entering your home, making for a more comfortable living environment.
-Glare Reduction: Tinted windows cut down on glare, which can be particularly beneficial in rooms with televisions or monitors.
-UV Protection: By blocking harmful UV rays, window tinting helps prevent the fading of interior furnishings, including carpets, hardwood floors, and other materials.
-Necessary Tools and Materials
Before embarking on your window tinting project, gathering the right tools and materials is crucial. 

Here's what you'll need:
Cleaning squeegee--------- https://amzn.to/42TS7Bo 
-Scotch Brite Blue pad (non-marring)-------https://amzn.to/3P0SEeS
-Olfa blade ---------https://amzn.to/4bWq9Js
Squeegee for installation --------- https://amzn.to/3TdslVn 
-Tape measure ------https://amzn.to/3uZx8jQ
-Hard card-------------https://amzn.to/3SWMRIp
-Spray bottle with a mixture of water and Dawn dish soap -----------https://amzn.to/3uWhcPl
-Paper towels (Bounty recommended for its durability) -------------https://amzn.to/3uZxC9E

Tools: 
https://amzn.to/3uSHOkn Pouch 
https://amzn.to/4bPCC1f Toolbelt
https://amzn.to/3IcbUT4 Tool-bag
https://amzn.to/3SVd2zh Caulking Tips 

Measuring and Cutting the Film
Accuracy is key in measuring your windows to ensure the tint film covers the entire glass surface without any excess. Measure the width and height of the window, adding an inch to each measurement to allow for an easy application. Depending on the size of your window, select either a 72-inch or 48-inch width material, keeping in mind the amount needed based on your measurements.

Installation Process
Preparation: Start with a thorough cleaning of the window to remove any debris and contamination. This ensures a smooth surface for the film application.
Application: Carefully apply the tint film to the window. Techniques such as avoiding contamination, ensuring the film's edges are aligned with the window's edges, and removing air bubbles are crucial for a successful application.
Finishing Touches: After the film is applied, remove excess water and air bubbles. Ensuring the edges are properly sealed will prevent peeling and ensure the longevity of your tint.

Conclusion
Window tinting is a rewarding DIY project that can significantly enhance the comfort and functionality of your home. By following the detailed steps provided by Max, even beginners can achieve professional-looking results. Remember, patience and precision are your best tools in this project. Share your experiences and any additional tips in the comments below to help others in their window tinting journey.

tab_title: Tesla's Valve Has No Moving Parts. Does It Really Work?
description:
Nikola Tesla patented a valve with no moving parts in 1916: just a channel with teardrop-shaped loops. The internet says it blocks flow one way almost completely. We tested that claim with real published measurements and with our own flow simulation.

What you'll learn:
How the Tesla valve works: forward flow passes straight, reverse flow is thrown back against itself
Why it's a toll road, not a gate: same pump, ~10 L/min forward, ~7 L/min backward
Diodicity: the one number that measures a fluidic diode
Why the Reynolds number decides everything
What the 2021 NYU experiments found, and what our 2D simulation shows
The twist: why pulsing flow makes it work better, and how four valves can make a pump
Where a Tesla valve makes sense, and where you still need a check valve

⏱ Chapters
0:00 Valves with no moving parts
0:30 Tesla's 1916 patent
1:05 Our simulation: forward vs reverse
1:51 Diodicity: the one number that matters
2:30 Reynolds number and the real measurements
3:57 What 2× really means: a toll road, not a gate
4:44 The twist: pulsing flow (two steps forward, one step back)
6:16 Where it makes sense (and where it does not)
7:13 Recap
7:50 Bonus for engineers: how we simulated it

📚 Sources
N. Tesla, US Patent 1,329,559, "Valvular Conduit" (filed 1916, granted 1920)
Q. M. Nguyen, J. Abouezzi, L. Ristroph, "Early turbulence and pulsatile flows enhance diodicity of Tesla's macrofluidic valve", Nature Communications 12 (2021). doi:10.1038/s41467-021-23009-y · arXiv: 2103.17222
Xiaomi Loop LiquidCool announcement, reported by The Register, 5 Nov 2021

🧪 About our simulation
2D lattice-Boltzmann model (D2Q9) of a six-loop Tesla-style valve, about 23,000 fluid grid points. It is simplified and two-dimensional, shown as an illustration, not a lab test. Our results: diodicity 0.94 at Re 100, 1.84 at Re 1000, 2.03 at Re 1500; with an equal back-and-forth push, net forward flow of about 4% of peak.

tab_title: Why Your Furnace Vent Pipe Can Leak Years Later Even When the Joint Looks Finished - Part 2
description:
In this episode of HVAC Know It All, host Gary McCreadie talks with Gaetano Altomare, Category Manager - Plumbing at IPEX by Aliaxis, about installing nonmetallic flue gas venting correctly. They cover pipe preparation, solvent welding, inspection, primer requirements, and combustion testing. Listeners will learn how to avoid weak connections and preserve vent integrity during installation and service.

Gaetano brings firsthand knowledge of certified venting products, manufacturer installation guidelines, and the development of dedicated combustion-testing fittings. His manufacturer's perspective connects the mechanics of pipe-and-fitting fusion with practical field decisions, including cutting older pipe, verifying compatible components, and sealing test-access plugs.

Key Takeaways
How square cuts, beveled ends, clean pipe surfaces, and a dry-fit interference check help produce a properly fused vent connection.
Why certified vent systems require components from one manufacturer and how optical brighteners help inspectors verify primer and solvent cement use.
How local requirements, installation temperatures of 32°F and colder, and pipe sizes of six inches and larger determine primer use for the products discussed.
How a dedicated combustion-testing fitting installed within two feet of the appliance provides probe access without drilling the vent pipe.
Why the test-access plug discussed requires two full turns of Teflon tape rather than relying on plastic threads alone to seal.

tab_title: Ductless Mini Split Basics
description:
Why select a ductless mini-split system? Our guide has all the answers you need to know if a ductless mini-split system is the right choice for heating and cooling your home or business. Learn the key components, capabilities, and benefits of installing a ductless mini-split. For more resources, visit us online or contact our experts today!

For all your heating & cooling needs: https://www.alpinehomeair.com/

Contact our experts: https://www.alpinehomeair.com/contact...

Ductless Mini-Split Air Conditioning (and Heating) Systems consist of three main components. First, there is the indoor air handler. This component mounts to an inside wall and is used to deliver heated or cooled air as well as to control the entire system. Our Blueridge Mini-Splits are controlled with easy-to-use remotes. Some units can be controlled with an app on your smart phone.

The second component of a ductless mini-split system is the outdoor air condenser or heat pump. This can be wall mounted or installed on a pad on the ground like a traditional heating and cooling unit. Each room being heated or cooled needs its own indoor air handler but a single outdoor unit supply to between one and five air handlers. Single Zone, or room, and multi-zone systems are available at Alpine Home Air Products. 

The third component of a ductless mini-split system is the line set. This necessary accessory is used to connect the indoor and outdoor units, provide power, and allow for drainage. There are 2 copper lines, a drain hose, and a power line. These parts can be purchased separately or as part of a ductless mini-split system kit at Alpine Home Air Products.

Shop Blueridge Mini-Splits: https://www.alpinehomeair.com/viewcat...
title: Ductless Mini Split Basics

tab_title: How to Install a Ductless Mini-Split Air Conditioner - Blueridge
description:
Learn how to install a ductless mini-split air conditioner in just nine minutes. A Blueridge Ductless Mini-Split is one of the most affordable ways to heat and cool your home. They’re perfect for additions, garages, or rooms where ductwork isn’t available. Mini-splits are energy efficient, quiet, and easy to install. There are two units to install. First, the indoor air handler and then the outdoor condenser. The two components are connected by copper tubing, called a line set. You can complete most of the work by yourself, however, the last 10% of the work should be completed by a trained professional. 

When you purchase a Blueridge Mini-Split at Alpine Home Air Products you will receive complete installation instructions as well as an installation DVD with select mini-splits. Visit us online for more installation information, to purchase a Blueridge Mini-Split, or to talk with one of our experts about any HVAC related issue.

Adjustable wrench, torque wrench, hex keys or allen wrenches, drill and drill bits, hole saw, utility knife, wire cutter and stripper, phillips and flat blade screwdrivers, a level, safety glasses, & work gloves

0:01:35 – Install the Indoor Air Handler

Choose location, install wall mount, cut hole for lines, drain hose, and electrical wires, connect drain hose and feed lines, hose, and electrical wires through wall, mount unit, connect multi-conductor wire inside unit (refer to manual for proper terminal connections)

0:04:38 – Install the Outdoor Heat Pump Air Condenser

Choose location, install pad or mounting brackets, securely mount condenser, install optional line set covers if desired, make outside connections, connect drain hose, connect copper line set, connect the multi-conductor wire (refer to manual for proper terminal connections)

0:06:32 – Consulting a trained professional for remaining connections is recommended, cut and flare copper lines as needed, properly pressurize the system, check for leaks, release refrigerant into system

0:08:24 – Make electrical connections, a trained professional is recommended

0:08:45 – Power up and test system

Congratulations on completing your ductless mini-split installation!

tab_title: No Heating For 10 years!! Every Plumber Failed - Can we fix it?
description:
For over 10 years this house has had no working heating on one side of the house it’s slowly been getting worse and worse— multiple plumbers have tried, failed, and walked away. Now two plumbers take on the challenge to finally bring the system back to life. description:
Could your basement walls be quietly wasting the heat you pay for? 🏠🔥❄️
In this video, Larry Janesky from Dr. Energy Saver uses a thermal imaging camera to show how much heat can escape through uninsulated foundation walls during the winter.

You'll see why an "unheated" basement may actually be warmer than you think, thanks to heat coming from boilers, furnaces, water heaters, ductwork, and other equipment. Larry explains how the temperature difference between your basement and the outdoors causes heat to move through cold foundation walls, and how this heat loss can continue throughout the heating season.

Then, he takes the thermal imaging camera outside to show the results: a foundation wall that is dramatically warmer than the outdoor air, melted snow along the foundation, and soil that is still thawed near the house.

Don't let uninsulated foundation walls quietly drive up your heating costs. Basement wall insulation can help keep the heat inside, improve comfort, and make your home more energy-efficient.

description:
http://www.drenergysaver.com | 1-866-607-0191

In Episode 71 of the On the Job Video series, Larry Janesky, owner and founder of Dr. Energy Saver, walks us through the attic of a home in Connecticut that had been previously insulated by another contractor to illustrate common mistakes being perpetrated by many insulation contractors across the country. 

The owners of this home had serious comfort issues, with uneven temperatures around the house and rooms that were just drafty and hard to heat. They called contractors from the state energy program for help. After a quick energy audit, the contractors informed the homeowners that they would benefit from additional attic insulation -- and the contractor was then hired to add inches of blown fiberglass to the attic. 

After the work was performed, however, the home was still just as uncomfortable as it was before. That is when they decided to call in Dr. Energy Saver and find out what went wrong. After performing a blower door test, Larry and his team realized that there was a significant amount of air leaking in and out of the house, greatly impacting comfort and energy savings. 

According to Larry, installing attic insulation without air sealing is malpractice, yet it is a very common practice among contractors because homeowners aren’t always aware of the problem. We hope this video will help homeowners across the U.S. make informed decisions when it comes to improving comfort and energy efficiency in their homes.
title: Attic Insulation Done Wrong… and How to Do It Right!

tab_title: Replacing Evaporator HVAC Repair
description:
I am replacing a leaking evaporator coil on an HVAC system. I found the AC evaporator coil leaking at the end of last summer. First I pump down the air conditioning unit. Second I disconnect the condensate drain and open the paneling of the unit up. Third I cut the copper refrigerant lines and pull out the coil. Finally I push the new coil back into place and seal up the pipes.
Once the Evap coil is in place and piped then I placed the AC unit into a pressure test. A pressure test verifies that there’s no leaks on the HVAC system. After the pressure test I evacuated the refrigeration circuit of the ac unit down to 400 microns. And evacuation/vacuum is performed to pull any contaminant and moisture is out of the AC system. Finally I charge up the AC system. Then test the air conditioning system.
title: Replacing Evaporator HVAC Repair

tab_title: Fix NEST dead battery : How to install a  C-Wire
description:
​Is your Nest thermostat dead, blinking red/green, or constantly losing connection?
​If your Nest was installed without a C-wire (Common Wire), it relies on "Power Sharing" from your heating and cooling equipment. Over time, power sharing often fails, draining the internal lithium battery until the thermostat completely shuts off.
​In this step-by-step HVAC tutorial, we cover how to identify power-sharing battery drain and correctly wire a C-wire directly from your air handler / furnace control board to your Nest thermostat baseplate for a permanent fix.

​⚠️ Safety Disclaimer
​Always turn off power to your HVAC equipment at the breaker or power switch before removing thermostat wires or accessing the furnace control board.

​#NestThermostat #CWire #HVACTips #SmartHome #HomeRepair

Cutting takeoffs and proper attachment to trunklines (Mechanical Training # 104)
1.  When setting your hole cuter size you should;
A.  set it for the exact size hole you are cutting
B.  set it about a ¼” larger than the size you want to cut so that you have room for error when setting your takeoff
C.  adjust the speed setting on your hole cutter
D.  all of the above
2.  When using your hole cutter you should;
A:  cut in a clockwise rotation
B.  slightly angle your hole cutter so that it cuts faster
C.  pull back on the hole cutter towards the end of the cut so that the material doesn’t collapse.
D.  all of the above
3.  Whenever possible before starting takeoffs you should;
A.  route all of your supply runs to the trunkline 
B.  mark your takeoff and then strap your run to the takeoff
C.  mastic the trunkline
D.  all of the above
4.  When cutting takeoffs you should;
A.  start and finish installing each takeoff individually
B.  if possible mark all takeoffs at once, then cut all takeoffs at once, then install all takeoffs at once
C.  carry all your tools with you while cutting takeoffs
D.  all of the above
5.  When installing takeoffs in a crawlspace the runs should be; 
A.  perfectly level
B.  cut takeoffs towards the top of the trunkline and add an elbow to keep the runs high
C.  cut the takeoff at a slight angle and angle then run upwards to allow more room for crawling
D.  cut the takeoff towards the bottom of the trunkline to allow room to crawl over
6.  When marking takeoffs avoid placing takeoffs;
A.  closer than 12” of the endcap
B.  on a transition
C.  on an elbow 
D.  all of the above
7.  When marking takoffs, takeoffs should be;
A.  at least 6” apart if not more
B.  staggered from each other and not directly across 
C.  on the correct size duct outlined on the plans
D.  all of the above
8.  After setting a takeoff you should inspect and confirm that
A.  there is no material obstructing the opening
B.  that the radius of the takeoff aligns well with the duct
C.  there is a good seal around the takeoff, mastic tape if necessary 
D.  all of the above
9.  When working with flex duct it is important to
A.  stretch the flex out after opening the box
B.  keep your ends tucked when working with flex
C.  immediately strap flex that it is hanging off a boot or fitting 
D.  all of the above
10.  When planning runs out each run should have
A.  a strap every 8’
B.  downward slope for proper air flow
C.  at least 4-6 feet of flex with two 90 degree turns to avoid excessive noise and airflow
D.  all of the above
11.  Before hanging boots they should; 
A.  always have flex attached
B.  have mastic applied if application allows
C.  have boot clips or plaster flanges if needed
D.  all of the above 
12.  Flex runs should be routed and strapped to the trunkline prior to cutting takeoffs.  When doing this it is important to consider;
A.  planning the most efficient route to the takeoff while considering attic access 
B.  strapping every 4’ and avoiding any sagging
C.  strapping properly to avoid a kink at the boot
D.  all of the above  
13.  When determining where to cut flex for trunkline attachment it is important to  
A.  cut flex about 6”-8” longer to allow for connection loss, adjust if cut too long
B.  cut flex exact length to takeoff
C.  allow plenty of extra flex so that there is plenty for a connection even if the run ends up being too long
D.  cut flex short and add splice later
14.  When making a flex connection to the trunkline you should
A.  tuck the end of your flex duct so that the insulation is doubled up
B.  gently tighten the flex with a double piece of duct tape
C.  use double pieces of duct tape about 5” long, rounding them while sticking them in place
D.  all of the above  
15.  When applying mastic to a takeoff you should
A.  only mastic tape seems
B.  solid mastic a clean circle around the takeoff
C.  mastic before you tape
D.  all of the above
title: Cutting takeoffs and proper attachment to trunklines (Mechanical Training # 104)

Este video muestra cómo sacar la licencia construcción para pinturas residentiales y comerciales en california . 

Esta clasificación es para contratistas de nivel oficial.


Además de 4 años de experiencia como pintor, también deberá documentar esa experiencia en talones de cheques, declaraciones de impuestos, recibos o copias de los contratos. 


La CSLB (Contractors State License Board) también posiblemente querrá ver la firma de un contratista general, titular de la licencia de pintura, capataz o compañero de viaje.

Esta firma verifica que tienes la experiencia como pintor que dices que tienes.

Los requisitos de licencia de contratista en California para obtener una licencia de contratista de pintura son que usted tenga al menos 18 años de edad.

Actualmente no está en libertad condicional o bajo palabra. Tiene una licencia de conducir o identificación válida y un seguro social o un número de ITIN.

Si usted es un pintur que busca expandir sus servicios y escalar su negocio, obtener la licencia de pintura puede ser un paso increíble en su carrera.

En California, cualquier persona que quiera cobrar más de $ 500 por trabajos de pintura, mantenimiento o fabricación debe tener la licencia de contratista pintura C33.

Las grandes compañías de construccion que diseñan e instalan redes y sistemas eléctricos complejos, todas tienen la licencia de construccion y un contrato de construcción.

Todo el mundo obtiene una licencia de contratista por diferentes razones. En algunos lugares, antes que puedes tramitar la licencia de contratista, necesitas ser certificado.

El tiempo de procesamiento de la solicitud para la licencia de pinturas suele ser de 90 días, pero hay muchos factores que pueden hacer que esto tome mucho más tiempo.

La CSLB es la agencia que rige a los contratistas de construcción en California.

Hay 73 diferentes clasificaciones de licencias en California. Cada licencia, aparte de la clasificación de especialidad limitada C-61, requiere que apruebe dos exámenes. El examen de contratista pintura.

115 preguntas de LEY y 115 preguntas de Oficio.

Para una guia más profunda a la licencia de contratista C33, le recomendaría que vea el video anterior y visite nuestro sitio web.

Hay dos niveles de licencia para pintura en California. 

Estudiar para su examen de licencia de contratista es muy importante. 

Querrá asegurarse de estar familiarizado con todas las leyes de la licencia de contratista. También hay certificaciones de construccion disponibles, así como ofrecidas por el Departamento de seguridad y riesgos laborales.

He ayudado a miles de contratistas a obtener una licencia en todo el país. Solo porque cumpla con los requisitos básicos de pintura, no significa que necesariamente tendrá un tiempo fácil en el examen.

He visto situaciones en las que los muchachos tenían décadas de experiencia solo para fallar en el examen porque no estaban familiarizados con todos los aspectos de su oficio. La licencia de contratista de California requiere diferentes áreas de especialización.

Debe recordar que a pesar de sus décadas de experiencia como pintura, la CSLB puede presentarle preguntas para las que no está preparado. Debes usar este video como referencia para los requisitos para licencia de contratista.

Para obtener más información sobre los costos actuales de una licencia de contratista de California, consulte este video:    • California Contractor License Cost - (2022...  

Asegúrese de que está utilizando todos los recursos disponibles para usted, para que puedas ser pintur residencial autorizado.

Los exámenes de práctica de la licencia C-33, las guías de estudio de la licencia de contratista de pintura, las escuelas para la licencia de contratista y las tarjetas de memoria son excelentes recursos para prepararlo para el examen de licencia de contratista.

tab_title: Heat Pump Making Loud Noises During Defrost: Finding the Real Problem EP285
description:
I received a service call for a heat pump with an outdoor fan that stopped spinning, loud grinding noises, and water dripping from the unit. At first, I suspected it was simply going through a normal defrost cycle, something many homeowners aren't familiar with. But just because a heat pump is going into defrost doesn't mean everything is working properly.

After checking refrigerant pressures and testing the defrost cycle, I discovered the reversing valve wasn't switching completely due to a weak solenoid coil. The valve was slipping back and forth between heating and cooling, causing unusual noises and preventing the system from defrosting properly.

Fortunately, I had a replacement reversing valve coil on my truck and was able to get the heat pump operating normally again without replacing the entire reversing valve.

tab_title: Federal Energy Incentives: Unlocking HOMES, HEAR, and Contractor Advocacy
description:
Federal energy rebate programs are back in motion, offering crucial financial incentives that contractors can leverage to grow their business and help homeowners save energy. Discover how contractor-led policy advocacy and peer accountability networks are creating new opportunities across the home performance industry.

On this episode of the R-Value Podcast, IDI expert Ken Allison interviews Kara Saul Rinaldi and Keith O'Hara.

Federal energy rebate programs are actively expanding across the country, providing new momentum for home performance, insulation, and HVAC upgrades. Policy expert Kara Saul Rinaldi outlines the latest developments surrounding the HOMES and HEAR rebate initiatives, breaking down the distinction between prescriptive appliance incentives and performance-based energy savings pathways. She highlights crucial program requirements—including why assessing thermal envelope insulation and air sealing is vital before sizing new heating and cooling systems—and explains how state-level implementations are unfolding nationwide.

Contractor and Building Performance Association board member Keith O'Hara brings the boots-on-the-ground contractor perspective to the conversation. He explains how BPA’s Policy Power-Up initiative allows market-rate contractors to fund direct policy work and gain a direct seat at the legislative table in Washington. Additionally, Keith reveals how contractor peer accountability groups, on-site audits, and direct congressional engagement help business owners solve operational pain points while building a stronger, more profitable industry.

Inside this episode...
01:30 – Clarifying the current national status of the HOMES and HEAR rebate programs
04:15 – Comparing prescriptive HEAR appliance incentives against performance-based HOMES pathways
07:00 – Why thermal insulation and air sealing take priority in HVAC sizing and rebate compliance

About EPA 608 Exam
The EPA Section 608 Certification is a federal requirement in the U.S. for all HVAC technicians who work with refrigerants. The exam ensures that technicians understand safe refrigerant handling, recovery, recycling, disposal, and environmental protection.
The exam is divided into two parts:
Core Section – Required for all certifications. Covers the Clean Air Act, ozone depletion, refrigerant properties, recovery/recycling procedures, and safety.
Type Exams – Focused on specific applications:
Type I – Small appliances
Type II – High-pressure systems
Type III – Low-pressure systems
Universal – Covers all types (Core + Type I, II, III)
Passing the EPA 608 Exam is essential for anyone working in the HVAC industry, as it ensures compliance with federal law and establishes professional credibility.

Today topic: Air Conditioning

Subscribe for new free practice tests every week: 
   / @trueprep  

About HVAC exam

Heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) is the technology of indoor and vehicular environmental comfort. Its goal is to provide thermal comfort and acceptable indoor air quality. HVAC system design is a subdiscipline of mechanical engineering, based on the principles of thermodynamics, fluid mechanics, and heat transfer. Refrigeration is sometimes added to the field's abbreviation as HVAC&R or HVACR, or ventilating is dropped as in HACR (such as the designation of HACR-rated circuit breakers).

HVAC CERTIFICATION
For aspiring heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) specialists, pursuing certification can be a way to show one’s competencies to prospective employers or clients. These credentials can demonstrate a wide range of skills in the field such as: installing, repairing, and maintaining HVAC units in residential or commercial spaces; analyzing air quality, humidity levels, and temperature control mechanisms; understanding the fundamentals of heating and refrigeration systems.

HOW TO BECOME A CERTIFIED HVAC TECHNICIAN
Some job-ready HVAC programs include the certification process as part of their training program such as the one at North American Training Center. That said, there is a wide array of agencies offering HVAC certifications for those looking to enhance their credentials. The North American Technician Excellence (NATE) hosts the “industry competency exam” and provides a number of HVAC-R specialty certifications such as air distribution (AD), HVAC efficiency analyst (senior level), and HVAC performance verifier. HVAC Excellence not only provides program accreditation, but has employment-ready certification exams for air conditioning, light commercial air conditioning, and basic refrigeration and charging procedures. The Refrigeration Service Engineers Society (RSES) has a partnership with NATE and provides additional certification exams including EPA section 608, commercial air conditioning, commercial refrigeration, heating, and HVAC-R electrical.
title: HVAC Exam Prep #1 - Air Conditioning | TruePrep

tab_title: I thought it was the compressor... I was Wrong
description:
I was convinced this rooftop unit had a bad compressor… but the diagnosis took an unexpected turn.
In this video, I walk through a commercial HVAC service call where a tripped breaker initially pointed me toward a failed compressor. After testing the system, checking the windings, and digging deeper into the electrical side, I found the real culprit: a bad condenser fan motor.
This is a great reminder that assumptions can cost you time—and replacing parts without proper testing can cost your customer a lot of money.
In this video you’ll see:✅ Diagnosing a tripped breaker✅ Compressor electrical testing✅ Condenser fan motor troubleshooting✅ Continuity and resistance checks✅ Real-world commercial HVAC diagnostics✅ How a bad fan motor can mimic a compressor failure
Whether you’re an HVAC apprentice, service technician, or seasoned mechanic, hopefully this service call helps you avoid the same trap.
Have you ever been 100% sure of a diagnosis, only to find out it was something completely different? Let me know in the comments!
👍 If you enjoyed the video, please Like, Subscribe, and hit the notification bell for more real-world HVAC service calls every week.

tab_title: What are the Pros and Cons of Heat Pumps?
description:
In the video we break down the Pros and Cons of Heat Pumps. 

Chapters
0:34 - What are the Pros and Cons of Heat Pumps
3:00 - What are the cons of Heat Pumps?

Read the full article below.
https://www.monkeywrenchplumbers.com/...

Air-source heat pumps are becoming an increasingly popular way to heat and cool homes, but like any technology, they have both advantages and disadvantages.

On the pro side, air-source heat pumps are energy-efficient, using much less energy than traditional heating and cooling systems. They also provide both heating and cooling, making them a versatile option for year-round comfort. Additionally, air-source heat pumps don't produce any emissions on-site, making them a more environmentally-friendly option than some other heating and cooling methods.

However, there are also some cons to consider. One is that air-source heat pumps may struggle to provide enough heat in extremely cold temperatures, so they may not be the best option for those living in very cold climates. They can also be more expensive to install than traditional heating and cooling systems, although the long-term energy savings may make up for this cost over time.

Overall, whether or not an air-source heat pump is the right choice for your home will depend on a number of factors, including your climate, energy needs, and budget. In this video, we'll be diving into the details of these pros and cons to help you make an informed decision about whether an air-source heat pump is the right choice for you.
title: What are the Pros and Cons of Heat Pumps?

tab_title: My AC Is Blowing Hot Air! What Should I Do?
description:
Current average price of an AC service call with the outcome of an AC capacitor replacement as shown: $406

When your boss is blowing hot hair … it’s a day of the week ending in Y. When your home’s vents are blowing hot air during the dog days of summer? It’s a day ending in C — as in, emergen-cy. To determine whether this is an issue you can solve for yourself, you can start the process of elimination by checking these four common causes of issues with your air conditioning:

1. Check Your Thermostat, Stat!

The issue could be as simple as someone bumped or otherwise unwittingly altered the setting on the thermostat — such as moving it to the heat setting or raising the temperature above the room temperature — or perhaps the batteries are dead and need to be replaced. Make sure your thermostat is functioning and that the settings are in the right place.

2. Is Your Condensate Drain Line Draining Condensate?

Your AC drain line catches and diverts the condensation created by your system. If this line becomes clogged due to neglect, it could cause a malfunction — not to mention water damage if it overflows. Make sure it’s draining freely into a floor drain or outside.

3. Is Your Furnace Filter Filtering Your Furnace?

If you’ve neglected your HVAC filter replacement routine — you should be changing it quarterly — your filter can get clogged up with crud, making your system struggle to pull air through it, working less and less efficiently and, eventually, choking it off to the point it shuts down altogether. If you haven’t changed your HVAC filter in a while, go ahead and do this asap, regardless of whether it’s the likely culprit.

4. Breaker, Breaker, Do You Read?

Check your circuit breaker box in the garage or basement. Perhaps you have a tripped switch that shut down your outdoor AC compressor. If so, flip it back, check your settings and see if things improve.

If none of these obvious issues solves your climate control catastrophe, you’re gonna need to call a pro! While tending to one’s own household maintenance obligations can be rewarding and is, in many cases, doable if not necessary, some tasks are just too much to ask of your everyday DIYer. That’s why we called in reinforcements for this particular project. Our HomeServe homie, Randy Boutte, who’s a bona fide HomeServe HVAC tech, showed us how he investigates an AC outage, what he does to address it, and what homeowners should expect in terms of time, cost, labor … and sweat.

Watch the video and let us know what you think in the comments section, homeowners: Is this a DIY dilemma, or a problem for the pros?

tab_title: Before You Install: Making Better Choices for HVAC Applications
description:
Good HVAC performance starts before the equipment is installed. Choosing a system that fits the space means looking beyond capacity to consider airflow, humidity, service access, and what the homeowner actually needs.

In this episode of Talking Comfort LIVE, Craig Lynch and JD McCarty discuss how application decisions, ductwork design, and proper commissioning affect comfort, efficiency, and long-term system performance.

The discussion covers HVAC system selection, installation planning, and commissioning, including:

02:17 – Before You Install: Plan for Performance - The team introduces the key application considerations, including comfort, airflow, efficiency, installation cost, serviceability, and homeowner expectations.

02:48 – Bigger Isn’t Always Better - Why choosing a larger system isn’t necessarily the answer to comfort complaints, and how sizing affects humidity control.

03:29 – Solving Hot & Cold Rooms - Craig and JD share examples of using ductless systems to address uncomfortable spaces that a central system wasn’t adequately serving.

08:03 – When Airflow Problems Become Charging Mistakes - JD shares a field story about a system with 30 pounds of excess refrigerant after technicians tried to charge it using supply and return temperatures alone.

09:26 – Serviceability Starts with Equipment Placement - Why installation planning should account for maintenance access—not just whether the equipment fits.

11:10 – Where Does the Air Go? - A discussion of supply and return placement, duct layout, and how conditioned air moves through the occupied space.

15:47 – Choosing the Right Application - Comparing traditional ducted systems, high-wall mini splits, cassettes, concealed ducted units, and hybrid solutions.

17:41 – Plan for Airflow Testing & Balancing - How grille selection, balancing dampers, and documented airflow measurements help deliver the comfort the customer paid for.

23:19 – Attic Installations: Access, Condensation & Drain Risks - Field examples highlight the service challenges and potential water damage associated with equipment installed in attics.

26:24 – “I Want This, Not That”: Managing Customer Expectations - How to explain the tradeoffs when homeowner preferences conflict with sizing, humidity control, airflow, or maintenance needs.

36:20 – From the Jobsite: Ductwork Mistakes - Craig walks through installation photos showing misplaced returns, kinked flex duct, and layouts that left rooms without adequate airflow.

43:48 – Off the Rack: The Inverter Commissioning Gap - The team discusses an industry article on why inverter heat pumps can underperform when installation and commissioning practices don’t match the equipment.

48:24 – Verify Settings & Document Your Startup - A reminder to read the instructions, confirm DIP switch settings, measure static pressure, and record commissioning details for future service.

51:04 – Auxiliary Heat, Staging & Efficiency - How backup heat operation and control configuration can undermine the performance customers expect from a high-efficiency heat pump.

52:56 – Build Good Habits, Not Callbacks - Why practical checklists, technician training, and thorough commissioning matter to both system performance and the company’s bottom line.

55:24 – From the Field: YouTube Questions & Comments - Viewer questions cover compressor wiring, communicating capabilities on older GREE Flex equipment, and static pressure probe placement at the coil.

The takeaway: choosing the right equipment is only part of the job—good planning, verified airflow, and proper commissioning help turn that choice into dependable comfort.

Subscribe for more #HVACtraining and technical discussions, and leave your questions or field experiences in the comments.
title: Before You Install: Making Better Choices for HVAC Applications

tab_title: Massively Improve Energy Efficiency by Upgrading Your Attic Flex Ducts!
description:
Duct systems in unconditioned spaces like attics are notoriously problematic.  When duct systems leak air in unconditioned spaces like attics, crawl spaces, garages, etc, that conditioned air is lost completely from the home.  This requires air conditioners and furnaces to run longer in order to bring the house to temperature, which drives up energy costs.  Duct leakage also causes comfort problems in homes.  When that hot or cold air is lost to an attic or crawl space, rather than going to a bedroom or living room, the result is rooms that are hotter or colder than they should be, depending on the season.  Flexible ducts tend to be be fairly tight themselves, but where they leak is where flexible ducts connect to the trunk line and register boots.  And this is the case here as you'll see.  

In this video we look at a really bad, leaky duct system that's in an attic and we show the process of changing out the old leaky take-offs for new air tight ones, and also changing out the old poorly insulated flexible duct for new, highly insulated R-8 rated flexible ducts.  We also show the proper techniques for attaching the take-off's to the trunk line, making sure they're sealed, attaching flexible duct to take-offs / collars and making sure they they are permanently sealed and attached, etc. 

The finished result is a duct system that is far tighter than before we started, resulting in massively improved energy efficiency for this home and comfort for this homeowner!

tab_title: Insulation Expert Reveals the BEST Way to Air Seal Your Attic
description:
This video from Insulwise in Pittsburgh explains how to insulate an attic that is already insulated, as well as the importance of air sealing attics in the first place.  There are three primary reasons to air seal an attic which are to reduce energy loss, improve comfort in the home, and reduce the flow of moisture (in the form of water vapor) from the home to the attic space so as to limit the risks for mold growth.  

The main trick in locating air leaks that may be hidden beneath insulation is to first create a map of all of the air leaks in the attic floor before going up into the attic.  These attic air leaks consist of wire holes, top plates, bathroom fans, drop ceilings and bulk heads, recessed lights, etc.  Once the map is complete it is then much easier for a team to go into the attic and methodically track down all of the penetrations in the attic floor.  Learn more about our air duck sealing process and service here: https://www.insulwise.com/duct-sealin...

tab_title: Impossible 15 Ton Aluminum Condenser Header repair
description:
This videos shows how to solder a large aluminum condenser header to 3/4 copper pipe.   The factory solder joint cracked after 10 years from vibration.   I sum up the key points that I learned below:
1)  Use brand new copper.
2)  Remove all the solder by heating the joint to 900 degrees and either blowing the excess solder off with air, or use a stainless brush in the heat to remove all the extra solder
3)  Use two torches even for smaller headers.
4)  Use two people to hold two Lucas Milhaupt AL822 brazing rods to braze both sides simultaneously
5)  Make sure to degrease with non flammable brake cleaner
6)  Try not to overheat.   The temperature window is very small around 950 deg F.
7)  Do the joint in a single attempt.   If the joint doesn't hold, pull it apart, remove the solder with heat and a stainless brush and use new copper.   The flux creates a barrier that prevents any more solder from sticking.  You really can't solder on top of solder.   

Here is how a robot solders this joint:       • Microchannel Transition Joint Brazing  

Notice the robot just jams the solder in very fast to fill the joint.   The actual soldering is less than 4 seconds.

Here is the Lucas Milhaupt factory instruction video on the tube of solder:      • Learn how to braze aluminum using Lucas Mi...
title: Impossible 15 Ton Aluminum Condenser Header repair

tab_title: Insulating Knee Walls | Making Finished Attics Energy Efficient in Cleveland
description:
http://www.drenergysaver.com | 1-888-225-6260

Knee walls are usually present in finished attics. The sloped roof creates a small space that can hardly be used for anything other than storage or, in some cases, to house air ducts. 

So when finishing the attic, builders usually build a small, finished wall to close that space, many times with small doors to allow access for storage, sometimes with no access at all. 

The problem with knee walls is that, for the most part, the space behind them remains unconditioned and the knee walls themselves are often poorly insulated. 
The soffit vents, built to keep the roof cool, allow a lot of air in the space year round. 

During the summer, that compartment can reach scorching temperatures, and because it is improperly insulated and air sealed, that heat will be transferred to the adjacent room through walls and floor and to the rooms below through the ceiling. 

 Larry Janesky from Dr. Energy Saver, proposes a different approach to knee wall insulation. The knee wall system developed by Dr. Energy Saver includes that small space into the building envelope, while preserving roof ventilation. SilverGlo, a special type of rigid foam board lined with radiant foil on both sides, is attached to the bottom of the rafters with special fasteners. The seams are then sealed with spray foam to prevent air leakages. The idea is to keep the temperature in the compartment behind the knee wall, as close as possible as the temperature in the adjacent rooms. 

The SilverGlo foam is infused with graphite for higher R-Value, and the foil liner will reflect heat back into the room during the winter and back to the outside during the summer. 

For more information on the SilverGlo attic and knee wall insulation system and for tips on how to save a lot of energy and money visit our website or call us for a comprehensive home energy audit!
title: Insulating Knee Walls | Making Finished Attics Energy Efficient in Cleveland

description:

Every day, HVAC contractors pull out their tape measures, run a load calc, and quote equipment—but there's one question almost nobody asks before they size that system, and skipping it turns a perfect Manual J on paper into a short-cycling, humidity-failing, callback-generating system that has your customer sweating upstairs while freezing downstairs. That question is how much air is actually leaking in and out of this house—and with the Department of Energy showing air leakage accounts for 25 to 40 percent of heating and cooling energy in a typical home, guessing at infiltration rates isn't doing a load calculation, it's doing a load estimation with your reputation on the line. In this video, I walk you through exactly why infiltration is the most guessed-at number in residential load calculations, and show you three measurable checkpoints—blower door, duct leakage, and thermal envelope—that let you size equipment to the real house in front of you instead of the assumed one on paper.

tab_title: Installing Radiant Heat Between Joists. Retrofit radiant heat into your home or for new construction
description:
This video walks you through installing radiant heat between the floor joists, how to staple it up using aluminum heat emission plates, and how to install the reflective barrier and insulation. We also show you how to connect to a Radiantec radiant tubing manifold and how to do the pressure test. 

The staple-up radiant floor installation method is very popular because as long as you can see the joists from below, you can install radiant heat. This method works well for new construction and retrofits. In fact, it works so well that it has almost entirely replaced the thin suspended slab applications.

While the slab application is pretty forgiving, it is our opinion that a staple up installation needs to be done exactly right for it to work properly. The following methods MUST be followed to have and effective and efficient staple-up installation:
1) Install Aluminum Heat Emission Fins. These are also called heat transfer plates or aluminum fins. A study conducted by Kansas State University some years ago showed that systems using heat transfer plates vs. systems that do not are able to transfer twice as many btu’s. The significance is that you can typically lower the water temperature and reduce cycle times which can lower your operational cost. 

Radiantec also conducted our own plate study experiments and you can find the results here. The most cost effective solution is to install the thin heat transfer plates in continuous coverage. We did find that the thicker, extruded aluminum plates transferred about 6% more heat but at more than double the cost.

Ideally, the heat transfer plates should be spaced continuously but they don’t have to be. Our general rule of thumb is to space the aluminum plates continuously in carpeted rooms, bathrooms, and high heat loss areas such as great rooms. Space them about every 8″ or so in all other areas.

2) Install An Aluminum Reflective Barrier. About 1-2″ below the radiant tubing and plates, you should install an aluminum reflective barrier. This is nothing more than a craft paper with an aluminum facing. It has fibers that run through it so it doesn’t rip or tear but it can be cut with a pair of scissors. The reflective barrier comes on a roll that is 50″ wide and must be cut so that it can fit between the joists. We have an installation video that shows how to do this. The purpose of the reflective barrier installation is to reflect the radiant heat waves back up towards the sub-floor. We are also trying to create a small dead air pocket that further helps to equalize the heat transfer. Some will argue that the reflective barrier isn’t necessary and that it will become covered up with dust and lose its effectiveness over the years. We still feel it’s an important piece and since it’s relatively inexpensive, it should be installed. Insulation is usually put in after this (see next step) so if you can find a foil faced insulation with high enough R-value, you can forgo this product.

3) Install Insulation. Many people ask us if it’s necessary to also install insulation below the radiant tubing, heat transfer plates, and reflective barrier. If you can only do this once because the ceiling will be finished then the answer is absolutely yes. The amount of insulation is dependent on what is above and below. If there is carpeting or a high heat loss area above then you should put in R-19. If not, you can probably get away with R-13 but R-19 is better. The type of insulation doesn’t really matter all that much. If there is an unheated basement below then you should use R-19. Most people don’t mind if they lose a little bit of heat downward in this scenario. If the heat loss downward is entirely wasted to a crawl space, for example, then your insulation method should be extensive. You should try to get in a minimum of R-30. Some will insulate between the joists with fiberglass and then seal the entire underside with rigid foam. If the ceiling will not be finished, some will wait and see how the system performs and then add the insulation after if necessary. What can happen if you don’t insulate? Since radiant heat will go in all directions, the heat will just as easily go downward. The basement will get too warm and you won’t get enough heat into the space above.
 
Will a radiant system without aluminum plates work? The best answer is “maybe.” If plates are not used then you are relying on air and the few locations where tubing is in contact with the floor to transfer the heat. The problem is, air is an insulator and Pex directly in contact with wood is a poor conductor. In order to make up for this poor heat transfer, the water temperature must be raised significantly. In some cases, as high as 180 degrees F.! Even then, on a cold day, the floor may not put out enough heat to heat the room if the home is older and not energy efficient.
title: Installing Radiant Heat Between Joists. Retrofit radiant heat into your home or for new construction

tab_title: Radiant heating in a concrete slab. Let us show you how easy it can be to  install radiant heat!
description:
Installing Pex tubing in a concrete slab is one of the easiest ways to install radiant heat. When installed in a concrete slab, radiant underfloor heating is very efficient and comfortable. Since the concrete slab radiant installation is fairly simple, many people fail to follow some simple yet very important steps thinking that it will work no matter what. To make sure you do the work right, please watch this video and read our manuals at: https://www.radiantec.com/installatio...

When you buy the tubing from Radiantec, we’ll provide you with a custom tubing layout. This layout is part of our free design assistance and many of our customers find it very helpful. Since concrete is a decent conductor for radiant heat, having an exact and perfect tubing arrangement isn’t necessary for most projects. You should try to use all of the tubing that was specified, space it out reasonably well, and make sure the tubing lengths are neither too short or too long. In areas with a lot of windows, the tubing can be spaced closer. In the middle of the room or in closets, space it further apart.

Here are some general rules of thumb for concrete slab radiant heating installations. These recommendations are general in nature. As with any building project, be certain to check with your code official before starting the work.

1) On top of the compacted earth or sand, install a vapor barrier.
2) Lay down at least 2″ of rigid foam insulation. Extruded or expanded polystyrene is the material of choice. Radiantec doesn’t recommend using radiant barriers or “bubble wrap” insulation for radiant floor heating.
3) Install the wire mesh or rebar for the concrete slab.
4) Attach the tubing to the wire mesh or rebar using plastic zip ties. If there is no steel, it is acceptable to staple the tubing directly to the insulation.
5) Connect the radiant tubing to a Radiantec slab manifold and pressure test.
Be sure to also read our Design and Construction Manual and to give us a call with any questions. We’re here to help make sure your radiant heating project is installed correctly and will provide many years of trouble-free operation.

tab_title: Attic Duct Replacement: Fixing Sweating Ducts & High Humidity
description:
Watch our dedicated HVAC team take on a full 3-day attic ductwork replacement

The Problem: Sweating Ductwork, High Humidity & Poor Airflow
Before this project, the homeowner was dealing with several common HVAC problems in Northeast Florida, including:
• Sweating ductwork and excessive condensation in the attic
• High indoor humidity and excessive household dust
• Negative air pressure and restricted or unbalanced airflow
• Hot and uncomfortable rooms throughout the home
• An HVAC system running excessively and contributing to high electric bills

Damaged, poorly sealed or improperly installed ductwork can contribute to air leakage, uneven temperatures, humidity concerns and reduced HVAC efficiency.

The Solution: Complete Attic Ductwork Replacement
Our HVAC crew spent three full days removing the old ductwork and installing a new duct system in this Orange Park home.
This project included removing the existing ductwork, installing duct supports and insulated flexible duct, connecting the ductwork to distribution boxes and ceiling register boots, sealing connections with duct mastic, and positioning the new duct runs to support balanced airflow.
Attic work in North Florida can be challenging, even in winter. Although this project took place in January, the heat trapped beneath the roof was so intense that our time-lapse cameras repeatedly overheated and shut down during installation. Our team kept working through the difficult conditions to complete the ductwork replacement.

The Results: Better Comfort Throughout the Home
After the ductwork replacement, the homeowner reported significant improvements in home comfort and HVAC performance, including:
• More balanced airflow and more consistent cooling from room to room
• Reduced indoor humidity and dust
• Shorter HVAC run times and noticeably lower monthly electric bills
• Consistent indoor comfort, with the system maintaining approximately 70°F throughout the summer

Actual results vary by home, equipment condition, duct design, insulation, and other factors. However, this project demonstrates how addressing ductwork problems can make a meaningful difference in home comfort.
If your HVAC unit is running constantly or your home suffers from humidity and airflow problems, our team is here to help. Contact us today for expert heating, cooling, and ductwork services throughout Jacksonville Florida and the surrounding areas!

tab_title: How to Waterproof a Basement | Ron Hazelton's House Calls feat. Basement Systems
description:
https;//www.basementsystems.com | 1-866-713-1443

Like many homeowners across the US, Ron Hazelton had a flooding basement which kept him awake during heavy rain periods. The problem was so serious that after each storm he had to use a mop and a floor sucker to get rid of the rising waters.

After a particularly messy flooding episode, he decided that it was time to get the problem solved once and for all. He scoured the internet for companies providing state-of-the-art basement waterproofing solutions -- and found Basement Systems.

Larry Janesky, the company's owner, came to inspect Ron's home. After a thorough evaluation, Larry was able to explain to Ron exactly what the problem was and what would be the perfect solution.

Like many others with similar problems, Ron's basement was flooding because during heavy rains the ground around his house would oversaturate with water. Hydrostatic pressure would begin to build up and push water against the wall. Following the path of least resistance, the water would then find its way into the basement through its weakest spot: the joint between the foundation walls and floor.

More evidence of this problem was found all over the basement walls, in the form of efflorescence. Efflorescence is a chalky, powdery substance that builds up on basement walls when mineral-saturated water infiltrates the concrete and then evaporates into the basement, leaving these mineral salts behind.

The solution for this type of problem resides in relieving the hydrostatic pressure by installing an internal perimeter drainage system. The system intercepts water before it enters the basement, diverts it to a sump pump system, and then evacuates it out and as far away from the foundation as possible.

Larry and his crew at Basement Systems installed a full perimeter WaterGuard basement drainage system, and a TripleSafe sump pump system with two backup pumps, so that Ron can rest assured his basement will stay dry no matter how heavy the rains -- and even in case of a power outage!

The unsightly, efflorescence stained walls were covered with BrightWall acrylic panels. These panels not only spruce up the look of the walls, they also act as a vapor barrier, and intercept any water coming through the concrete walls, diverting it to the perimeter drainage.

Ron can now enjoy peace of mind and sleep soundly through storms, knowing that his basement now has the best protection against flooding available in industry!

tab_title: How to Start a Harman Advance Pellet Stove: Auto and Manual
description:
The Harman Advance pellet stove runs from a panel you cannot see from the front: it sits behind the side door on the left, with six lights, three knobs and one switch. This video runs the stove out of its own owner's manual (Harman Advance owner's manual R34, 1-90-09730), every step with its page.

Two names for two controls: the faceplate says Feed Limit and Constant Burn; the manual's text also calls them the Feed Adjuster and Stove Temp. Same knobs. The panel on screen is the one page 8 draws.

The panel (page 8): power and status lights, one light each for the distribution blower, combustion blower, feed motor and igniter, the feed limit (1 to 6, plus TEST), the igniter switch (AUTO or MANUAL), the temperature dial (50 to 90 F outer ring, 1 to 7 inner ring) and the mode selector (Room Temp, Off, Constant Burn).

Automatic start (page 5): plugged into a 120 volt outlet with only the power light lit, no fuel in the ash pan, mode selector off, fill the hopper, scrape the burn pot if needed, one TEST cycle after an empty hopper, feed knob to 4, igniter switch up to AUTO, temperature dial, then Room Temp or Constant Burn.

Manual start (page 7): igniter switch to MANUAL, feed on 4, mode selector off and then the mode (that starts the combustion blower), fill the burn pot only level with the front edge, starting gel made for pellet stoves on a cold start only, light it with a match and close the door.

Then Room Temp versus Constant Burn on AUTO and on MANUAL (pages 4 and 6), setting the feed knob from the ash on the front of the burn pot (pages 4 and 5), and the shutdown: mode selector off, or let it run out of pellets, and never pull the plug (page 4).

tab_title: Hanging a Furnace Horizontal in a Basement | Full HVAC Install Part 4 (Final)
description:
This is the final episode of the basement HVAC install series. Everything we've been building comes together here.

In this video, I connect the remaining supply air ducts and then get the furnace and evaporator coil hung in the horizontal left position. Before suspending anything, I install a missing 4x4 support beam to hold up a floor joist. The furnace and coil can't hang from framing that isn't properly supported. From there, the furnace and coil are suspended with allthread and unistrut.

Once the equipment is hung, I connect:

Return air plenum
Supply air plenum
Gas line with sediment trap
Condensate pump
Flue pipe

Venting note for techs: because the furnace is installed horizontal left, the original right side of the furnace is now the top. I rotated the inducer draft motor assembly so the flue exits out the top of the unit. From there, the vent runs out the side of the home and up the exterior wall past the flat roof parapet.

I also cleaned the condenser, which was packed with leaves inside the coil. Unfortunately, I forgot to hit record during the cleaning, but you'll see the before and after. A condenser full of debris can't reject heat properly, which drives up head pressure, energy bills, and wear on the compressor.

The video ends with a final walkthrough of the finished furnace install in the basement.

Thanks for following this whole series. If it helped you, whether you're a homeowner or a tech learning the trade, please like, subscribe, and leave a comment with any questions.

tab_title: How NTC Temperature Sensor Thermistors Work
description:
This video demonstrates how NTC temperature sensor thermistors work.

Dear Diary,

Using the thermistors we pulled out of the Fujitsu unit last week, I demonstrate how to test them and also how they work with a glass of cold tap water and the piercing tips from my Jumper King kit (https://supco.com/web/supco_live/prod...)

NTC - negative temperature coefficient - means when the temperature rises, the resistance drops.  And when the temperature drops, the resistance increases.  

This is the opposite of a PTC - positive temperature coefficient - where both temperature and resistance rise and lower together. 

I forgot to mention that testing them will also confirm whether the thermistors are shorted or open.  

Thanks again for watching :)

tab_title: How to Test UPS Batteries Under Load (Battery Cell Tester vs Multimeter)
description:
The UPS battery self-test failed in about one second.
Its screen still showed 219 V and 100%... so I read the batteries at rest, then with the cell tester's load coil.
The meter showed 13.41 V. Under the tester's coil, I read 9.4 V.

A multimeter reads the voltage with very little load from the instrument, so a resting number can still look fine after the UPS has already failed its own test. This bank is sixteen 12 V batteries in one 192 V string. The cell tester's coil pulls current, and that is where a weak block shows. In the thumbnail, the meter and the coil sit on two different batteries from that same string. The charger stayed connected during the cabinet checks, so these are loaded-voltage readings, not an isolated capacity test. A short load check also cannot prove backup time. That still needs the full discharge test.

on top of the roof sheathing and vented above it?

In this video, Bryan Uhler (Pioneer Builders) walks through a vented insulated
over-roof assembly designed for the Pacific Northwest climate. This approach
virtually eliminates thermal bridging through the rafters, allows all mechanical
equipment and ductwork to live inside conditioned space, and achieves Zero Energy
Ready performance — without spray foam.

💡 Why this assembly matters:
• Eliminates thermal bridging through rafters
• High R-value (R-51+) with Rockwool Comfortboard + Comfortbatt
• All ductwork and HVAC lives inside conditioned space
• Foam-free roof assembly (easier to diagnose leaks)
• Venting pathway protects against moisture accumulation
• Works with I-joist rafters and conventional framing
• Qualifies for the $5,000 ZER tax credit

• Structural sheathing on I-joist rafters
• Airtight Zip Sheathing layer (taped)
• Comfortbatt insulation in rafter cavities
• 3” Comfortboard over roof sheathing
• 2x4 vent battens screwed with Simpson SWD fasteners
• Roof cladding installed over vent cavity

This is the first time we’ve built this assembly in Washington State — and it’s

Phillip shows us how to install a return vent using Thermo-Pan. This type of installation is particularly useful when installing a return vent in an older home and allows you to utilize the existing construction.

Transcript:
Today we're going to install a return air supply for this furnace. Return air comes in the bottom where the blower cavity is. This is a gas furnace, it heats air with the heating exchanger and it goes through the air conditioner coil and out through the supply duct. In order to pull the return air from parts of the house we need, we're going install ducts. It doesn't have to be as extensive as the supply ductwork, because it is not hot air going through. If you pull air from right by the furnace it's going to be noisy and the system is not going to balance well -it will pull more air from the room that it's in, rather than from other areas of the house. Behind the furnace, there is a filter that goes into a utility room; we're going to duct a channel for the air to flow through it and into the bottom of the furnace. We have the channel framed out and we're going to add some support. Where it comes through are pipes/electrical; on a return it's no problem, but for supply that's not allowed.  We've framed through the bay behind the furnace that going to go up into the floor base where TJI's run parallel. We need to go through the next TJI to duct into the hallway upstairs.  To do that we're going to use Thermo-pan, which is light cardboard inside metalized sheeting that has an R-3 insulation value; together with adhesives and staples, we're going to create the bay.

I'll use 2"x8" reinforcements to prevent vacuum pressure from collapsing the bay. This bay lets the pipes and electrical go through, but still supports the Thermo-pan. I'm going to use a staple-gun because it's faster, but you can use panning nails, small nails with wide heads to anchor the Thermo-pan. Use caution with a staple gun because it can punch right through. Next piece is going to angle in and then go up into the base. I have two gaps I'll need to fill.  I'm going to pan off the inside of it first and then I'll do a cover for the outside. To do the cover we need something to attach to and a support in the middle, so we're going to use some 2"x4"s. We have Thermo-pan connectors, are going to slip this one on. This will give us a good seal without having to use duct-sealant. With the angle-joint we will have to use sealant to connect this. Now I'm going to use Hardcast 550 duct sealant on the joints in order to seal and to keep it together. Now our return-air is sealed up to this point here. We have to block this off a little bit on the inside so air doesn't escape, but it's all in this bay. This bay has been blocked, so what we need to do now is block this other one so that the air can travel through these vent holes and into this bay. 
The air will travel down the bay along the hallway, where it will hit one return, and then jump bays and go into the one upstairs.

Customer called saying their Carrier heat pump was “completely frozen” and wouldn’t heat the house. The aux heat was running nonstop, but no warmth from the outdoor unit. When I arrived, the coil was indeed iced over… but the real problem wasn’t the refrigerant or a bad defrost cycle. Massive icicles from the gutter directly above the unit had frozen the fan in place! Once I cleared the ice and got that fan spinning again, everything came back to life. Classic winter surprise most folks never see coming. If your heat pump isn’t blowing warm air this season, watch this before you assume it’s dead!

What happens when your A/C condensate drain backs up and there's nothing to shut the system down? You could end up with thousands of dollars in water damage, ruined drywall, damaged insulation, and even a collapsed ceiling!

In today's video, we're talking about one of the most overlooked but IMPORTANT safety devices in the HVAC industry: CONDENSATE DRAIN SAFETY SWITCHES!

I'll be discussing why these switches are so important, how they help protect your home from costly water damage, and why proper condensate drainage and overflow protection should NEVER be overlooked during an HVAC installation or service.

🔧 In this video, we cover:

Why A/C condensate drains become clogged
The importance of primary and secondary drain safety switches
How float switches shut down your cooling system
The consequences of improper condensate overflow protection
Why spending a little on prevention can save THOUSANDS in repairs

Whether you're an HVAC technician, an apprentice learning the trade, or a homeowner wanting to protect your investment, this is something EVERYONE should understand!

tab_title: How to Clear Your Clogged AC Drain Line
description:
In this video, we thoroughly detail the proper way to clear your AC's primary drain line.  A clogged primary drain line is our #1 service call in Florida, so this should be done BEFORE it gets clogged; no less than once every 6 months.

Need that Milwaukee vacuum? Here it is! ➡️  https://geni.us/KCkX3m6

Here is a step-by-step procedure to go with the video:
-locate your primary drain line access "Tee" at your indoor unit, and it's termination point outside.
-turn off power to system to prevent unit from running while clearing the drain.
-hook up the vacuum to the drain line at the outside termination/opening and turn it on
-go to the inside unit and remove your drain access cap; wait to hear the shop vac has completed emptying the drain line
-pour down water (~1 gallon) as fast as you can without the drain overflowing
-proceed to turn shop vac off and remove from exterior drain line opening
-dispose of shop vac contaminants and wash your equipment/hands!
**  BE SURE TO POUR WATER DOWN DRAIN LINE AT INSIDE LOCATION UNTIL IT DRAINS OUTSIDE AGAIN!  **

Still stumped with that stubborn clog?  Try this! ➡️. https://geni.us/FA81Zmk

description:

Looking to insulate your attic and want the best option for your house and budget? Come along with Amanda as she explores an attic that's being air-sealed and having blown-in fiberglass insulation installed.

0:00 - Intro
0:28 - The installation crew uses either canned foam or a froth pack to seal all of the seams in the attic and other penetrations where air can leak into and out of the space.
0:48 - Areas around recessed lighting, electrical wiring, plumbing, and vents are other places where the spray foam is applied.
1:03 - Baffles are installed in the attic to ensure proper ventilation.
1:17 - Once the air sealing is done, the crew will blow in the insulation. In this instance, blown-in fiberglass is being installed.
1:37 - Blown-in fiberglass benefits include coverage, improved home comfort, and less work for the HVAC system.
4:35 - Spray foam can be expensive, so this method gives the benefits of an air seal in spots known for high air leakage, while also giving the recommended insulation coverage and R-Value for the particular climate zone.
